# THE HERMETIC MUSEUM <note>original: "Musaeum Hermeticum." In the 17th century, a "Museum" was often used to describe a library or a collection of scholarly works dedicated to the Muses—the Greek goddesses of inspiration and knowledge.</note>

## RESTORED AND ENLARGED. <note>original: "Reformatum et Amplificatum." This indicates that the current edition is an improved version of the earlier 1625 publication, containing more than double the amount of alchemical treatises.</note>

<term>Hermeticism: An ancient philosophical and spiritual tradition based on the "Hermetica"—writings attributed to the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus. It focuses on the hidden laws of nature and the relationship between the human soul and the universe.</term>

<term>Alchemy: A precursor to modern chemistry that blended laboratory work with spiritual philosophy. Its practitioners sought to "ennoble" matter, most famously by attempting to turn base metals into gold or searching for a universal medicine.</term>

<margin>Engraved by Matthäus Merian</margin> <note>The original Latin reads "M Merian fe." [fecit], which identifies the creator of the illustration. Matthäus Merian (1593–1650) was a renowned Swiss-German engraver famous for his intricate scientific and alchemical illustrations.</note>

<note>The title page is framed by an elaborate engraving rich in symbolic imagery. At the top, a **Phoenix**—a mythical bird that rises from its own ashes—represents rebirth and the final stage of the alchemical process. Opposite it is a **Pelican**, often used in alchemy to symbolize the "nourishing" of the Great Work, as it was believed to feed its young with its own blood. The central figures include planetary deities such as **Sol** (the Sun/Gold) and **Luna** (the Moon/Silver), alongside **Mercury**, the messenger god who represents the vital transformative substance used by alchemists. At the bottom, a figure holds a **Seal of Solomon** (a hexagram), signifying the union of opposites: fire and water, spirit and matter.</note>

# PREFACE
## TO THE ENGLISH EDITION.

T<gloss>Large decorative drop cap</gloss>HE HERMETIC MUSEUM RESTORED AND ENLARGED <note>original: "Musaeum Hermeticum Reformatum et Amplificatum." This 1678 Frankfort edition is the most famous version of this collection.</note> was published in Latin at Frankfort, in the year 1678, and, as its title implies, it was an enlarged form of an earlier work which, appearing in 1625, is more scarce, but, essentially, of less value. Its design was apparently to supply in a compact form a representative collection of the more brief and less ancient alchemical writers ; in this respect, it may be regarded as a supplement to those large storehouses of <term>Hermetic<gloss>The secret or "sealed" tradition of alchemy, named after the mythical founder Hermes Trismegistus.</gloss></term> learning such as the *Chemical Theater* <note>original: "Theatrum Chemicum," a massive six-volume collection of alchemical tracts published throughout the 17th century.</note>, and that scarcely less colossal work of <term>Mangetus<note>Jean-Jacques Manget (1652–1742), a Swiss physician and scholar who compiled the most comprehensive library of alchemical texts ever printed.</note></term>, the *Curious Chemical Library* <note>original: "Bibliotheca Chemica Curiosa."</note>, which are largely concerned with the finest examples of the ancient literature, with the works of <term>Geber<note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century scholar often called the father of chemistry.</note></term> and the <term>adepts<gloss>Those who have successfully achieved the "Great Work" of transmuting base metals into gold or attaining spiritual enlightenment.</gloss></term> of the school of Arabia, with the writings attributed to <term>Hermes<note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the foundation of alchemy is credited.</note></term>, with those of Raymond Lully, Arnold de Villa Nova, Bernard Trevisan, and others.

THE HERMETIC MUSEUM would also seem to represent a distinctive school in Alchemy, not altogether committed to certain modes and terminology which derived most of their prestige from the past, and sufficiently enigmatical as it was, still inclined to be less obscure and misleading than was the

habit of the older masters. For it belonged to a period which had inherited a bitter experience of the failures, impostures, and misery surrounding the *Magnum Opus* <note>Latin for "The Great Work," the ultimate goal of alchemy: the creation of the Philosopher's Stone or the transformation of the soul.</note> and its mystical quest, which was weary of unequipped experiment, weary of wandering "multipliers," <note>Fraudulent alchemists who claimed they could "multiply" gold or silver to swindle investors.</note> and pretentious "bellows-blowers," <note>A derogatory term (from the French "souffleurs") for those who obsessively worked at the furnace without understanding the spiritual or philosophical principles of the art.</note> while it was just being awakened to the conviction that if Alchemy were true at all, it was not to be learned from books, or, at least, from any books which had hitherto been written on the subject. Running through all the tracts which are comprised in the following volumes, the reader will recognize traces of a central claim in alchemical initiation—that the secrets, whatever they were, must be understood as the property of a college of adepts <gloss>A secret society of masters who have achieved the Great Work.</gloss>, pretending to have subsisted from time almost immemorial, and revealing themselves to the select and the few, while the literature, large as it is, appears chiefly as an instrument of intercommunication between those who knew. At the same time, it may also be regarded as a sign and omen to the likely seeker, an advertisement that there was a mystery, and that he must go further who would unravel it.

While the treatises now translated are for the most part anonymous, as befits veiled masters, the literary reader will remember that the name of John de Meung <note>Jean de Meun (c. 1240–1305), a French poet famous for completing the "Romance of the Rose," which many alchemists believed contained hidden chemical allegories.</note> connects the allegorical "*Romance of the Rose*" with the parables of Alchemy; Flamel <note>Nicolas Flamel (c. 1330–1418), a Parisian scribe who became the most famous legendary figure of French alchemy, said to have discovered the secret of eternal life.</note> will be familiar to all Hermetic students as the most celebrated of the French adepts; the saintly name of Basil Valentine <note>A legendary 15th-century monk; his writings are a crucial link between medieval alchemy and the early science of chemistry.</note>, investigator of the properties of antimony <note>A metallic element used in the purification of gold; its study led to many early chemical breakthroughs.</note>, will not even now be unhonoured by the chemist; Eirenaeus Philalethes <note>The pseudonym (meaning "peaceful lover of truth") of an influential 17th-century alchemist, now widely believed to be the American-born George Starkey.</note>, equally revered and unknown by all devout <term>Spagyrites<gloss>A term coined by Paracelsus to describe alchemists who use the processes of "separating and recombining" to create medicines.</gloss></term>, is supposed to have been the most lucid

### PREFACE TO ENGLISH EDITION.

of hierophants <note>A term for priests or officials who interpreted sacred mysteries in ancient Greece; here referring to the secret masters of alchemy.</note>, and the “Open Entrance” <note>Full title: *Introitus Apertus ad Occlusum Regis Palatium* (An Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King), a famous alchemical text first published in 1667 and attributed to Eirenaeus Philalethes.</note> to be the clearest of all his works. Helvetius <note>Johann Friedrich Schweitzer (1630–1709), a Dutch physician of German origin who famously claimed to have performed a transmutation with the help of a mysterious stranger.</note> was an illustrious chemist, and Michael Maier <note>A German physician and counselor to Emperor Rudolf II; he was a prolific author of alchemical emblems and a defender of the Rosicrucians.</note> is a person of some repute in the Rosicrucian controversy. Michael Sendivogius was an uninstructed disciple of Alexander Seton, and the “New Chemical Light,” <note>Original Latin title: *Novum Lumen Chymicum* (1604).</note> which he published and claimed as his own, was really the work of his master, who has been called the chief martyr of Alchemy <note>Seton was reportedly imprisoned and tortured by the Elector of Saxony to reveal the secret of the Philosopher's Stone, dying shortly after being rescued by Sendivogius.</note>. It may be added in this connection that some critics have cast doubt upon the genuine nature of the “Testament of John Cremer,” and it is true that the annals of Westminster do not include an abbot of that name.

It should be understood that the writer of this brief note must not be accredited with the translation which it seeks to introduce. That is the work of a gentleman who is said to have had a life-long acquaintance with alchemical literature; it has been subjected to a searching revision at the hands of the present editor, who may himself be permitted to claim some experience in Hermetic <term>Hermetic: Relating to the mystical and alchemical tradition supposedly founded by Hermes Trismegistus.</term> antiquities; the version as it stands does not uncreditably represent both the spirit and the sense of the original without the original’s prolixity <note>Excessive wordiness or tedious length in speech or writing.</note>. While affording to the modern student of secret doctrines an unique opportunity for acquiring in English a collection of alchemical writers, this edition of **THE HERMETIC MUSEUM** <note>Original Latin: *Musaeum Hermeticum*.</note> also claims consideration at the hands of the historian as a contribution of real value to the early history of chemistry.

**I**T would be unjust to doubt, most gentle reader, that of all the arts invented for the use of life by the reason of man, that of *Alchemy* <term>Alchemy: The ancient branch of natural philosophy that sought to purify or perfect materials, most famously by turning base metals into gold or creating a universal medicine.</term> is the most noble and glorious. For all philosophers exclaim, as it were, with one voice, albeit in many languages, that this art is not only true, but (after the Divine Law <term>Divine Law: The religious and moral codes through which, according to the author, the soul is saved.</term> by which our souls are saved) the best and most magnificent gift bestowed upon man by God; and that it should therefore be investigated with all zeal and with the greatest pains. But as good wine needs no praise, so neither does this art require a herald; for its truth is undoubted, and its utility in human life universally acknowledged, and shewn forth, not only in the Art of Medicine, in Pharmacy, and many other sciences, but more especially in the Art of Transmuting Metals <term>Transmutation: The alchemical process of changing one metal into another, specifically "base" metals like lead into "noble" metals like gold.</term>, is so clearly and perspicuously demonstrated, that it in no way requires to be adorned by the splendour of oratory, or tricked out with the device of language. I will not enlarge upon the blessing which the elaboration of minerals and metals has bestowed upon our race. I merely point it out, but refrain from discussing it at length. Different men devote themselves to the study of this science from different motives. The philosopher is impelled by the love of truth, and the thirst after wisdom. Worthy reader, and true enquirer into the secrets of nature, do not marvel that in the old age of this world—when it seems to have one foot already in the grave <note>At the time of writing, many believed the world was in a period of "senescence" or natural decay, nearing its final days.</note>—I have determined to write this tract. I do this although all libraries are already full of books on this subject—of which, however, the greater part are false and wear merely the "rouge and powder" <note>The author uses this cosmetic metaphor to describe books that are superficially attractive or use fancy language to hide a lack of real alchemical knowledge.</note> of <term>philosophy<gloss>In this context, "philosophy" refers specifically to "Natural Philosophy" or alchemy—the study of how the physical world and its materials work.</gloss></term>. 

I have written it not for my own pleasure, but for your advantage, so that by pointing to the foundation of truth, I might lead you back from the pathless wilderness into the right way—which is certainly for your own interest. As far as I am concerned, I have long known all that I seek to know in regard to this matter and have no need of many books, seeing that during the last twenty-two years I have read and re-read all the works that fell into my hands—including numerous manuscripts, as well as many printed volumes.

In this my tract you will find the subject set forth and the true solution given, not only theoretically, but also from a practical and <term>allegorical<gloss>Alchemists used symbolic stories (allegories) involving kings, queens, and dragons to describe chemical reactions and spiritual processes.</gloss></term> point of view, with a clearness and lucidity such as I believe to be almost unparalleled in any previous philosophical treatise. In quoting, I have always been careful to give the exact reference, so that you may look out the passage for yourself, and by diligently considering it, sharpen your understanding. I could more easily have composed this treatise, and made myself known to the <term>Brethren of the Golden<gloss>This likely refers to the "Brethren of the Golden and Rosy Cross" (the Rosicrucians), a secret society of mystics and alchemists that became famous in the early 1600s.</gloss></term>

Why then should I place myself at the mercy of this impure world? Permit me rather, dear friend, to follow the example of the sages, and leave the rest to the thrice good and great God, who will make my true self known to you in good time, if it be for the glory of His name, and for your and my good.

# THE GOLDEN TRACT

## CONCERNING THE STONE OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.

---

Ancient as well as modern philosophers, most beloved reader and devoted seeker after true wisdom, when through the grace of God they had reached the goal of their desires, have endeavoured to make their discovery known to their fellow inquirers in all parts of the world—not only because they wished to inform them that the thrice great and good God had enlightened their minds, blessed the labours of their hands, and shewn to them the greatest and most profound secret of earthly wisdom (for which benefit all praise, honour, and glory are justly due to Him)—but also that they might afford assistance to beginners in the <term>Art<gloss>The "Art" (often called the "Sacred Art" or the "Great Work") refers to the practice of alchemy, which was viewed as a blend of natural science, philosophy, and divine revelation.</gloss></term>, by which, with God’s permission, they too might attain to the knowledge of this most holy mystery. Such men there have been in all countries.

Amongst the Egyptians <term>Hermes Trismegistus<gloss>Original Latin: "Hermes Trismegistus." Though the aforementioned <term>Sages<gloss>Specifically referring to the "Philosophi" or true masters who have successfully achieved the creation of the Philosophers' Stone.</gloss></term> wrote at different times, and in different languages, yet their works exhibit so marvellous an agreement, that any true philosopher may easily see that all their hearts had been gladdened by God in the discovery of this <term>stone<gloss>The Philosophers' Stone: a legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and serving as a universal medicine for the body and soul.</gloss></term>, and that they all had performed this work with their own hands. Now, as the truth of their views is perceived by their agreement, so the disagreement of certain others marks them as false philosophers. For, not knowing the foundation of this glorious <term>Art</term>, and making up fanciful theories out of their own heads, they exhibit their ignorance to all.

Nay, what is more, He not only restricted everything to its own kind, but gave each created thing its own seed, by which it might be propagated after its own manner—always remaining in its own class, and not overstepping the bounds of some other <term>species</term>. That retarding, combustible, and fœtid sulphur is not the true fire that fashions metals; but quicksilver has its own sulphur in itself, which is sufficient for the purpose of fashioning it, as Bernard, Count of Trevisan <note>A 15th-century Italian nobleman and famous alchemist who claimed to have discovered the philosopher's stone.</note>, says: 

> "Some believe that in the generation of metals, a sulphuric substance is introduced from without; but, on the contrary, it is clear that in the working of Nature sulphur is already enclosed in the mercury. Yet it has no power in it except through the moving heat, by which the said sulphur is changed, and with it two other qualities of the mercury. In this way, then, Nature generates by means of this sulphur the different kinds of metals in the veins of the earth, according to the diversity of degrees and alterations."

For in metals, according to Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a renowned physician and alchemist.</note> (part I., chapter iii.), 

> "there is a two-fold superfluity <note>excess or unnecessary material</note>: one that is enclosed in the innermost nature of the quicksilver, and got there at the first mingling of the metal; the other does not belong to the essence of it, is external to it, and corruptible. To remove the former is a difficult task; the latter may be removed without any difficulty. The combustible sulphur is taken away by being subjected to the action of fire, or is destroyed by foreign bodies; but the other, which is in the quicksilver, is preserved by it from combustion <note>burning or destruction by fire.</note>."

But again, that inward sulphur which fashions the <term>quicksilver<gloss>Also known as mercury, the principle of fluidity and transformation.</gloss></term> belonging to it, and matures it towards perfection, is either pure or impure, combustible or incombustible. Impure sulphur hinders the

When common <term>sulphur</term> is added to copper, and the whole brought in contact with fire (for art can do by intense heat in a few moments what it takes the gentle heat of Nature a long time to accomplish) it corrodes the copper, and changes it into <term>vitriol</term>, and, in proportion to the quantity of the <term>sulphur</term>, the <term>vitriol</term> assumes a richer or fainter colour; whence it comes that some <term>vitriol</term> contains more copper and some less. ...in the spirit of **vitriol**, <term>vitriol</term> <note>A historical name for metal sulfates (like iron or copper sulfate), used to produce highly acidic "spirits" or oils through distillation.</note> and the spirit of sulphur, like the spirit of vitriol, has power to change into vitriol. Since, then, this corrosive sulphur is hid in vitriol, and since it contains so small a quantity of impure mercury, we may be sure that it cannot be the object of our search. In this we agree with **Alphidius**, <note>An early alchemical authority, likely of Arabic origin, whose sayings were frequently cited in medieval European collections.</note> who says: "Take heed, my son, and eschew dead bodies, and stones; in these things there is no true way of procedure, for their life preserves not, but destroys. Such are salts, orpiments, arsenic, magnesia, bismuth, **tutty**, <note>A crude zinc oxide collected from the chimneys of smelting furnaces, used in medicinal salves and early chemistry.</note> and the like." And **Arnold** in his *Flower of Flowers* <note>original: "Flos Flor." or *Flos Florum*, a treatise on the transformation of metals attributed to Arnold of Villanova.</note> says: "The reason of these mistakes is that the four spirits, *namely*, orpiment, salt of ammonia, mercury, and sulphur, are not the seed of perfect or imperfect metals (except, of course, mercury and sulphur by themselves)."

But from these last words of Arnold it might be inferred that common mercury and quicksilver are the substance of the stone, seeing that these are referred to the four spirits, and that sulphur is supposed to consolidate the mercury. But I answer, with **Richard the Englishman**, <note>Also known as Ricardus Anglicus, a 13th-century writer often associated with the "Correctorium Alchemiae."</note> in his eleventh chapter, that it does not really do so. For every kind of common sulphur is repugnant to metals, as the Sage says: "Indeed you must know that sulphur comes forth out of the fatness of the earth, and is thickened in the **mine** <note>original: "minera," referring to the natural underground site where minerals and ores are formed.</note> by gentle heat; when it becomes hard it is called sulphur."

Now there are two kinds of sulphur, the living and the combustible. **Quick sulphur** is the active principle of metals, and, when purged from all foreign matter, is the **Matter of our Stone**. But the common combustible variety is not the Matter of metals or of our Stone; rather, it is injurious to them. Common, combustible sulphur—so we are told by **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose theories on the formation of metals dominated Western alchemy for centuries.</note> and Richard the Englishman—has nothing to do with our art. However carefully prepared, it still disintegrates and destroys metals, because it has no affinity with them. When enclosed in metals, it retards their fusion. This is clearly seen in the case of iron, which contains hard, gross, and impure sulphur. When this sulphur is burned it is nothing but a dead, earthy, powdery substance. How then can it impart life to other things? For it has two principles of decay—its inflammability and its earthy impurity. The **sulphur of the Sages**, on the other hand, is **living fire**; it is quick, and quickens and matures lifeless...

This is that which overcomes fire, and delights in its amicable heat.” Here Geber clearly shews that the substance of our Stone cannot exist in imperfect metals; because things that are impure in themselves do not abide the fire which might purify them, while our mercury (on account of its purity) is not in the slightest degree...

But why do the philosophers call their gold now "water," and now "earth"? Do they not contradict themselves, or each other? No; our Sages, in expounding the truth, veil it under obscure and allegorical expressions, but nevertheless agree with each other so marvellously that they all seem to speak, as it were, with one mouth. They express themselves in mystic phrases to hide the truth from the unworthy and impious, lest they should seem to be casting pearls before swine <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6; alchemists frequently claimed their secrets were hidden by God from the greedy and immoral.</note>, and giving the holy thing to be trodden underfoot by these who think only of indulging their lustful desires. The Sages, then, do well to call their gold earth or water; for they have a perfect right to term it whatever they like. So they have frequently called their Stone their gold, their super-perfect gold, their regenerate gold, and by many other names besides. If any one does not perceive their meaning at the first glance, he must blame his own ignorance, not their jealousy.

The reader now knows that the substance of our Stone is neither animal nor vegetable, and that it does not belong to the minerals or the base metals, but that it must be extracted from gold and silver, and that our gold and silver are not the vulgar, dead gold and silver, but the living gold and silver of the Sages. The following instruction is from the “Preface to the Twelve Gates” <note>Original: "Procœmium of the Twelve Gates." For what are gold and silver (says <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose scientific and philosophical works were highly influential in medieval Europe.</note>) but pure red and white earth? Take away from it the aforesaid splendour, and it will be nothing but worthless earth. The whole compound we call our lead. The quality of splendour comes from the <term>Sun</term> and <term>Moon</term>. And, in brief, these are our solvents. Perfect bodies we naturally calcine with the first, without adding any impure body but *one*, commonly called by philosophers the <term>green lion</term> <note>A term often used for raw mineral matter or strong acidic solvents; here it serves as the unifying agent between the gold and silver tinctures.</note>, and this is the medium for perfectly combining the tinctures of the <term>Sun</term> and <term>Moon</term>. This is our natural, most sure fire, our mercury, our sulphur, our pure tincture, our soul, our <term>Stone</term> raised with the wind, born in the earth. These things take to heart. This <term>Stone</term>, I dare to tell thee, is the powerful essence of the metal, and thou must be careful how thou dost obtain it. For this solvent is invisible, although with the secondary philosophic water it may, by the separation of elements, become visible in the form of pure water. Out of this solvent, and with it, thou mayst obtain the sulphur of Nature, if it be naturally turned into a pure spirit. Then thou mayst with it dissolve thy fundamental mass [*i.e.* gold and silver].”

For towards evening I noticed that many vapours rose from the earth through the heat of the sun, and were lifted up as water is attracted by the sun; afterwards when night fell, they watered the earth as fertilising dew <note>This describes the process of circulation or distillation: the liquid evaporates (rises), condenses on the cool top of the vessel, and drips back down (the "dew") to wash the matter at the bottom.</note>, and washed our bodies, which became more beautiful and white the oftener this sprinkling took place. And the whiter they became, the more the quantity of moisture in the air diminished, until at last the atmosphere was too thin for the spirit and soul to remain therein any longer; so they were at length compelled to return to the clarified body of the Queen, which (to my great joy) was straightway restored to life. My joy was all the greater, because now she was arrayed in a beautiful and magnificent garment such as is rarely seen by mortal eye, and had a glorious crown, all made of diamonds, upon her head. Thus attired, she stood upon her feet and cried: 

> "Know this, ye mortals, and let it enter your hearts, that the most High God is one God, who has power to set up and pull down kings. He makes rich and poor as He wills. He has killed, and raised again. I was great, and was brought low; but now, having been humbled, I have been made Queen of many more kingdoms. After death life has been restored to me. When I was poor, the treasures of the wise and mighty were committed to me. Therefore I, too, can make the poor rich, give grace to the humble, and restore the health of the sick. But I am not yet able to raise my beloved brother, the most mighty King, from the dead. Nevertheless, when he comes, he will show that my words are true." 

When she had thus spoken the sun lighted up the world with his glorious rays, and the heat waxed great (for the <term>dog days</term> <note>original: *dies caniculares*. Historically, the hottest days of summer associated with the rising of the star Sirius. In alchemy, this refers to a period of sustained, intense heat.</note> were approaching). Long before this, garments of rich black silk, of grey or ash-coloured <term>damask</term> <note>A reversible figured fabric of silk or wool; here used to describe the shifting colors of the chemical matter during the "Peacock's Tail" stage.</note>,

Now, though I had been most strictly enjoined not to open the chamber, I was filled with awe by the majesty and persuasive speech of the King, and acceded to his request.

I gladly acceded to his request, and, after slaking his thirst with a deep draught, he returned to the chamber, requesting me to shut the door carefully so that no one might disturb him or rouse him from his sleep. ->*To the Worthy and Christian Reader.*<-

**B**ELOVED and pious reader, above all, ye who are <term>Sons of Wisdom</term> <note>A traditional term for initiates into the alchemical or hermetic mysteries.</note> and the Doctrine, some years ago Almighty God, in answer to my daily prayers, opened my eyes by the light of His Holy Spirit (Who was sent us through Christ by the Father, and from Whom we receive all wisdom), and enabled me to discover the True Centre in the Centre of the Triangle and the one true Matter of the precious <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>The legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and achieving physical and spiritual perfection.</note>, so that I now hold it in my hands; but it took me five years longer to discover how the blood of the <term>Red Lion</term> <note>The "Red Lion" is a metaphor for the "fixed" sulfur or the soul of the matter—the masculine, solar principle in the alchemical work.</note> and the glue of the <term>White Eagle</term> <note>The "White Eagle" represents the "volatile" mercury or the spirit—the feminine, lunar principle that must be joined with the Lion.</note> were to be extracted, and how these were to be mixed in their natural proportions, enclosed, sealed, and committed to the secret fire. Nor did I even then find the <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: "arcanum" — a profound secret or mystery, often referring to a powerful medicinal or chemical essence.</note> without constant and untiring application.

As I pondered in my mind the marvels of the Most High, and the duty of fervent love to our neighbours, which He laid upon us; I remembered the wheat harvest, when Reuben, the son of Leah, found <term>Dudaim</term> <note>original: "Dudaim"; likely referring to mandrakes, plants historically associated with fertility and mentioned in the Book of Genesis</note> in the field, which Leah gave to Rachel for the love of the <term>Patriarch Jacob</term>. Then I was carried forward, being plunged in profound thought, to the time of <term>Moses</term>, who rendered potable the <term>golden calf</term> <note>In alchemical tradition, Moses' ability to grind the gold calf into powder and dissolve it in water is seen as a supreme example of the "universal solvent" or the ability to manipulate the inner nature of metals</note> (which <term>Aaron</term> had formed) by reducing it to powder in the fire, throwing it into the water, and giving it the children of <term>Israel</term> to drink; and I marvelled greatly at the wonderful and masterly destruction of the metal by the man of God. 

But when I reflected upon the matter, the truth was borne in upon my mind, and my eyes were opened like those of the disciples at <term>Emmaus</term> <note>A biblical reference to the moment of sudden spiritual recognition or revelation</note>, who knew their Master in the breaking of bread; and my heart burned within me. Then I retired to rest, that I might consider the matter further on the morrow, and fell into a deep slumber; when, behold, <term>Solomon</term> appeared to me in all his power, wealth, and glory, and with him came his whole harem: sixty were queens, eight hundred concubines, and of virgins there was a countless number. 

One of them was his most beautiful dove, and was dearest to his heart. They formed a procession according to the <term>Catholic rite</term> <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or "canonical" order rather than specifically the Roman Catholic Church</note>, in the centre of which was one greatly praised and beloved, whose name was like ointment poured out, and whose fragrance was sweeter than that of spices; the fiery spirit of this person was the <term>Key</term> for the opening of the <term>Temple</term>, for entering the <term>Holy of Holies</term>, and taking hold on the <term>horns of the Altar</term>.

When the procession had been performed in the manner aforesaid, <term>Solomon</term> shewed me the <term>One Centre</term> in the <term>Triangle</term> <note>A geometric symbol common in alchemy, often representing the unity of the three principles (Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury) or the Holy Trinity</note>.

# WONDERFUL WATER STONE OF THE WISE,
->COMMONLY CALLED<-
# THE PHILOSOPHER’S STONE.

F**ROM** the beginning of the world, there have always been God-enlighted men and experienced philosophers and wise Gentiles who diligently studied the nature and properties of the lower Creation. They laboriously endeavoured and fervently longed to discover whether Nature contained anything that would preserve our earthly body from decay and death, and maintain it in perpetual health and vigour. For by the light of Nature, and Divine revelation, they intuitively perceived that the Almighty, in His love to men, must have concealed in the world some wonderful <term>arcanum<note>From the Latin "arcanum," meaning a secret or mystery. In alchemy, it refers to a hidden curative power or the "Great Secret" of nature.</note></term> by which every imperfect, diseased, and defective thing in the whole world might be renewed, and restored to its former vigour.

By the most diligent and careful search they gradually found out that there was nothing in this world that could procure for our earthly and corruptible body immunity from *death*, since death was laid upon the <term>Protoplasts<note>Literally "the first-formed," referring to Adam and Eve as the original human beings.</note></term>, Adam and Eve, and their posterity, as a perpetual penalty. But they did discover *one thing* which, being itself incorruptible, has been ordained of God for the good of man, to remove disease, to cure all imperfection, to purge old age, and to prolong our brief life—a boon actually enjoyed by the <term>Patriarchs<note>The biblical fathers of the human race, such as Noah or Methuselah, who were famously credited with living for several centuries.</note></term>.

This wonderful remedy was industriously sought by the wise and understanding, until they discovered it, and its precious virtue. Thus, the <term>Patriarchs</term> used it to restore their bodily

## PART II.

### ISAIAH XXVIII.

> “ *Therefore, thus saith the Lord: Behold I lay in Zion for a foundation a Stone, a tried Stone, a precious corner Stone, a sure foundation. He that has it shall not be confounded.* ”

The numerous writers on our most noble <term>Art</term><note>The "Art" is the standard term for Alchemy, emphasizing that it is a skilled craft requiring both practical knowledge and divine inspiration.</note> have never wearied of singing its praises, and inventing for it new and glorious names. Its most precious object they have called the <term>PHILOSOPHER’S STONE</term><note>The goal of the "Great Work," believed to be a substance that could transmute base metals into gold and act as a universal medicine.</note>, or the most ancient, secret, natural, incomprehensible, heavenly, blessed, beatified, and triune universal Stone of the Sages. Their reason for naming it a stone, or likening it to a stone, was this: First because its original <term>Matter</term><note>The *Prima Materia*, or the raw, chaotic starting material of the alchemical process.</note> is really a kind of stone, which, being hard and solid like a stone, may be pounded, reduced to powder, and resolved into its three elements (which Nature herself has joined together), and then again may be re-combined into a solid stone of the fusibility of wax by the skilled hand of the artist adjusting the law of Nature.

The importance of starting with an exact knowledge of the first or otherwise the second <term>Matter</term> of the <term>Philosophical Stone</term> has been largely dwelt upon by all writers on this subject. This <term>Matter</term> is found in one thing, out of which alone our Stone is prepared (although it is called by a thousand names), without any foreign admixture; and its quality, appearance, and properties have been set forth in the following manner. It is composed of three things, yet it is only *one*. Likewise, having been created and made of one, two, three, four, and five, it is everywhere found in one and two.<note>This refers to alchemical numerology: One (the Source), Two (Opposites like Sulfur/Mercury), Three (the Principles of Salt/Sulfur/Mercury), Four (the Elements), and Five (the Quintessence).</note> They also call it the <term>universal Magnesia</term><note>In alchemy, "Magnesia" does not refer to the chemical element magnesium, but rather to the "magnetic" primary substance that attracts the celestial spirit.</note>, or the seed of the world, from which all natural objects take their origin. Its properties are of a singular kind; for, in addition to its marvellous nature and form, it is neither hot and dry like fire, nor cold and wet like water, nor cold and dry like earth, but a perfect preparation of all the elements. Its body is incorruptible, and is not destroyed by any of the four elements, but its properties far exceed those of the four elements, and the four qualities, like heaven and the <term>Quintessence</term><note>The "fifth essence" or highest element, which was thought to be the material that composed the celestial bodies.</note>. With respect to its outward appearance,

It is named the **water of life**, the purest and most blessed water, yet not the water of the clouds, or of any common spring, but a thick, permanent, salt, and (in a certain sense) dry water, which wets not the hand, a slimy water which springs out of the fatness of the earth. Likewise, it is a double mercury and <term>Azoth</term><note>Azoth was considered the "universal curative" or "universal solvent" in alchemy, often symbolized by a mercury-like substance that contains the beginning and end of all things.</note>, which, being supported by the vapour or exudation of the greater and lesser heavenly and the earthly globe, cannot be consumed by fire. For itself is the universal and sparkling flame of the light of Nature, which has the heavenly Spirit in itself, with which it was animated at first by God, Who pervades all things, and is called by <term>Avicenna</term><note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), known in the West as Avicenna, was a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational to later European alchemy.</note>, the **Soul of the world**. For as the soul lives and moves in all the members of the body, so that spirit lives and moves in all elementary creatures, and is the indissoluble bond of body and soul, the purest and most noble essence in which lie hid all mysteries in their inexhaustible fulness of marvellous virtue and efficacy. Moreover, they ascribe to it infinite Divine power and virtue when they say that it is the **Spirit of the Lord** who fills the Universe, and in the beginning moved upon the face of the waters. They also call it the spirit of truth that is hid in the world, and cannot be understood without the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, or the teaching of those who know it. It is found *potentially* everywhere, and in everything, but in all its perfection and fulness only in one thing. In short, it is a <term>Spiritual Essence</term> which is neither celestial nor infernal, but an aërial, pure, and precious body, in the middle between the highest and lowest, the choicest and noblest thing under heaven. But by the ignorant and the beginner it is thought to be the vilest and meanest of things. It is sought by many Sages, and found by few; suspected by those that are far away, and received by those that are near; seen by all, but known by few, as you may see from the following lines:

> “ Into three the great good is divided, yet it is *one*, and highly esteemed by the world. Men have it before their eyes, handle it with their hands, yet know it not, though they constantly tread it under their feet. It is the greatest wealth, and he who knows the **Art** may rival the richest. ”

# THE SOPHIC HYDROLITH.

## AN ENIGMA OF THE SAGES,

In which the underlying substance of the Art, called the **Phoenix of the Sages** <note>The Phoenix is a mythical bird that burns itself to ashes and is reborn; in alchemy, it symbolizes the process of "multiplication" or the final stage of perfecting the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, is found to be thrice threefold.

> "If I tell you three parts of a thing you have no cause to complain. Seek one of three, and of the three one will be there: for where there is body and soul, there is also Spirit, and there shine **salt, sulphur, and mercury** <note>These are the 'Tria Prima,' the three fundamental principles of all matter according to Paracelsus. Salt represents the body (solidity), Sulphur the soul (flammability/oiliness), and Mercury the spirit (volatility/fluidity).</note>. Trust my word, seek the grass that is **trefoil** <note>Literally a three-leafed plant like clover, used here as a metaphor for the 'three-in-one' nature of the alchemical substance.</note>. Thou knowest the name, and art wise and cunning if thou findest it."

## ANOTHER ENIGMA.

->(Much easier.)<-

> "There is one thing in this world which is found occasionally. It is bluish-grey and green, and, wonderful to say, there is in this thing a red and white colour. It flows like water, yet it makes not wet; it is of great weight, and of small. I might give it a thousand names, yet the thousand know it not. It is mean to look upon, yet to the Sage it is precious. He who solves it with the second and condenses it with the third, he has our glorious subject."

## YET ANOTHER ENIGMA.

Everything contributes to the formation of this **Stone** <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the Great Work, capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting longevity.</note>. It is conceived below the earth, born in the earth, quickened in heaven, dies in time, obtains eternal glory.

Now when you have the substance indicated (which is in part heavenly, in part earthly, and in its natural state a mere confused chaos without certain name or colour), and know it well (for this knowledge the Sages have always accounted the principal part of this work), then you must give your whole mind to manipulating it in the proper manner. But before doing anything to it with his hands, the student should remember not to begin the preparation of this great and inscrutable <term>arcanum</term> <note>From the Latin 'arcanum,' meaning a deep secret or a powerful hidden mystery of nature.</note> before he knows well the spirit that lurks in it according to its essential qualities and properties. "With this spirit," says a certain philosopher, "you should not meddle until you first have a full and exact knowledge of it. For God is marvellous in His works, and He is not mocked. I could give some instances of..."

If these defects are not immediately seen to, they will speedily become incorrigible. A cunning adept should be acquainted with the various devices by which they may be remedied; and I will recount them here for the sake of the beginner.

If one or more of the above defects are observed, the whole compound must again be taken out of the phial, and once more solved in the aforesaid <term>water of mercury</term> <note>Also known as "philosophical mercury," this is not common quicksilver but a specialized solvent believed to dissolve metals into their primary components.</note> (also called <term>virgin's milk</term> <note>A poetic term for the white, corrosive, or milky-looking liquid used as a solvent in the early stages of the Work.</note>, or the milk, blood, and sweat of the <term>First Matter</term> <note>The *Materia Prima*; the chaotic, original substance from which the Philosopher's Stone is made.</note>, or the never-failing fountain, or the <term>water of life</term>, which nevertheless contains the most malignant poison); with this water it must once more be moistened and saturated, and then subjected to the action of the fire, until there is no longer any <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process where a solid turns directly into a gas; here, it refers to the volatile parts of the mixture rising to the top of the glass.</note> or formation of gaseous vapours; or till the final <term>coagulation</term> <note>The thickening or hardening of the substance into a solid state.</note> has duly taken place, as described above. Of its subsequent <term>fermentation</term> and <term>multiplication</term> <note>The final stages where the power of the Stone is increased so that a small amount can transform a large amount of base metal.</note>, and of its uses, more will be said in the third part.

*Of the time required for the whole process*, it is impossible to say anything very definite; and, indeed, the Sages have put forward the most conflicting opinions on this point—no doubt because some have been occupied with it longer than others. But if any man will carefully observe the working of Nature, and be guided by her teaching, and in all things hold a middle course, he will gain his object sooner than one that trusts too blindly to his own wisdom.

But I tell thee not to go beyond the middle point of the letter **X** <note>The author uses the Roman numeral **X** (10) as a symbolic timeline for the operation.</note> either in the former or latter stage of the operation, but to take one half (**V**) <note>Roman numeral 5.</note> for the time of the solution and the other half for the composition. Then, again, for the final union, the number **XX** <note>Roman numeral 20.</note> should be thy guide (unless anything unforeseen should occur). Be satisfied with that space of time. On the other hand, do not try to hurry on the consummation, for one hour's mistake may throw thee back a whole month. If thou strivest unduly to shorten the time thou wilt produce an abortion. Many persons have, through their ignorance, or self-opinionated haste, obtained a <term>Nihilixir</term> <note>A clever alchemical pun combining the Latin *nihil* (nothing) and *elixir*. It refers to a failed, worthless potion.</note> instead of the hoped for <term>Elixir</term>.

# THE SOPHIC HYDROLITH.
<note>The title "Sophic Hydrolith" translates to the "Wise Man's Water-Stone," a poetic name for the Philosopher’s Stone, suggesting it is a substance that is both solid and liquid, or born of water.</note>

In view of the importance of this <term>magical science</term> <note>In this context, "magical science" refers to Alchemy, which was viewed as a sacred art that investigated the hidden "magic" or spiritual forces within the natural world.</note>, I have thought it right to lay this before the <term>sons of knowledge</term> <note>A traditional term for initiates or students of alchemy who were deemed worthy of its secrets.</note>, for their careful consideration.

## RIDDLE.

“There are seven cities, seven metals, seven days, and the number seven; seven letters, seven words in order meet, seven times, and as many places; seven herbs, seven arts, and seven stones. Divide seven by three, and thou shalt be wise. No one will then strive to precipitate the half. In brief, all will proceed favourably in this number.”
<note>The number seven is central to alchemy, representing the seven classical planets and their corresponding metals: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Mercury (Mercury), Copper (Venus), Iron (Mars), Tin (Jupiter), and Lead (Saturn).</note>

In the following lines the whole <term>Process</term> <note>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is briefly described:—

### (I.)—THE FIRST STAGE.

> “Dissolve your substance, and then let it be decomposed; then let it be distilled, and once more condensed.”

### (II.)—THE SECOND STAGE.

> “Combine two things, decompose them, let them become black. Digest them and change them to white by your skill; at last let the compound change to a deep red, let it be coagulated, and fix it; and you will be a favoured man. If, afterwards, you cause it to ferment, you will have conducted the whole work prosperously. Then tinge therewith whatsoever you will, and it will multiply to you infinite treasure.”
<note>This describes the three main alchemical stages: Nigredo (blackness/decay), Albedo (whiteness/purification), and Rubedo (redness/perfection). "Tinging" refers to the final step where the Stone is used to transform base metals into gold.</note>

Or, more briefly, thus:—

> “Seek three in one, again seek one in three. Dissolve, and condense, and thou shalt be master of the Art.”
<note>This refers to the "Tria Prima" (Three Primes): Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which alchemists believed were the three components of all matter.</note>

A Riddle in which also the <term>Process</term> is indicated:—

> “A spirit is given for a time to the body, and that spirit is the life of a soul. If the spirit draw the soul to itself, they are both severed from the body. Then are there three abiding in the same place, until the precious body is dissolved, and is decomposed and dies. But after a time the spirit and the soul are brought back by gentle warmth, and hold once more their former seat. Then you have the essence; no perfection is wanting, and the work is glorified by a joyful end.”
<note>This allegory describes the chemical process of "death and rebirth," where a substance is broken down (the spirit and soul leaving the body) and then reunited in a purified, "glorified" state.</note>

### PROV. XXIII.

> “My son, give me thy heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways.”
<note>A quote from Proverbs 23:26, used here to emphasize that the alchemist must be pious and dedicated to God to succeed in the Work.</note>

### PART III.

*Sirach xliii*: <note>This refers to chapter 43 of the Book of Sirach (also known as Ecclesiasticus). Alchemists frequently cited this text to argue that the secrets of nature are gifts from God that reveal His hidden glory.</note> "Who has seen Him that he should tell of Him? Who can exalt Him according to His greatness? We see but the smallest of His works: those that are much greater are hidden from us. For God has made all, and gives understanding thereof to those that fear Him."

Concerning the end <note>In this context, "end" refers to the ultimate goal or final purpose.</note> of this great Art, and the excellence, virtue, efficacy, and unspeakable utility of the marvellous <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>The legendary "Stone" was not a literal rock, but a refined substance—often described as a red powder or a heavy liquid—capable of perfecting both metals (turning them to gold) and the human body (healing all illness).</note>, much has been written: yet has no one been able to tell out its thought-surpassing glory or to adequately set forth its fame. All Sages have regarded it as the chief felicity <note>Happiness or intense good fortune.</note> that this earth can afford, without which no one can attain perfection in this world. For *Morienus* <note>Morienus was a semi-legendary alchemist, famously depicted as a hermit living near Jerusalem who taught the secrets of the Stone to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "He who has this Stone has all, and needs no other help." For it includes all temporal felicity, bodily health, and solid good fortune.

They have also commended the Stone for that the spirit and efficacy which lie concealed in it are the spirit of the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>Literally the "fifth essence," the spiritual core of matter that remains after the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) are purified and balanced.</note> of all things beneath the <term>disc of the moon</term> <note>This refers to the "sublunary sphere," the earthly realm where things are subject to change, decay, and death, as opposed to the eternal, unchanging heavens.</note>; on this account they say that it upholds the sky, and moves the sea. They also describe it as the most elect, the most subtle, the purest, and noblest of all the heavenly spirits, to which all the rest yield obedience as to their King, that bestows on men all health and prosperity, heals all diseases, gives to the God-fearing temporal honour and a long life, but to the wicked, who abuse it, eternal punishment. It is also extolled by the Sages because it has never been known to fail of effecting its purpose, but is found to be in all proved, perfect, and unerring. Therefore *Hermes* <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founding father of alchemy.</note> and *Aristotle* call it the true, undeceiving, and unfailing <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: "arcanum arcanorum" (secret of secrets). In alchemy, an arcanum is a deep mystery or a potent medicine containing the concentrated power of nature.</note> of all arcana, the Divine Virtue which is hidden from the foolish. In brief, they have designated it the chief of all things under heaven, the marvellous conclusion or epilogue of all philosophic works. Hence some devout Sages have affirmed that it was Divinely revealed to *Adam*, and by him handed down to all the holy Patriarchs.

The <term>Stone</term> or <term>Elixir</term> cannot be used for this purpose in the form in which we left it at the completion of the previous stage of our process; but it should be still further fermented and augmented in the following manner, as otherwise it could not be conveniently applied to imperfect metals and bodies.

Take one part of the <term>Essence</term>, and add to it three parts of purest gold, which has been purged and melted by means of <term>antimony</term> <note>In alchemy, antimony was called the "Grey Wolf" because it was used to "devour" impurities in gold during the refining process.</note>, and reduced to very thin plates. Let them be placed together in the <term>crucible</term> <note>A heat-resistant container used for melting metals at very high temperatures.</note>.

Thereupon the whole compound will be transformed into a pure and efficacious <term>Tincture</term>, which, when applied to base metals, in the ratio of 1 : 1000, will change them into pure gold.

# PART IV.

## PSALM 78 AND MATTHEW 13.

->*“I will open my mouth in parables, and declare things hidden from the foundation of the world.”*<-

When it pleases Almighty God, through His Divine Word, to reveal His marvelous, deep, and heavenly mysteries to the human race, He usually does so through parables. He shadows forth His meaning using things familiar to our eyes, which are placed visibly before us. For instance, when He pronounced the sentence of death upon Adam in Paradise after the Fall, He told him that because he was made and formed from dust, he should also return to dust—dust being a substance which has no life in itself. Again, when He promised Abraham a lineage too large to count, He illustrated His meaning by pointing to the stars in the heavens, the sand on the seashore, and the dust of the earth. 

In the same way, God used various precious <term>types</term> <note>In theology, a "type" is a person, event, or thing in the Old Testament that foreshadows something in the New Testament.</note> to declare His will to the children of Israel through the Prophets. This practice was also adopted in the New Testament by Christ Himself—the Foundation and <term>Express Image of the Truth</term> <note>original: "character veritatis." A reference to Christ as the exact representation of God’s nature (Hebrews 1:3).</note>—who presented His teaching in parables so that it might be better understood. Thus, He compares His Divine and Blessed Gospel—the greatest happiness for mankind—to seed sown in a field where an enemy scatters weeds; to a hidden treasure; to a pearl of great price; to a grain of wheat; to a mustard seed; and to leaven.

[Compare Luke 8, Matthew 13 and 22, Luke 19, and Matthew 20.]

He describes the Kingdom of Heaven under the image of a great Wedding Feast. The Christian Church, likewise, He compares to a Vineyard, and to a King calling upon his servants to settle their accounts. He also uses the <term>similitude</term> <note>An older word for a comparison or likeness; a parable.</note> of a noble lord who entrusted his goods to his servants, of a lost sheep, a prodigal son, and other similar stories.

[Compare Matthew 18, Luke 16, Matthew 25, Luke 18, Mark 12, Luke 18, and Luke 10.]

These types and similitudes were given to us because of our human infirmity <note>Our natural weakness or limited intellectual capacity as humans.</note>, which prevents us from understanding and...

It argues that this biblical tradition justifies the use of symbolic language in the pursuit of spiritual and alchemical knowledge.</summary>

I speak of the thrice refined Word of God (*Psalm cxix.*) <note>Psalm 119.</note>, which proceeds out of the mouth of God, and is declared by His Holy Spirit—which is not, as these false teachers presumptuously assert, a vain and empty sound, but the Spirit, the life, and the saving power of God to all that believe. Of it the **Royal Seer** <note>A poetic title for King David, traditionally considered the author of the Psalms.</note> David speaks as follows: “I will hear what the Lord shall say unto me.” Of this inward and Divine hearing of the Word of God, as from a kind of fountain-head, good and living faith, which works by love, takes its source. For it is, as S. Paul says (*Rom. x.*) <note>Romans 10.</note>: “Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God.”

Now if the Word is pure and undefiled, the hearing, too, may be pure and undefiled, and the faith which comes of such hearing will also be true, and show itself by love and humble obedience to the will of God in prayer, praise, and thanksgiving. It will also find expression in all good works towards our neighbour. To the exercise of this love Christ exhorts us in His long valedictory discourse (*John xiii.*) <note>John 13.</note>, and leaves it with us as His farewell saying: “This is my commandment that ye love each other, even as I also loved you.” “If any one say, I know God, and love not his brother, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him. And if a regenerate man bear himself thus lovingly and humbly in all his life, he will never lack fruit in due season. For such a man is placed by God in the furnace of affliction, and (like the <term>hermetic compound</term> <note>The alchemical substance undergoing transformation, here symbolizing the soul of the believer within the "vessel" of the body.</note>) is purged with the fire of suffering until the **old Adam** <note>A theological term for the sinful human nature inherited from the biblical Adam that must be "slain" for spiritual rebirth.</note> is dead, and there arises a new man created after God in righteousness and true holiness, as **St. Paul** says (Rom. vi.): "We are buried with Christ by baptism into death, that like as Christ was raised up from the dead, even so we also should walk in newness of life." When this has been accomplished, and a man is no longer under the dominion of sin, then there begins in him something analogous to the solution of the gold added to the substance of our <term>chemical process</term> <note>Refers to the "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) of alchemy—the process of purifying base matter into perfection.</note>.

The old nature is destroyed, dissolved, decomposed, and, in a longer or shorter period of time, transmuted into something else. ### EPILOGUE.

Thus, gentle and well-wishing reader, I have briefly and simply set forth to you the perfect analogy which exists between our earthly and chemical and the true and heavenly Stone, Jesus Christ, whereby we may attain unto certain beatitude and perfection, not only in earthly but also in eternal life. I might have done so more grandly and copiously; but you must know that I am neither a theologian, nor, according to the modern fashion, an <term>Aristotelico-theologian</term> <note>A scholar who combines the logic of the Greek philosopher Aristotle with Christian theology—a style of "book-learning" that the author considers overly complicated compared to direct spiritual experience.</note>, but a simple and unsophisticated layman. For the knowledge which God has committed to me, I have obtained, not at any learned academy, but in the universal school of Nature, and by perusing the open book of God. For this reason I have expressed my thoughts simply, and not tricked them out in <term>sesquipedalian</term> <note>From the Latin meaning "a foot and a half long." It refers to the use of very long, complex, and often pretentious words.</note> words, as is the manner of professional theologians; nor do I pretend to have exhausted the subject; all that I have done is to throw out some hints for the guidance of those who wish to investigate it more carefully. In doing my best, I have also endeavoured to do my duty; for every lover of the truth is bound to praise God by revealing the knowledge entrusted to him. Besides all this, I desired to profess publicly my belief in the true Christian faith; since at the present time many devout and godly Christians are falsely represented and decried by lying slanderers as heretics. Let not the blasphemies and reckless judgment of the wicked world trouble the true Christian, against whom they are directed; for the Devil and his servants have at all times done to the followers of Christ what they did to Christ Himself. Therefore I will say no more on this subject, but I will leave it to be decided by the Judge of all the world.

As to the earthly Stone itself <note>The physical "Philosopher's Stone" used in laboratory alchemy to transmute metals.</note> I must ask the reader to study diligently what has gone before in our treatise as to this subject.

<summary>The author concludes his work by affirming the parallel between the alchemical Stone and Jesus Christ, while humbly identifying as a layman who learns from Nature rather than academic theology. He defends his faith against accusations of heresy and encourages the reader to revisit the practical instructions for creating the earthly Stone.</summary>

For as in an excellent poem a verse is sometimes repeated at least once, so on this point we are accustomed to do the same, because the reader ought not to direct his aims and thoughts to the earthly <term>Philosophical Stone</term> <note>The legendary substance believed to transform base metals into gold and provide a universal cure.</note> until he has attained a right knowledge of the <term>Celestial Stone</term> <note>The author’s term for Jesus Christ, viewed as the spiritual foundation and ultimate goal of the universe.</note>, and has prepared it, or, at least, has commenced with the utmost zeal the preparations of both together. For the earthly Stone is a gift from God, descending by the clemency of the Celestial Stone. I agree with all the Sages that it would be folly to attempt the study of so profound a mystery without a good previous knowledge of Nature and her properties. But I also say that it is not merely difficult, but quite impossible, to prepare the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> without a true knowledge of Christ, the heavenly Corner Stone, in whom all Nature lives and moves, and has its being <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Acts 17:28, used here to bridge the gap between theology and natural science.</note>. This warning should be duly considered; and he who would not expose himself to the certainty of ignominious failure, should reflect that the mastery of any art requires persevering exercise, and that, before setting about this search after the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term>, he must prepare himself by careful and patient study. If any neglect this warning, his failure will be the result of his own ignorance and mental immaturity.

But I wonder still more that there are to be found some men, who not only study this <term>Art</term> <note>The "Sacred Art" of alchemy.</note>, but even try to practice it, and yet do not quite know whether it proceeds by natural and legitimate magic, or whether it is not after all a <term>necromantic</term> <note>A form of dark magic involving the conjuration of the dead or demonic spirits.</note>, or black art, which is exercised by the illegitimate aid of the powers of hell. No, my good friend. The Devil, wicked angels, and wicked men, have no power but that which God suffers them to possess—and with our present glorious <term>Art</term> they positively have nothing whatever to do. It is entirely in the hand of God, who imparts it to whom He will, and takes it away from whom He will; and He does not suffer any votaries of pleasure, or evil spirits, to partake of it. He gives it only to the pure, true, and humble of heart. This excellence is neither known, nor understood, by the majority of the present generation; and when the sound of it strikes upon their ears, and they do not comprehend it, they straightway call it foolishness. On account of this their blindness, that spirit will always be hidden from their minds, and will at length be entirely taken away from them.

Let me, however, be permitted to impress one thing on the minds of my pious and devout readers. In so far as a man orders his life, soul, heart, and actions aright in the sight of God, in so far will he perceive that he is making good progress in the discovery, preparation, and use of the <term>Stone</term> <note>The "Philosopher’s Stone," the legendary substance capable of curing all diseases and turning base metals into gold.</note>. This assertion is the result of my own personal experience during many years, and it embodies my deliberate conviction. Therefore, the best preparation for this study is, in my judgment, a diligent amendment of heart and life.

I am aware that I here lay myself open to the objection that it is possible to enumerate several men who actually possessed this <term>Stone</term>, or <term>Tincture</term> <note>A term often used interchangeably with the "Stone," specifically referring to its ability to "stain" or "infuse" other metals with its own golden perfection.</note>, and with it transmuted base metals into gold and silver; and who yet were not good men, but vain, profligate, and without knowledge of God. To this objection, I answer that from whencesoever these men may have obtained the <term>Tincture</term>, I certainly never will believe that they prepared it—*i.e.*, the true and right <term>Tincture</term>—themselves. The tragic end of many of these men, and the headlong destruction brought upon them by their <term>Tincture</term>, prove but too clearly the truth of what I say. Moreover, all that call themselves <term>alchemists</term> <note>In this context, the author refers to anyone practicing the "Art," but he distinguishes between the sincere philosopher and the greedy "puffer."</note> are not therefore necessarily true possessors of the <term>Stone</term>. For, as in other branches of knowledge, there are found many different schools and sects, so all that are in search of this precious <term>Tincture</term> are called <term>alchemists</term>, without necessarily deserving the name.

In this tract I have spoken of true, natural, and scientific <term>alchemy</term>, which teaches us to distinguish the evil and impure from the good and pure, and thus, to aid the weakness, and correct the corruption, of Nature. We help the metals to arrive at maturity <note>The alchemical belief that all metals naturally "grow" toward gold within the earth; the alchemist merely accelerates this process in the lab.</note>, just as a gardener may assist fruit, which by some accident is prevented from ripening, or as a seed or grain of corn may easily be multiplied by being sown in the ground. Of <term>pseudo-alchemy</term> <note>False alchemy, often called "sophistry," which focused on tricks or chemical mimics rather than the true transformation of matter and spirit.</note> I neither pretend, nor care, to know anything, because I perceive that the ways of its teachers are crooked, and that they promise mountains of gold, without being able to redeem the least part of their pledge; I also see that those who follow them incur great expense, ceaseless toil, and are often ruined in body and soul. Therefore, if you encounter <term>alchemists</term> of this description, who speak boastfully of their <term>Art</term> <note>The "Great Art" (Ars Magna), the traditional name for the practice of alchemy.</note>, and offer—

...to teach it to you for money, I warn you to be on your guard against them. For with such men, there is usually a "serpent lurking in the grass" <note>original: "latet anguis in herba," a Latin idiom meaning a hidden danger or a treacherous person.</note> (Micah 2 <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Micah, chapter 2, which denounces those who plot evil and practice fraud.</note>).

I think I may confidently assert that the cost of preparing the <term>Tincture</term> <note>The refined alchemical substance used to transform base metals into gold or to create an elixir of life.</note> (apart from your own daily maintenance and the fuel required for the furnace) does not exceed three <term>florins</term> <note>A common gold coin of the period; the author emphasizes that the work is spiritually expensive but materially cheap.</note>. For the <term>Matter</term> <note>The "Prima Materia" or starting substance of the alchemical work, which many authors claimed could be found anywhere, even in common waste.</note>, as has already been said, is for the most part very common and may be obtained everywhere in abundance; and the *labour* is easy and simple. In brief, the whole design presents no difficulty whatever to those whom God has chosen for this purpose—that is, to those who love Him—but to the wicked, it is beset with insurmountable obstacles. 

In conclusion, let me tell you that if God, in His gracious mercy, should deign to reveal to you this "open secret," it will then become your sacred duty to use it well and to conceal your knowledge from the unworthy. You must put a seal upon your lips and preserve unbroken silence about it. If you neglect this well-intentioned warning, you may bring upon yourself the anger of God and the persecution of wicked men, being justly punished with both worldly and eternal ruin.

-> “If anyone seeks riches by means of this sacred Art,” <-

All this, beloved Reader, I desired to urge upon you as a final farewell. I devoutly hope that God has opened your eyes and that you have fully grasped my meaning. I am forbidden by my vow to explain the matter more clearly or openly than I have already done. I can only ask you once more to read through this treatise carefully and to ask God to enlighten your understanding.

## APPENDIX

If, after obtaining this knowledge, you give way to pride or greed (under the guise of "thrift" or "prudence") and thus gradually turn away from God, the secret will most certainly fade from your mind in a way you do not understand. This has actually happened to many who refused to listen to this warning.

# EPIGRAM.

"It is an easy matter to prepare gold in the furnace out of metals: at times there is found a man to whom the secret is revealed. Why is not every alchemist rich? The reason is that one thing is wanting which many seek with anxious care. Common gold is not fixed, and, when brought to the test of fire, quickly disappears and perishes. But he who knows the fixed gold <note>Alchemical "fixed" gold refers to a substance that has been purified to the point that it can withstand the highest heat without losing weight or property, unlike "volatile" or common metals.</note>, which at all times remains the same, and from which nothing is lost, he is the possessor of the true <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy—the sacred science of transformation.</note>, and may be called a good and practical <term>Sage</term> <note>A wise practitioner who has achieved the "Great Work."</note> and <term>Chemist</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Chemist" and "Alchemist" were used interchangeably to describe those who studied the properties of matter.</note>."

# ANOTHER EPIGRAM.

"**Theology** without **alchemy** is like a noble body without its right hand. This is graphically shewn and exhibited in the picture before us <note>The author is referring to an "emblem," a symbolic illustration common in alchemical texts that encodes secret processes through visual allegory.</note>. First look at the helmet and the two wings, which signify the love of the **Art**. They bear us onward to **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sophia"</note>, who is bright like the **Sun-God** <note>original: "Phœbus," an epithet for Apollo, symbolizing the clarity and perfection of the alchemical Sun or gold.</note>. Her body is naked because she is ardently loved. She is loved because she has at her disposal the riches of the whole world. He that gazes upon her beauteous form cannot refrain himself from loving her, goddess as she is. Although this love is, as it were, hidden, yet it is constant; and that is indicated by the mask. Her heart is sincere, her words are modest, righteousness upholds her steps, she is free from malice and guile. Her valiant appearance shews that she is of an open mind. Yet she seems to be falling, too: that is because the base world hates her, and with fierce truculence tries to cast her down to the ground. But evermore she bravely rises on high, though ambition moves her not. She is beloved by God and man. Though mockery is to her for a garment, as is shewn by the noisy cymbals, yet she cares nothing for it, but cleaves all the more faithfully to wisdom; to it she lifts her eyes, to it she directs her steps. For she knows that it is the only true salvation, and therefore she occupies herself with it by day and by night. She is not anxious for worldly praise, nor does she heed the hatred and injustice of men, or care for their opinion too little or too much. Much suffering and tribulation are inflicted upon her by this wicked world, yet she bears it with a valiant heart and holds it in disdain. For she possesses the treasure which gives her all...

**G**OOD heavens, how deeply I am often saddened at seeing the human race, which God created perfect, in His own image, and appointed to be the lords of the earth, depart so far away from me! I allude more particularly to you, O stolid <term>philosophaster</term> <note>A "philosophaster" is a pretender to philosophy; a person who possesses only a superficial or false knowledge of the subject.</note>, who presume to style yourself a practical chemist, a good philosopher, and yet are entirely destitute of all knowledge of me, of the true <term>Matter</term> <note>Referring to the "Prima Materia" or First Matter, the primitive, formless base substance that alchemists believed could be transformed into any other substance.</note>, and of the whole <term>Art</term> <note>The "Great Art" (Ars Magna), a common name for the practice of alchemy.</note> which you profess! For, behold, you break vials, and consume coals, only to soften your brain still more with the vapours. You also digest <term>alum</term>, salt, <term>orpiment</term> <note>A yellow mineral consisting of arsenic trisulfide, historically used as a pigment and in alchemical experiments.</note>, and <term>atrament</term> <note>A term for any dark or black substance, usually referring to vitriol (metallic sulfates) or ink.</note>; you melt metals, build small and large furnaces, and use many vessels: nevertheless, I am sick of your folly, and you suffocate me with your sulphurous smoke. With most intense heat you seek to fix your <term>quicksilver</term> <note>The common name for mercury.</note>, which is the vulgar volatile substance, and not that out of which I make metals; therefore you effect nothing. For you do not follow my guidance, or strive to imitate my methods, rather mistaking my whole artifice. You would do better to mind your own business, than to dissolve and distil so many absurd substances, and then to pass them through <term>alembics</term>, <term>cucurbitas</term>, <term>stills</term>, and <term>pelicans</term> <note>These are all types of glassware used in distillation. A "pelican" is a circulatory vessel with two "arms" that return the condensed liquid to the base, resembling a pelican pecking its own breast.</note>. By this method you will never succeed in congealing <term>quicksilver</term>. For the revivification you use a <term>reverberatory fire</term> <note>A type of furnace that directs heat or flames downward onto the material being heated, rather than heating it from below.</note>, and make it so hot as to render everything liquid—thus do you finish your work, and in the end ruin yourself and others. You will never discover anything unless you first enter my workshop, where, in the inmost bowels of the earth I ceaselessly forge metals: there you may find the substance which I use, and discover the method of my work. 
Do not suppose that I will reveal my secret to you unless you first find the growing <term>seed of all metals</term> <note>Alchemists believed that metals were not dead matter but grew like plants from a "seed" or "sperm" within the earth.</note> (resembling that of

***Metals Exist, vegetables Live and Grow, and animals Feel***, which is more than merely to grow. <note>This follows the Aristotelian "Great Chain of Being," where minerals have existence, plants have life, and animals possess sentience.</note> I make metals, stones, and the <term>atramental substances</term> <note>Mineral salts or vitriols, often dark in color, used in alchemical processes and the making of ink.</note> out of certain elements, which I mix and compound in a certain way. Metals have no life, or principle of generation and growth, if they lack their own proper seed. The first is accomplished by the <term>four elements</term> <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> in nine days; the <term>Moon</term> goes through the twelve <term>heavenly signs</term> <note>The twelve constellations of the Zodiac.</note> in twenty-nine and a half days.
