Thus all things in heaven which are comprehended under the <term>Moon</term> <note>In the medieval worldview, the "sublunary" sphere (everything below the Moon) was the realm of change, decay, and the mixing of elements.</note>, do work, and impart their influence to the substance, which, like a woman, longs to conceive seed. Each star influences its own substance, and according to their peculiar nature, they produce different things. They work first in heaven above, then in the earth beneath in the elements, each according to its own peculiar virtue; and hence arise species and individual things.

You are to know that these manifold influences do not pour themselves fruitlessly upon the earthly elements. For though their working is invisible, yet it is a most certain and real thing. The earth is surrounded by heaven, and from it obtains her best influences and substances. Every sphere is ready to communicate its truth, and therewith to pervade her centre. After the <term>putrefaction</term> <note>A stage of decay and blackening (nigredo) where the old form is broken down to allow for new life.</note> comes the <term>generation</term> <note>The birth or creation of a new substance.</note>, which is brought about by the internal incombustible warmth heating the coldness of the <term>quicksilver</term>, which gladly submits to this heat because it wishes to be united to its <term>sulphur</term>. Mary</term>" <note>A 'bain-marie' or water bath used for gentle, indirect heating.</note>, or other sophisticated contrivances. Thus I extract my <term>quicksilver</term> from the <term>four elements</term>, or their substance. This is always accompanied by its <term>sulphur</term>, which is its second self, and warms it gradually, gently, and pleasantly. Thus the cold becomes warm, and the dry moist and oily. 

But the moist is not without its dry substance, nor is the dry without its moist: one is conserved by the other in its first essence (which is the elementary spirit of the essence, or the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The 'fifth essence,' a pure, spiritual substance that permeates the four physical elements.</note>) from which proceeds the generation of our child. The fire brings it forth, and nourishes it in the air, but before that, it is decomposed in virgin earth; then water flows forth (or it flows forth from the water), which we must seek, since it is my first Matter, and the source of my mineral. For contrary resists strenuously to contrary, and doth in such wise fortify itself, lest perchance it be carried away in operating; then does it suffer <term>transmutation</term> <note>The fundamental change of one species or metal into another.</note>, and is stripped of its form by the concupiscence of matter, which incessantly attracts a new form.

By my wisdom I govern the first principle of motion. My hands are the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>In the ancient cosmos, the sphere of the fixed stars which surrounds the planets.</note>, as my Father ordained; my hammers are the <term>seven planets</term> <note>The Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, which were believed to influence the growth of metals.</note>, with which I forge beautiful things. The Earth is really dry, but it is also cold; its great dryness renders it akin to fire. *Fire*, however, is the first of elements which causes life and growth by its heat.

Now all these elements influence and qualify each other, so that each in its turn is now active, now passive. For instance, Fire works upon air and earth. Earth is the mother and nurse of all things, and sustains all that is liable to decay under heaven. Now God has given me power to resolve the four elements into their <term>quintessence</term>; this is that <term>first substance</term> which in every element is generically qualified. Every sane person must see that nothing can be accomplished without a perfect knowledge of the heavenly bodies <note>Astrological influence was considered essential in alchemy, as the movements of planets were thought to govern the growth of metals in the earth.</note>, or apart from the efficacy which abides in them; without these everything is error and misuse; and yet, whence is a mere man to obtain this influence, and how is he to apply it to the substance? How can he mingle the elements in their right proportions? Even if a man were to spend a long life in the investigation of this secret (says <term>Avicenna</term> <note>A Latinized name for Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose works on medicine and philosophy were foundational in Europe.</note> in his book *On the Powers of the Heart* <note>original: *De Viribus Cordis*</note>, chapter 2), he would not get any nearer to its solution. It is entrusted to my keeping alone, and can never be known to any man. By my virtue and efficacy I make the imperfect perfect, whether it be a metal or a human body. I mix its ingredients, and temper the <term>four elements</term> <note>Fire, Air, Water, and Earth; the building blocks of the physical world.</note>. I reconcile opposites, and calm their discord.

This is the golden chain which I have linked together of my heavenly virtues and earthly substances. I accomplish my works with such unerring accuracy that in them all my power is shewn forth, and with so much skill that the wisest of men cannot attain to my perfection. I acknowledge and confess that thou art the Mother and Empress of the great world, made for the little world of man’s mind. Thou movest the bodies above, and transmutest the elements below. At the bidding of thy Lord thou dost accomplish both small things and great, and renewest, by ceaseless decay and generation, the face of the earth and of the heavens. I confess that nothing can live without a soul, and that all that exists and is endued with being flows forth from thee by virtue of the power that God has given to thee. All matter is ruled by thee, and the elements are under thy governance. From them thou takest the <term>first substance</term> <note>Also known as *materia prima*, the formless primal matter from which all elements and physical objects were thought to be composed.</note>, and from the heavens thou dost obtain the form. That substance is formless and void until it is modified and individualized by thee. First thou givest it a substantial, and then an individual form. In thy great wisdom thou dost cunningly mould all thy works through the heavenly influences, so that no mortal hand can utterly destroy them. Now, whether I lie, or stand, or walk, I can think of nothing but thy great mystery. And yet I am unable to conceive what substance and form I must take for it. Thou didst sternly rebuke me for not following thy way; but thou knowest that, if I do not obey thee, it is only because I do not know what thou wouldst have me do. I shall never be able to attain any satisfactory result in this <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, the sacred process of purifying and perfecting both matter and the practitioner's soul.</note>, unless thou wilt enlighten my blindness. Gold and silver, however, are strong enough to resist its violence; although it is well-known that mercury, when exposed to an exceptional degree of heat, devours and swallows even these two metals. Yet neither of them is changed into the nature of the mercury, howbeit, they are enclosed in its womb; for gold and silver are more permanent and more perfect than crude mercury, this being an imperfect metal, notwithstanding that there is in it the substance of perfection. -># A PHILOSOPHICAL SUMMARY.<-

mercury. For this reason, the ancient Sages have called it the **Mother of the Metals**, and hence, being itself a metal, it must contain a two-fold metallic substance, namely, the inner substance of the <term>Moon</term> <note>In alchemical texts, "Moon" (Luna) refers to Silver.</note>, and that of the <term>Sun</term> <note>In alchemical texts, "Sun" (Sol) refers to Gold.</note> (which is unlike the other). Of these two substances mercury is formed, and they are cherished in its body in the form of <term>spiritual essences</term> <note>In this context, "spirits" or "essences" refer to the intangible, energetic properties of the metals before they take a solid, physical form.</note>. Now, as soon as Nature has formed that mercury of these two spirits, she strives to <term>transmute</term> <note>To change from one nature, substance, or form into another.</note> them into a perfect bodily form; and therefore, when those two spirits have grown up, and their two varieties of seed awake, they desire to assume their own proper bodies; and then the Mother, mercury, must **die** <note>In alchemy, "death" or "mortification" refers to the breakdown of a substance's original form so that its inner essence can be reborn as something more "perfect."</note>, and having died a natural death, can never be quickened any more into that which it was previously.

Vainglorious and arrogant Alchemists have obscurely hinted that perfect and imperfect bodies must be transmuted into fluid mercury, but this assertion is only a trap for the unwary. It is true that mercury consumes imperfect metals, like lead and tin, and thus increases in quantity; but, by doing so, it loses its perfection, and is no longer the mercury that it was before. If, indeed, it could be so **mortified** by a chemical process as to shut out all hope of its ever quickening itself again, it would be changed into something else, as happens with <term>cinnabar</term> <note>A toxic, bright red mineral (mercury sulfide) which is the primary source of mercury.</note>, or in <term>sublimate</term> <note>Likely "mercury sublimate" or "corrosive sublimate," a powdery solid created by heating mercury with acids.</note>. But, when it is <term>coagulated</term> <note>The process of a liquid becoming a solid.</note> by a chemical process, whether by a swift or a slow method, its two bodies do not assume a permanent form. 

By the natural process this coagulation is indeed successfully carried out; and thus we never find a vein of lead, for instance, which does not contain a few permanent grains, at least, of gold and silver. It is Nature that creates all things, whether they be animal, vegetable, or mineral, and warms them, each at its own proper degree.

## THE ONLY TRUE WAY.

---

**B**ELOVED friend and brother, under the name of this glorious <term>Art</term> <note>Alchemy, historically referred to as the "Great Art" (Ars Magna), which sought both the perfection of metals and the soul.</note> there is to be found much false teaching, which is put forward by <term>pseudo-alchemists</term> <note>Commonly called "puffers" because of their constant use of bellows; these were individuals who sought only material gold through trial and error rather than natural philosophy.</note>, whose writings are nothing but imposture and deceit, and are yet highly esteemed by people of the simpler sort. These charlatans induce their dupes to waste much money and time on that which can profit them nothing; for unless a thing be well begun, it can never be brought to a good end. Yet most men, who, nowadays, have devoted themselves to this exalted art of <term>chemistry</term> <note>In the 17th century, the terms "chemistry" and "alchemy" were often used interchangeably (sometimes spelled "chymistry").</note>, are pursuing a wrong course, and are deceivers or deceived. The deceivers are conscious of their own ignorance, and try to veil it under an obscure and allegorical style. The less they really know, the more pompous and the more unintelligible do their speculations become. But the reader, who is puzzled by their perplexing style, may at least comfort himself with the assurance that he knows as much about the matter as the authors. That assurance must serve for a kind of clue to the endless labyrinth of their false <term>sublimations</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again.</note>, <term>calcinations</term> <note>Reducing a substance to a powder or ash by applying high heat.</note>, <term>distillations</term> <note>The purification of a liquid by heating it to vapor and condensing it back into a liquid.</note>, <term>solutions</term>, <term>coagulations</term>, <term>putrefactions</term> <note>The intentional "rotting" or breakdown of the "Prime Matter" to allow for new growth.</note>, and <term>corruptions</term>. Nevertheless, we may almost every day see foolish persons spend their whole substance on those absurd experiments, being induced to do so by the aforesaid pseudo-alchemists, who impose on them with a false process, and fanciful perversions of Nature.

With these useless and unnecessary experiments the true Alchemists will have nothing to do. They follow the method pursued by Nature in the veins of the earth, which is very simple, and includes no solutions, putrefactions, coagulations, or anything of the kind. Can Nature, in the heart of the earth, where the metals do grow and receive increase, have anything <note>The sentence breaks off here at the end of the page, continuing the argument that natural metal growth is a simple, organic process rather than a complex laboratory ritual.</note>

...corresponding to all those pseudo-alchemical instruments, <term>alembics</term> <note>A distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling pot and a cooling cap (the head) with a tube to collect the condensate.</note>, <term>retorts</term> <note>Spherical glass vessels with long, downward-sloping necks, used for distilling substances at high heat.</note>, circulatory and sublimatory phials, fires, and other materials, such as cobbler's wax, salt, arsenic, mercury, sulphur, and so forth? Can all these things really be necessary for the growth and increase of the metals? It is surprising that any one not entirely bereft of his senses can spend many years in the study of <term>alchemy</term> <note>The ancient philosophical and proto-scientific tradition aimed at perfecting nature, most famously through the transmutation of base metals into gold.</note>, and yet never get beyond those foolish and frivolous solutions, coagulations, putrefactions, and distillations, while Nature is so simple and unsophisticated in her methods. Surely every true Artist must look upon this elaborate tissue of baseless operations as the merest folly, and can only wonder that the eyes of those silly dupes are not at last opened, that they may see something besides such absurd sophisms, and read something besides those stupid and deceitful books. It seems that they are so entangled in their sophisms that they can never attain to the freedom of true philosophy.

But let me tell you that so long as you love lies, and turn away from <term>rational philosophy</term> <note>A systematic approach to understanding the world through logic and the observation of natural laws, rather than through superstitious or haphazard experiments.</note>, you will never find the right way. I can speak from bitter experience. For I, too, toiled for many years in accordance with those sophistic methods, and endeavoured to reach the coveted goal by <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance into a vapor and then cooling it back into a solid form to purify it.</note>, <term>distillation</term> <note>The boiling of a liquid to separate its components based on their different volatility.</note>, <term>calcination</term> <note>Reducing a substance to a fine powder by heating it to high temperatures in the presence of air.</note>, <term>circulation</term> <note>A repetitive cycle of distillation and condensation within a sealed vessel, intended to "refine" the spirit of the substance.</note>, and so forth, and to fashion the <term>Stone</term> <note>The "Philosopher’s Stone," a legendary substance believed to be capable of transmuting metals and providing a universal cure for illness.</note> out of substances such as urine, salt, atrament <note>A historical term for sulfate minerals like vitriol, often used to make ink or acid.</note>, alum, etc. I have tried hard to evolve it out of hairs, wine, eggs, bones, and all manner of herbs; out of arsenic, mercury, and sulphur, and all the minerals and metals. I have striven to elicit it by means of <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "aqua fortis"; Latin for "strong water," a term for nitric acid, a powerful solvent.</note> and <term>alkali</term> <note>Basic chemical substances, such as potash, used to react with acids.</note>. I have spent nights and days in dissolving, coagulating, amalgamating, and precipitating. Yet from all these things I derived neither profit nor joy. I had hoped much from the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth element," believed to be the purest, most spiritual essence of a physical substance.</note>, but it disappointed me like the rest.

Therefore, beloved brother, let me warn you to have nothing to do with sublimations of sulphur and mercury, or the solution of bodies, or the coagulation of spirits, or with all the innumerable alembics, which bear little profit unto veritable art. So long as you do not seek the true essence of Nature, your labours will be doomed to failure; therefore, if you desire success, you must once for all renounce your allegiance to all those old methods, and enlist under the standards of that method which proceeds in...

-># THE ONLY TRUE WAY <-

...strict obedience to the teaching of Nature—in short, the method which Nature herself pursues in the bowels of the earth. For you see that Nature uses only **one substance** in her work of developing and perfecting the metals, and that this substance includes everything that is required. Now, this substance appears to call for no special treatment, except that of <term>digestion</term> <note>In alchemy, digestion refers to the process of exposing a substance to a gentle, constant heat over a long period, mimicking the internal heat of a living body or the earth.</note> by gentle heat, which must be continued until it has reached its highest possible degree of development. 

For this simple heating process the cunning <term>sophists</term> <note>The author uses "sophists" to describe false alchemists who use clever but fallacious arguments and overly complex language to hide their lack of true knowledge.</note> have substituted solutions, <term>coagulations</term> <note>The process of turning a liquid into a solid or semi-solid state.</note>, <term>calcinations</term> <note>The reduction of a substance to powder or ash through high heat.</note>, <term>putrefactions</term> <note>The stage of decomposition where the matter "dies" and turns black; alchemists believed this was a prerequisite for new growth.</note>, <term>sublimations</term> <note>The process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then collects again as a solid in the cooler part of the vessel.</note>, and other fantastical operations—which are only different names for the same thing; and thereby they have multiplied a thousand-fold the difficulties of this undertaking, and given rise to the popular notion that it is a most arduous, hazardous, and ruinously expensive enterprise. This they have simply done out of jealousy and malice, to put others off the right track, and to involve them in poverty and ruin. But they will find it difficult to justify their conduct before God, who has commanded us to love our neighbours as ourselves. For out of sheer malice they have rendered the road of truth impassable, and perplexed a simple natural process with such an elaborate tissue of circumstantial nomenclature, as to make the <term>amelioration</term> <note>Literally "improvement"; in this context, the transmutation of base metals into "perfect" gold.</note> of the metals appear a hopelessly difficult task.

For while you heat, you also putrefy, or decompose, as you may see by the changes which a grain of wheat undergoes in the ground under the influence of the rain and of the sun; you know that it must first decay before new life can spring forth. It is this process which they have denominated putrefaction and solution. Again when you heat, you also sublime, and to this <term>coction</term> <note>From the Latin "coctio," meaning cooking; it refers to the "ripening" of the alchemical matter through heat.</note> they have applied the terms sublimation and <term>multiplication</term> <note>The stage where the power or quantity of the alchemical Elixir is increased.</note>, that the simple man might err more easily. In like manner coagulation takes place in heating; for they say that coagulation takes place when humidity is changed into the nature of fire, so as to be able to resist the action of fire, without evaporating, or being consumed. And heating also includes that which they call “<term>circulation</term>,” <note>A process where vapors rise and fall within a vessel, creating a continuous cycle of refinement.</note> or conjunction, or the union of fire with water to prevent complete combustion.

Thus you see that that which they have called by so many names is really but **one simple process**. The substance, which...

is *one*, they have described under a similar variety of appellations <note>Appellations: different names or titles used to describe the same thing.</note>, to prevent men from finding that which, by the grace of God, can provide for them so many precious blessings. In the first place they call it “our mercury,” by which they mean nothing but moisture, which begins to unite itself with the fire, and therefore may be compared to mercury <note>In alchemy, "mercury" often symbolizes the liquid, feminine, or volatile principle in nature, rather than just the metal quicksilver.</note>. Again, they use the expression, “our sulphur,” whereby they mean nothing but the fire itself, which lies hid beneath the water, or humidity, and is heated by the water to its highest degree <note>Alchemical "sulphur" represents the active, masculine, or combustible principle—the "inner fire" of a substance.</note>. Then, again, they call it <term>Hyle</term> <note>Original Greek: *hyle* (ὕλη). A philosophical term for "primordial matter" or the raw substance of the universe before it takes a specific form.</note>, or the **First Substance**, because all things are first generated out of water and fire. Other names, such as Arsenic, Orpiment, Bismuth <note>The author dismisses these specific minerals as the "wrong" materials used by people who take alchemical recipes too literally.</note>, are not used by the Sages at all, but only by certain ignorant charlatans, of whom we need not take any further notice. *Let us follow the guidance of Nature: she will not lead us astray.*

If you let this be your motto, you will surely be able to call to mind the **first substance**, out of which all metallic substances are generated. But before we consider this question, it will much behove you to understand why the Sun, Moon, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn <note>These are the traditional alchemical names for the seven metals of antiquity: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Copper (Venus), Iron (Mars), Tin (Jupiter), and Lead (Saturn).</note>, are metals, and what is their origin. Besides finding an answer to this question, you must also bear in mind that all created things are divided into **three kingdoms**, viz., the animal, the vegetable, and the mineral. To the first belong all living things that have flesh and blood; to the second all herbs, plants, and trees; to the third all metals, stones, and everything that cannot be burned.

But, though divided into three classes, yet all things, O my brother, may be traced back to **one common Principle**, from which they derive their generation, or birth. The <term>coction</term> <note>From the Latin *coctio*, meaning "cooking" or "digestion." In alchemy, this refers to the process of maturing or purifying a substance through steady heat, much like fruit ripening in the sun.</note> of the *animal* is almost as imperfect as that of the vegetable substance: for its essence is easily burned. The coction of the mineral substances is the most perfect of all, because in them the metallic liquid is more closely united (by coction) to its elementary fire. Hence metals are better able to resist common fire than the vegetable and animal substances. When a metal is placed in the fire, it does not burn with a bright flame like wood; for the liquid of wood is not so completely joined (by coction) to its essence, as the liquid of metals is to its essence. The union of the liquid with the essence is not metallic, but vegetable, for which reason the latter is consumed with a black smoke. When, by a higher degree of coction, the vegetable has been transmuted into a metallic essence, it no longer gives out a black smoke in common fire, but a white smoke, as you may see when imperfect metals <note>“Imperfect metals” usually refers to base metals like lead or tin, which oxidize or vaporize when heated, unlike “perfect” gold.</note> are melted in the fire. That is why the Ancients said that you must first make the substance black before you make it white, *i.e.*, it must first give out a black smoke before it gives out a white. Again they say: You must first make it white before you make it red. To make red is to make perfect, because gold and silver have been rendered perfect by coction, their essence being fully united to their liquid, and changed into pure fire.

Do not then suffer yourself to be thrown off your guard by the obscure phraseology of the Ancients. If you thoroughly study the simple fundamental nature of the metals, you will know what their enigmatic expressions mean, and will not, like some moderns, conclude from their writings that you must take a certain substance and dissolve it until it turns black, then again purify and <term>calcine</term> <note>To calcine is to heat a substance to high temperatures in order to drive off volatile parts or reduce it to a powder (calx).</note> it until the blackness disappears and it begins to turn white; and after that, once more increase the fire and calcine and toil until the substance turns red. But where are they to obtain it, and how are they to bring it to perfection? The <term>metallic essence</term> <note>The internal "seed" or life-force of a metal that allows it to grow or change.</note> can not be separated from the <term>imperfect metals</term> <note>Base metals like lead or tin, which were believed to be "unfinished" gold.</note> without being injured ; for if it be separated with fire the liquid must evaporate, and the essence (with its earth) be consumed. For the liquid protects the fire against combustion, so that both remain fixed and unchanged in common fire. This perfected substance the Ancients have well called the <term>Elixir</term>, or fire which has undergone a process of perfect <term>cooking</term> : for that which before was crude and raw is "cooked," or <term>digested</term> <note>The process of slow "ripening" of the matter over time using gentle warmth.</note> by the process of maturation. That element which, by its imperfection, causes base metals to be broken up and disintegrated by fire, has been <term>digested</term> and perfected by natural heat.

## *There follow some Methods of Recognising our Stone.*

### I.

Know that our Stone is *one*, and that it is justly called a Stone. For it *is* a Stone, and could bear no name so characteristic, as that of the <term>Stone of the Sages</term> <note>Another name for the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note>. Yet it is not any one of our existing stones, but only derives its appellation from its similarity to them. For our Stone is so prepared as to be composed of the <term>four elements</term> <note>The classical elements of Fire, Air, Water, and Earth, which alchemists believed must be balanced to achieve perfection.</note>. On this account it has been called by different names, and assumes different forms, although it is *one* thing, and its like is not found upon earth. It is a Stone, and not a stone in the sense of having the nature of any one stone; it is fire, yet it has not the appearance, or properties, of fire; it is air, yet neither has it the appearance, or properties, of air; it is water, but has no resemblance, or affinity, to the nature of water. It is earth, though it has not the nature, or appearance, of earth, seeing that it is a thing by itself.

## *Another way of Knowing our Precious Stone.*

### II.

An ancient philosopher says: Our Stone is called the sacred rock, and is divided, or signified, in four ways. Firstly, into earth; secondly, into its accretion; thirdly, into fire; and fourthly, into the flame of fire. If any one knows the method of dissolving it, of extracting its <term>salt</term> <note>Alchemical Salt represents the "body" or the fixed, non-combustible principle of a substance.</note>, and of perfectly <term>coagulating</term> <note>The process of "coagulation" involves turning a liquid or dissolved substance into a solid state, a key step in the alchemical cycle of "solve et coagula" (dissolve and congeal).</note> it, he is initiated in the mysteries of the Sages. Therefore if the salt turn white, and assume an oily appearance, then it <term>tinges</term> <note>To "tinge" means to project the Stone's power onto a base metal to transform its color and nature into gold or silver.</note>. There are three stages in our Art. Firstly, the transmutation of the whole thing into one salt; secondly, the rendering of three subtle bodies intangible; thirdly, the repetition of the whole solution of the whole thing. If you understand this, set your hand to the work. For the Matter is only one thing, and would

## *Yet Another Way of Knowing our Blessed Stone.*

The philosopher, <term>Morienus</term> <note>Morienus (or Morienus Romanus) was a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit, said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>, calls our <term>Stone</term>, water: and he had good reasons for the name. O water of bitter taste, that preservest the elements! O glorious nature, that overcomest Nature herself! O thou that resemblest Nature, which dissolvest her tractable nature, that exaltest Nature—that art crowned with light, and preservest in thyself the four elements, out of which the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance, which alchemists believed could be extracted to create the Stone.</note> is made! Thou art for the simple, seeing that thou art most simple in thy operation. Having conceived by a natural process, thou bringest forth vapour, and art a good mother. Thou needest no outward help; nature preserves nature, and is not separated from nature by the operation of nature. The thing is easy to find, the knowledge is easy, altogether familiar, yet it is as a miracle to many. Thy solution is great glory, and all thy lovers are named above. Thou art a great <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: "arcanum" — a Latin word meaning a profound secret or mystery known only to the initiated.</note> and to the many thou appearest impossible!

Then the body loses all its grossness, and becomes new and pure; nor can this body and soul ever die, seeing that they have entered into an eternal union, such as the union of our bodies and souls shall be at the last day.

### *Another Description of our Stone.*

The Enigma of the Wise <note>This refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the elusive goal of the alchemical "Great Work."</note> is the Salt and Root of the whole Art, and, as it were, its Key, without which no one is able either to lock or unlock its secret entrance. No man can understand this Art who does not know the Salt and its preparation, which takes place in a convenient spot that is both moist and warm; there the dissolution of its liquid must be accomplished, while its substance remains unimpaired. These are the words of Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary 8th-century Islamic polymath often regarded as the father of chemistry.</note>.

### *Explanation.*

Know that the Salt of which Geber speaks has none of the specific properties of salt <note>The author clarifies that alchemical "Salt" is a philosophical principle representing solidity and fixity, not common table salt.</note>, and yet is called a Salt, and *is* a Salt. It is black and fetid, and when chemically prepared, assumes the appearance of blood, and is at length rendered white, pure, and clear. It is a good and precious Salt which, by its own operation, is first impure and then pure. It dissolves and coagulates itself, or, as the Sage says, it locks and unlocks itself. No Salt has this property but the Salt of the Sages. Its chemical development it may undergo in a moist and convenient place, where its moisture (as the Sage says) may be dissolved in the <term>Bath of Mary</term> <note>original: "Balneum Mariae"; a double boiler or water bath used to provide gentle, consistent heat.</note>. He means that it must be warm enough for its water to be distilled, yet not warmer than the excrement of horses <note>Decaying horse manure was a common source of steady, gentle heat in historical laboratories before the invention of regulated gas or electric heaters.</note>, which is not fresh.

### *Another Description of our Stone.*

Alexander the Great <note>While a historical king, medieval alchemists often attributed secret texts to Alexander to lend them authority.</note>, King of Macedonia, in his "Philosophy" has the following words: Know that the Salt is fire and dryness. Fire coagulates, and its nature is hot, dry, and penetrating, even unto the inmost part. Its property is to become white even as the Sun and the Moon <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents gold and the Moon represents silver.</note> with the variations in the extremes of fire, to wit, of the natural fire, while the Sun restores redness and the Moon whiteness, and brings bodies to their spiritual condition at the same time that it removes their blackness and bad sulphur. With it bodies are calcined <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve decomposition or oxidation.</note>: it is the secret of the red and white <term>tincture</term> <note>A "tincture" is a concentrated essence capable of transforming or "staining" base metals into gold (red) or silver (white).</note>, the foundation and root of all things, and the best of all created things after the rational soul of man. For no Stone in the whole world has a greater efficacy, nor can any child of this earth find the Art without this Stone. Blessed be

### *The Purging the “Earth” of Its Superfluous Earth.*

The quantity of this water is so great that it flows over the whole earth, yet leads to nothing but the knowledge of this **Art**. The same also is misused too often by those who desire it.

Take also the "fire," and in it you will find the **Stone**, and nowhere else in the whole world. It is familiar to all men, both young and old, is found in the country, in the village, in the town, in all things created by God; yet it is despised by all. Rich and poor handle it every day. Yet no one prizes it, though, next to the human soul, it is the most beautiful and the most precious thing upon earth, and has power to pull down kings and princes. The oil is the fire, or the Sun, the water is air, or the Moon; and Sun and Moon are silver and gold which must enter into union. Be thou, therefore, a lover of the **Art** <note>The "Art" or the "Great Work" (Ars Magna) refers to the sacred practice of alchemy.</note>, and commended unto God the Almighty even unto all eternity. Know also that by so much as the earthly part is wanting, by also so much does the heavenly part abound more fully. It contains within itself all healing and **transmuting** <note>The power to change one substance into another, specifically base metals into gold, or sickness into health.</note> virtue, breathed into it by God.

->### *A Simple Account of the True Art.*<-

According to the Sages, no body is dissolved without the coagulation of the spirit. For as soon as the spirit is transmuted into the body, the **Stone** receives its power. So long as the spirit is volatile and liable to evaporate, it cannot produce any effect; however, when it is fixed, it immediately begins to operate. 

You must therefore prepare it as the baker prepares the bread. Take a little of the spirit and add it to the body, just as the baker adds leaven to the meal, until the whole substance is leavened. It is the same with our spirit, or leaven. The Substance must be continuously penetrated with the leaven until it is wholly leavened. Thus the spirit purges and spiritualizes the body until they are both transmuted into one. Then they transmute all things into which they are injected into their own nature. 

The two must be united by a gentle and continuous fire, affording the same degree of warmth as that with which a hen hatches her eggs. It must then be placed in a <term>St. Mary's Bath</term> <note>original: "Balneum Mariae." A vessel of hot water used to heat a secondary container slowly and evenly; the ancestor of the modern double-boiler or bain-marie.</note>, which is neither too warm nor too cold. The humid must be separated from the dry and again joined to it. When united, they change mercury into pure gold and silver. 

Thenceforward you will be safe from the pangs of poverty. But take heed that you render thanks unto God for His gracious gift which is hidden from many. He has revealed the secret to you so that you may praise His holy name and succour your needy neighbor. Therefore, take diligent heed, lest you hide the talent committed to your care. Rather, put it out at interest for the glory of God and the good of your neighbor. For every man is bound to help his fellow man and to be an instrument in the hand of God for relieving his necessities. Of this rule Holy Scripture affords an illustration in the examples of Joseph, Habakkuk, Susanna, and others. <note>These biblical figures are cited as examples of those who were providentially aided by God or who used their positions to save and provide for others during times of crisis.</note>

### HERE FOLLOWS THE SECOND PART OF THIS BOOK.

In the beginning, when God Almighty had created our first parent Adam, together with all other earthly and heavenly bodies, He set him in Paradise, and forbade him, under penalty of eternal death, to eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. So long as Adam obeyed the Divine precept he had immortality, and possessed all that he needed for perfect happiness. But when he had partaken of the forbidden fruit, he was, by the command of God, driven forth into this world, where he and his descendants have since that time suffered nothing but poverty, disease, anxiety, bitter sorrow, and death. If he had been obedient to the Divine injunction, he would have lived a thousand years in Paradise in perfect happiness, and would then have been translated to heaven; and a like happy destiny would have awaited all his descendants. For his disobedience God visited him with all manner of sufferings and diseases; but in His mercy also showed him a medicine whereby the different defects brought in by sin might be remedied, and the pangs of hunger and disease resisted, as we are, for instance, preserved and strengthened by bodily meat and drink.

### *An Account of the True Art.*

I make known to all ingenuous students of this <term>Art</term> <note>Alchemy, often called the "Sacred Art."</note> that the <term>Sages</term> <note>The "Philosophers" or master alchemists of antiquity.</note> are in the habit of using words which may convey either a true or a false impression; the former to their own disciples and children, the latter to the ignorant, the foolish, and the unworthy. ### *Concerning the Origin of Metals.*

My son, I will now proceed to explain to you more in detail the generation of the metals, and the way in which they receive their growth and development, with their special form and quality. You will thereby be enabled to understand, even from the very foundation, with marvellous accuracy and clearness, the principle that underlies our whole Art. Permit me, therefore, to inform you that all animals, trees, herbs, stones, metals, and minerals, grow and attain to perfection, without being necessarily touched by any human hand: for the seed is raised up from the ground, puts forth flowers, and bears fruit, simply through the agency of natural influences. As it is with plants, so it is with metals.

While metals lie in the heart of the earth in their natural ore, they grow and are developed day by day through the influence of the four elements. Their internal fire is the radiance of the Sun and Moon; the earth conceives this solar radiance in her womb, and by it, the "seeds" of the metals are warmed thoroughly and evenly, just like grain growing in the fields. <note>The author is describing the "vitalist" theory of minerals—the ancient belief that metals were living things that grew inside the earth like plants or embryos.</note> 

Through this warmth, a vapor or spirit is produced in the earth, which rises upward and carries with it the most subtle <note>In this context, "subtle" means refined, pure, or intangible, as opposed to "gross" or heavy matter.</note> parts of the elements. It might well be called a <term>fifth element</term> <note>Also known as the *quintessence*, this was believed to be a pure, celestial substance that existed beyond the four physical elements (earth, air, fire, and water).</note>, for it is a quintessence and contains the most volatile parts of all the elements. This vapor strives to float upward through the summits of the mountains, but because they are covered with heavy rocks, the vapor is prevented from escaping. When it strikes against these rocks, it is compelled to descend again. 

It is drawn up by the Sun and forced down again by the rocks; as it falls, the vapor is transmuted into a liquid—that is, into <term>sulphur</term> and <term>mercury</term>. <note>In alchemical theory, all metals were thought to be composed of varying proportions and purities of "philosophical" Sulphur (the active, combustible principle) and Mercury (the passive, fluid principle).</note> Of each of these, a part is left behind, while that which is volatile continues to rise and descend, with more and more of it remaining behind and becoming <term>fixed</term> <note>A "fixed" substance is one that has become solid and stable enough to resist being evaporated by fire.</note> after each descent. 

This "fixed" substance is the metals, which cleave so firmly to the earth and the stones that they must be smelted out in a red-hot furnace. The coarser the stones and the earth of the mountains are, the less pure the metal will be; the more refined the soil and stones are, the more refined the vapor will be, along with the sulphur and mercury formed by its condensation. The purer these latter are, the purer, of course, the metals themselves will be. When the earth and stones of the mountain are crude, the sulphur and mercury must partake of this crudeness and cannot attain their proper development. 

This is how the different metals arise, each according to its own kind. For just as each tree in a field has its own unique shape, appearance, and fruit, so each mountain bears its own particular ore; those stones and that earth are the "soil" in which the metals grow. The quality of this soil is to a great extent dependent upon <term>planetary influences</term>. <note>Traditional alchemy linked the seven metals to the seven "planets" of the ancient world: Gold to the Sun, Silver to the Moon, Copper to Venus, Iron to Mars, Tin to Jupiter, Lead to Saturn, and Quicksilver to Mercury.</note> The nearer the mountains lie to the planets, the more do metals grow in them; for the qualities of metals are determined by planetary influences. Mountains that are turned towards the Sun have refined stones and earth, and produce nothing but gold. If they are situated more favorably to be influenced by the Moon, their metallic substance is turned into silver. For all—

For the <term>Sun</term> and <term>Moon</term> are the <term>mercury</term> in our <term>Matter</term>. The <term>Sun</term> is warm and dry, the <term>Moon</term> warm and moist; for in [the] earth is hid a warm and dry fire, and in that fire dwells warm and moist air—and from these is generated <term>mercury</term> which is both warm and moist. Hence there may be distinguished two chief <term>constituent principles</term>, to wit, moist and dry, that is, earth, wind, and water, unto which <term>mercury</term> is conjoined, and the same is warm and moist. 

<term>Mercury</term> and <term>sulphur</term>, in our substance, and in all things, spring from the moist and dry, the moist and dry being stirred by the warmth of the <term>Sun</term>, and distilled and sublimed,—in each thing according to its specific nature. Thus our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> is that <term>mercury</term> which is mixed of the dry and the moist. But the common <term>mercury</term> <note>Common quicksilver.</note> is useless for our purpose—for it is volatile, while our <term>mercury</term> is fixed and constant. Therefore have nothing to do with the common <term>mercury</term>, but take our <term>mercury</term> which is the principle of growth in all bodies, whether human, vegetable, or metallic; which imparts to all flowers their fragrance and colour. 

This <term>mercury</term> represents an harmonious mixture of the <term>four elements</term>, hot and dry, <term>Sun</term> and <term>Moon</term>. It is generated in the form of a vapour in the fields and on the mountains, by the warmth of the <term>Sun</term>: that vapour is condensed into a moisture, from which arise <term>sulphur</term> and <term>mercury</term>, and from them again metals. The same process takes place in our <term>Art</term> <note>Alchemy.</note>, which represents the union of the warm and moist, by means of warmth. For our substance is generated in the form of a vapour out of warmth and moisture, and changed into <term>sulphur</term>. In this fire and water, and nowhere else, is our <term>Stone</term> to be found. For the vapour carries upward with it most subtle earth, most subtle fire, most subtle water, and most subtle air, and thus presents a close union of the most subtle elements. This is the <term>first Matter</term> <note>The primordial substance from which the Stone is made.</note>, and may be divided into water and earth, which two are again joined together by gentle heat, even as in the woods and mountains <term>mercury</term> is joined with

It is the most precious fire that God has created in the earth, and has a thousand virtues—nay, it is so precious that men have averred that the Divine Power itself works effectually in it. It has the purifying virtue of Purgatory, and everything is rendered better by it. It is not wonderful, therefore, that a fire should be able to fix <note>"Fixing" refers to the process of making a volatile, liquid, or airy substance solid and resistant to heat.</note> and clarify <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemical theory, Mercury is the "spirit" or liquid principle of all metals, not just the common liquid metal quicksilver.</note>, and to cleanse it from all grossness and impurity. The Sages call it the living fire, because God has endowed it with His own Divine, and vitalizing power.

In the writings of the Sages, this fire goes by different names. Some call it “burnt” wine, others assign to it three names from the analogy of the Three Persons of the Holy Trinity, God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost; Body, Soul, and Fire, or Spirit.

The Sages further say: The fire is fire, and also water, containing within itself both cold and heat, moisture, and dryness, nor can anything extinguish it but itself. Hence others say that it is an inextinguishable fire, which is continually burning, purifying, and tinging <note>"Tinging" refers to the process of the Stone or Tincture dyeing or transforming a base metal into gold or silver.</note> all metals, consuming all their impurities, and combining <term>Mercury</term> with the <term>Sun</term> <note>In alchemical texts, the "Sun" (Sol) is the symbolic name for gold.</note> in so close an union that they become one and inseparable.

Therefore our great Teachers say that as God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, are three Persons, and yet but one God; so this fire unites these three things, namely, the Body, Spirit, and Soul, or Sun, <term>Mercury</term>, and Soul. The fire nourishes the Soul which binds together the Body and the Spirit, and thus all three become one, and remain united for ever. Again, as an ordinary fire, on being supplied with fuel, may spread and fill the whole world, so this <term>Tincture</term> <note>The Tincture is a powerful liquid or powder—often synonymous with the Philosopher's Stone—used to transform substances.</note> may be multiplied, and so this fire may enter into all metals; and one part of it has power to change two, three, or five hundred parts of other metals into gold.

Again, the Sages call this fire the fire of the Holy Spirit, because as the Divinity of Christ took upon itself true flesh and blood without forfeiting anything of its Divine Nature, so the <term>Sun</term>, the <term>Moon</term> <note>In alchemical texts, the "Moon" (Luna) is the symbolic name for silver.</note>, and <term>Mercury</term>, are transmuted into the true <term>Tincture</term>, which remains unaffected by all outward influences.

### *What is the Urine of Children?*

I will now truly inform you concerning the <term>Urine of Children</term> <note>A common alchemical metaphor or "deckname." Without this seed there is no consummation of our <term>Art</term> <note>Alchemy is frequently referred to as "The Art" or the "Sacred Art."</note>, and no <term>Tincture</term> <note>The "Tincture" is the potent substance (often the Philosopher's Stone in liquid form) used to transform base metals into gold or silver.</note>, either red or white. ### *What is the Mercury of the Sages?*

<term>Mercury</term> is nothing but water and salt, which have been subjected for a long space of time to natural heat so as to be united into one. This is <term>Mercury</term>, or dry water, which is not moist, and does not moisten anything; of course, I do not speak of crude common mercury <note>Refers to liquid quicksilver found in nature, which alchemists believed was "dead" or "crude" compared to their prepared version.</note>, but of the <term>Mercury of the Sages</term>. The <term>Sages</term> call it the <term>fifth element</term> <note>Also known as the "quintessence," it is the spiritual essence that permeates all physical matter beyond the four standard elements of earth, air, fire, and water.</note>. The other <term>quintessence</term>, which is in the earth, and partly material, contains within itself its own seed which grows out of its soil. The heavenly <term>quintessence</term> comes to the aid of the earthly, removes the grossness of its earth, and brings the aforesaid seed to maturity. For <term>Mercury</term>, and the <term>Celestial Quintessence</term>, drain off all harmful moisture from the <term>quintessence</term> of the earth. This <term>Mercury</term> is also called <term>sulphur of the air</term>, <term>sulphur</term> being a hardening of <term>mercury</term>; or we may describe them as husband and wife, from whom issue many children in the earth. Common <term>sulphur</term>, as you know, coagulates common <term>mercury</term>; for <term>sulphur</term> is poisonous, and <term>mercury</term> deadly. For the grossness of the air arises from the setting, the approach, and the rising of the Sun. v. **ANAXAGORAS** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who suggested that all things are composed of "seeds" containing every quality.</note> says: God and His goodness are the first principle of all things. Therefore, the mildness of God reigns even beneath the earth, being the substance of all things, and thus also the substance beneath the earth. For the mildness of God mirrors itself in creating, and His integrity in the solidity that is beneath the earth. Now we cannot see His goodness, except in bodily form.

vi. **SENIOR**, or **PANDOLPHUS**, <note>"Senior" usually refers to the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Zadith ben Hamuel. Pandolphus is another common figure in the alchemical tradition.</note> says: I make known to posterity that the thinness, or softness, of air is in water, and is not severed from the other elements. If the earth had not its vital juice, no moisture would remain in it.

vii. **ARISTEUS** <note>A legendary figure often associated with the secrets of nature and the preservation of alchemical knowledge.</note> delivers himself thus briefly: Know that the earth is round, and not flat. For if it were perfectly flat, the Sun would shine everywhere at the same moment.

viii. **PYTHAGORAS**: <note>The famous Greek mathematician, whom alchemists revered as a master of the harmony of the spheres and the elements.</note> That which is touched and not seen, also that which is known but not looked upon, these are only heaven and earth; again, that which is not known is in the world and is perceived by sight, hearing, smell, taste, or touch. Sight shews the difference between black and white; hearing, between good and evil; taste, between sweet and bitter; touch, between subtle and gross; smell, between fragrant and fetid.

ix. **ARISTEUS**, in his Second Table, says: Beat the body which I have made known to you into thin plates; pour thereon our salt water, *i.e.*, <term>water of life</term>, <note>Original Latin: *Aqua Vitae*. In this context, it refers to a specialized alchemical solvent or "mercury" rather than common brandy.</note> and heat it with a gentle fire until its blackness disappears, and it becomes first white, and then red.

x. **PARMENIDES**: <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who focused on the nature of being.</note> The Sages have written about many waters, stones, and metals, for the purpose of deceiving you. You that desire a knowledge of our **Art**, <note>The "Art" or "Great Work" of alchemy.</note> relinquish Sun, Moon, Saturn, and Venus, <note>These are planetary symbols for the metals: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Lead (Saturn), and Copper (Venus).</note> for our ore, and our earth, and why so? Every thing is of the nature of no thing. <note>An alchemical paradox suggesting that the true substance of the Stone is a "universal" that exists everywhere but is recognized by few.</note>

It emphasizes that the true alchemical materials are not common metals, but a hidden "ore" found through divine goodness and natural observation.</summary>

Then you have the <term>Medicine</term> <note>Another name for the Philosopher's Stone, believed to "heal" base metals into gold and grant long life to humans.</note>, which restores health, and imparts perfection to all things. xlii. **LAMECH**: In the <term>Stone of the Philosophers</term> are the first elements, and the final colours of minerals, or Soul, Spirit, and Body, joined unto one. The Stone which contains all these things is called **Zibeth** <note>A term often used in alchemy to refer to the "primordial matter" or a specific foul-smelling substance used at the start of the work; the name is derived from "civet," a musky secretion.</note>, and the working of Nature has left it imperfect.

xliii. **SOCRATES** <note>In alchemical literature, "Socrates" refers not to the historical Greek philosopher, but to a persona used in medieval dialogues to represent ancient wisdom.</note>: Our Mystery is the life of all things, or the water. For water dissolves the body into spirit, and summons the living spirit from among the dead. My son, despise not my **Practical Injunction**. For it gives you, in a brief form, everything that you really need.

xliv. **ALEXANDER** <note>Referring to Alexander the Great, who in alchemical legend was said to have discovered secret wisdom in the tomb of Hermes.</note>: The good need not remain concealed on account of the bad men that might abuse it. For God rules over all, according to His Divine Will. Observe, therefore, that the <term>salt of the Stone</term> is derived from mercury, and is that Matter, most excellent of all things, of which we are in search. The same also contains in itself all secrets. <term>Mercury</term> is our Stone, which is composed of the dry and the moist elements, which have been joined together by gentle heat in an inseparable union.

xlv. **SENIOR** <note>Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel), a prominent 10th-century Arab alchemist whose works were highly influential in the Latin West.</note> teaches us to make the Salt out of ashes, and then, by various processes, to change it into the **Mercury of the Sages**, because our <term>Magistery</term> <note>The mastery or the completed alchemical process.</note> is dependent on our water alone, and needs nothing else.

xlvi. **ROSARIUS** <note>Refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), one of the most famous illustrated alchemical manuscripts.</note>: It is a stone, and not a stone, viz., the **eagle-stone** <note>Also called *aetites*; a stone believed to be found in eagles' nests that contained another stone rattling inside it, symbolizing the "stone within a stone" or the spirit within the matter.</note>. The substance has in its womb a stone, and when it is dissolved, the water that was coagulated in it bursts forth. Thus the Stone is the extracted spirit of our indestructible body. It contains mercury, or liquid water, in its body, or fixed earth, which retains its nature. This explanation is sufficiently plain.

xlvii. **PAMPHILUS**: The **Salt of the Gem** is that which is in its own bowels ; it ascends with the water to the top of the <term>alembic</term> <note>A distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</note>, and, after separation, is once more united and made one body with it by means of natural warmth. It is of earth, water, air, and fire. It has no cause of corruption or other contrary quality.

For as Naaman the Syrian was purged of his leprosy by washing himself seven times in Jordan, so our substance must undergo a seven-fold cleansing, by calcining and dissolving, and exhibiting a variety of ever deepening colours. liv. **ANANIAS** <note>Likely referring to a legendary figure associated with early Judeo-Christian alchemical traditions.</note>: Know, ye <term>Scrutators of Nature</term> <note>Literally "searchers." A term for early scientists or philosophers who investigated the hidden laws of the physical world.</note>, that fire is the soul of everything, and that God Himself is fire and soul. And the body cannot live without fire. For without fire the other elements have no efficacy. It is, therefore, a most holy, awful, and divine fire which abides with God Himself in the Most Holy Trinity, for which also we give eternal thanks to God.

lv. **BONIDUS**: In the fountain of Nature our <term>Substance</term> <note>The "Prima Materia" or the raw starting material required for the Great Work.</note> is found, and nowhere else upon earth; and our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> is fire, and has been generated in fire, without, however, being consumed by fire.

lvi. **ROSINUS** <note>A Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Greco-Egyptian alchemist and mystic.</note>: Two things are hidden in two things, and indicate our Stone: in earth is fire, and air in water, yet there are only two outward things, viz., earth and water. For <term>Mercury</term> <note>In this context, Mercury is not just the liquid metal, but the "universal spirit" that mediates between the physical and spiritual realms.</note> is our Stone, consisting as it does both of moist and dry elements. Mercury is dry and moist in its very nature, and all things have their growth from the dry and moist elements.

lvii. **GEBER** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), an influential Islamic polymath considered the father of early chemistry.</note>: We cannot find anything permanent, or <term>fixed</term> <note>Stable and resistant to the transformative power of heat.</note>, in fire, but only a viscous natural moisture which is the root of all metals. For our venerable Stone nothing is required but mercurial substances, if they have been well purified by our <term>Art</term> <note>The "Sacred Art" or the practice of alchemy itself.</note>, and are able to resist the fierce heat of fire. This Substance penetrates to the very roots of metals, overcomes their imperfect nature, and transmutes them, according to the virtue of the <term>Elixir</term> <note>Also called the Medicine; a substance capable of perfecting both metals and the human body.</note>, or Medicine.

lviii. **AROS**: Our Medicine consists of two things, and one essence. There is one Mercury, of a fixed and a <term>volatile</term> <note>Easily evaporated or changed; representing the "spirit" that escapes the fire.</note> substance, composed of body and spirit, cold and moist, warm and dry.

lix. **ARNOLDUS** <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist credited with many medieval Hermetic texts.</note>: Let your only care be to regulate the <term>coction</term> <note>The process of "cooking" or slow-heating the alchemical substance in a sealed vessel.</note> of the Mercurial substance. In proportion as it is itself dignified shall it dignify bodies.

lx. **ALPHIDIUS**: Transmute the nature, and you will find what you want. For in our <term>Magistery</term> <note>The "Great Work" or the mastery of the alchemical process.</note> we obtain first from the gross the subtle, or the spirit; then from the moist the dry, *i.e.*, earth from water. Thus we transmute the corporeal into the spiritual, and the spiritual into the corporeal, the lowest into the highest, and the highest into the lowest.

lxi. **BERNARDUS** <note>Referring to Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century Italian alchemist renowned for his lifelong search for the Stone.</note>: The middle substance is nothing but coagulated mercury; and the first Matter is nothing but twofold mercury. For our <term>Medicine</term> <note>Another name for the Philosopher's Stone, believed not only to transmute metals but to heal all human ailments.</note> is composed of two things, the fixed and the volatile, the corporeal and the spiritual, the cold and the warm, the moist and the dry. Mercury must be subjected to <term>coction</term> <note>From the Latin 'coctio,' meaning cooking or ripening through heat.</note> in a vessel with three divisions, that the dryness of the active fire may be changed into vaporous moisture of the oil that surrounds the substance. A term used to describe the primordial, unformed matter of the universe.</note>, containing in a confused mixture the properties of every creature.

lxiv. **ALRIDOS** <note>A name likely referring to an Arabic alchemical authority, possibly a corruption of Al-Razi.</note>: The virtue and efficacy of everything is to be found in its quintessence, whether its nature be warm, cold, moist, or dry. This quintessence gives out the sweetest fragrance that can be imagined. Therefore the highest perfection is needed.

lxv. **LONGINUS** describes the process in the following terms: Let your vessel be tightly closed and exposed to an even warmth. This water is prepared in dry ashes, and is subjected to coction till the two become one. When one is joined to the other; the body is brought back to its spirit. Then the fire must be strengthened till the fixed body retains that which is not fixed by its own heat. With this you can <term>tinge</term> <note>To 'tinge' or 'tincture' is the alchemical act of projecting the Stone onto a base metal to transform its color and nature into gold.</note> ten thousand times ten thousand of other substances.

lxvi. **HERMES** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundation of alchemy is attributed.</note>, in his Mysteries, says: Know that our Stone is lightly esteemed by the thankless multitude; but it is very precious to the Sages. If princes knew how much gold can be made out of a particle of <term>Sun</term> <note>In alchemical texts, the 'Sun' (Sol) is the standard symbol for Gold.</note>, and of our Stone, they would never suffer it to be taken out of their dominions.

I now propose to say something about the meaning of the obscure and allegorical expressions used by some of the <term>Sages</term> whom I have quoted. Be sure that they all were true <term>Sages</term>, and really possessed our <term>Stone</term>. It may have been possessed by more persons since the time of Adam <note>Alchemists often traced their secret knowledge back to Adam, believing it was a divine gift given to the first man.</note>, but the above list includes all of whom I have heard. I need not here review all their sayings; for the words of the least of them are sufficient for imparting to you a knowledge of this <term>Art</term>; and my ambition goes no higher than that. If I have enumerated so large a number of authorities, I have only done so in order that you might the better understand both the theory and practice of this <term>Art</term>, and that you might be saved all unnecessary expense. For this reason I have declared this true philosophy with all the skill that God has given me. I hope the initiated will overlook any verbal inaccuracy into which I have fallen, and that they will be induced by my example to abstain from wilfully misleading anxious enquirers. I may have fallen into some errors of detail, but as to the gist of my work, I know what I have written, and that it is God's own truth.

### *Explanation of the Saying of Adam.*

When God had created our first parent <term>Adam</term> <note>In the alchemical tradition, Adam is often viewed as the "Primal Man" or "Microcosm," who possessed perfect knowledge of nature before the Fall.</note>, and set him in <term>Paradise</term>, He shewed him two things, namely, earth and water. Earth is fixed and indestructible, water is volatile and vaporous. These two contain the <term>elements</term> <note>The four building blocks of the universe: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> of all created things : water contains air, and earth fire—and of these four things the whole of creation is composed. In earth are enclosed fire, stones, minerals, salt, mercury, and all manner of metals ; in water, and in air, all manner of living and organic substances, such as beasts, birds, fishes, flesh, blood, bones, wood, trees, flowers, and leaves. To all these things God imparted their efficacy and virtue, and subjected them to the mastery and use of <term>Adam</term>. Hence you may see how all these things are adapted to the human body, and are such as to meet the requirements of his nature. He may incorporate the virtue of outward substances by assimilating them in the form of food. In the same way, his mind is suitably constructed for the purpose of gaining a rational knowledge of the physical world. That this is the case, you may see from the first chapter of <term>Genesis</term> <note>The first book of the Bible, detailing the creation of the world.</note>.

On the sixth day of the first year of the world, that is to say, on the 15th day of March, God created the first man, <term>Adam</term>, of red earth <note>The Hebrew name "Adam" is traditionally linked to the word "adama," meaning red earth or clay.</note>, in a field near <term>Damascus</term>, with a beautiful body, and after His own image. When <term>Adam</term> was created, he stood naked before the Lord, and with outstretched hands rendered thanks to Him, saying : 

> O Lord, Thy hands have shaped me : now remember, I pray Thee, the work of Thy hands, which Thou hast clothed with flesh, and strengthened with bones, and grant me life and loving-kindness.

So the Lord endowed <term>Adam</term> with great wisdom, and such marvellous insight that he immediately, without the help of any teacher—simply by virtue of his original righteousness—had a perfect knowledge of the <term>seven liberal arts</term> <note>The traditional curriculum of medieval education: grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note>, and of all animals, plants, stones, metals, and minerals. Nay, what is more, he had perfect understanding of the <term>Holy Trinity</term>, and of the coming of <term>Christ</term> in the flesh. Moreover, <term>Adam</term> was the Lord, King, and Ruler of all other creatures which, at the Divine bidding, were brought to him by the angel to receive their names. Thus all creatures acknowledged <term>Adam</term> as their Lord, seeing that it was he to whom the properties and virtues of all things were to be

made known. Now the wisdom, and knowledge of all things, which Adam had received, enabled him to observe the properties, the origin, and the end of all things. He noted the division and destruction, the birth and decay of physical substances. He saw that they derive their origin from the dry and the moist elements, and that they are again transmuted into the dry and the moist. Of all these things Adam took notice, and especially of that which is called the <term>first Matter</term> <note>Original: *materia prima*. In alchemy, this is the formless, original substance from which all things are created and to which they must be returned before they can be transformed.</note>. For he who knows how all things are transmuted into their <term>first Matter</term>, has no need to ask any questions. It was that which existed in the beginning before God created heaven and earth; and out of it may be made one new thing which did not exist before, a new earth, fire, water, air, Sun, Moon, Stars, in short, a new world.

As in the beginning all things were created new, so there is a kind of new creation out of the <term>first substance</term> in our <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" refers to alchemy, the practice of purifying and perfecting materials.</note>. Now although God warned Adam generally not to reveal this <term>first substance</term>—viz., the moist and the dry elements—yet He permitted him to impart the knowledge to his son Seth. Abel discovered the <term>Art</term> for himself, by the wisdom which God had given him, and inscribed an account of it on beechen tablets. He was also the first to discover the art of writing; further, he foretold the destruction of the world by the Flood, and wrote all these things on wooden tablets, and hid them in a pillar of stone, which was found, long afterwards, by the children of Israel. Thus you see that our <term>Art</term> was a secret from the beginning, and a secret it will remain to the end of the world. For this reason it is necessary carefully to consider all that is said about it, and especially the words of the Lord to Adam: for they exhibit in a succinct form the secret of the whole <term>Art</term>.

### *Explanation of the Saying of Abel.*

This saying partly explains itself, and is partly explained by what we said about God’s words to Adam. Yet I will add a few remarks concerning it. Man hath within him the virtue and efficiency of all things, whence he is called a <term>small world</term> <note>The Microcosm; the philosophical idea that the human body is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note>, and is compared to the <term>large world</term> <note>The Macrocosm; the universe as a whole.</note>, because the bones which are beneath his skin, and support his body, may be likened to the mountains and stones, his flesh to the earth, his veins to the rivers, and his small veins to the brooks which are discharged into them. The heart is the sea into which the great and small rivers flow; his hair resembles the growing herbs—and so with all other parts of his body. Again, his inward parts, such as the heart, lungs, and liver, are comparable to the <term>metals</term> <note>Alchemists traditionally linked internal organs to specific metals and planets; for example, the heart was often associated with gold and the Sun.</note>. The hairs have their head in the earth (that is, the flesh) and their roots in the air, as the Sages say, that the root of their minerals is in the air, and their head in the earth. That which ascends by <term>distillation</term> <note>The process of heating a liquid to create vapor and then condensing it back into liquid to purify it.</note> is <term>volatile</term> <note>Original: *volatile*. Refers to a substance that easily evaporates or "flies" upward when heated.</note>, and is in the air; that which remains at the bottom, and is <term>fixed</term> <note>A substance that remains stable and does not evaporate under heat.</note>, is the head, which is in the earth. Therefore, the one must always exist in conjunction with the other if it is to be effectual. Hence man may be compared to an inverted tree: for he has his roots, or his hair, in the air, while other trees have their hairs, or their roots, in the earth.

And of our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</note>, too, the Sages have justly said that it has its head in the earth, and its root in the air. This similitude has a two-fold interpretation. First, with regard to the place in which our <term>Matter</term> <note>The raw material or "subject" used to begin the alchemical work.</note> is found; secondly, with regard to the dissolution and second conjunction of the <term>Stone</term>. For when our <term>Stone</term> rises upward in the <term>alembic</term> <note>A specialized vessel used for distillation, consisting of a boiling pot and a cooling cap with a spout.</note>, it has its root in the air; but if it would regain its virtue and strength, it must once more return to its earth, and then it has its head and perfect potency in the earth. Hence our <term>Stone</term>, too, is not inaptly denominated a small world; it is called the mountain of mountains, from which our ore is derived, since it is evolved from the first substance in a way analogous to that in which the great world was created. Know that if you bury anything in the earth, and it rots, as food is digested in the human body, and the gross is separated from the subtle, and that which is fetid from that which is pure, then that which is pure is the <term>first Matter</term> <note>The primordial, formless substance from which all things originate.</note> which has been set free by decay. If you understand this, you know the true <term>Art</term> <note>Alchemy, often called "The Royal Art" or "The Sacred Art."</note>. But keep it to yourself, and cast not pearls before swine; for the vulgar regard our <term>Art</term> with ignorant contempt.

The volatile becomes fixed, and the fixed volatile, by dissolution and <term>coagulation</term>, and both assume, first a white, and then a red colour. ### *Explanation of the Saying of Isindrus.* <note>Isindrus is a name frequently appearing in the *Turba Philosophorum*, an influential early alchemical text. He is likely a fictionalized or corrupted version of an ancient Greek philosopher.</note>

Good Heavens! How skilfully the **Sages** <note>The "Sages" or "Philosophers" are the historical and legendary figures who were believed to have successfully discovered the secrets of alchemy.</note> have contrived to conceal this matter. It would surely have been far better if they had abstained from writing altogether. For the extreme obscurity of their style has overwhelmed thousands in ruin, and plunged them into the deepest poverty, especially those who set about this task without even the slightest knowledge of **Nature**, or of the requirements of our **Art**. What the **Sages** write is strictly true; but you cannot understand it unless you are already initiated in the secrets of this **Art**. Yea, even if you were a *Doctor of the Doctors*, and a *Light of the World*, you would be able to see no meaning in their words without this knowledge. They have written, but you are none the wiser. They half wished to communicate the secret to their posterity; but a jealous feeling prevented them from doing so in plain language. To the uninitiated reader these words of **Isindrus** must appear nothing short of nonsense: 

> "Great is the **air**, because the air corrects the thing, if it is thin or thick, hot or cold." 

But the **Sage** means that when it ascends with the water, it is hot air, for fire and air bear our **Stone** like secret fire concealed therein, and the water which ascends from the earth, by that ascension becomes air, and thin; and when it descends, it descends into water which contains fire; thus the earth is purified, seeing that the water takes [the] fire with it into the earth. For the **fire** is the **Soul**, and the **Moon** the **Spirit** <note>In this symbolic system, the "Soul" (Fire/Sun) provides the active life-force, while the "Spirit" (Water/Moon/Mercury) acts as the mediating link between the soul and the physical body.</note>. Therefore, the **air** is great, because it bears with it water and fire, and imparts them to all things, though thereby (by this loss of water) itself becomes cold. Then the air becomes thick, when with its fire it is <term>transmuted</term> <note>Transmutation is the fundamental alchemical change of one substance into another.</note> into the body, and thus the air corrects the thing by its thickness. For it bears out our **Stone** as it carries it in, and purifies it both in its ascent and in its descent. In the same way air purifies all things that grow

This temperate warmth, which resembles that of a bath <note>Likely referring to the *balneum Mariae* or water bath, a method of providing consistent, gentle heat.</note>, brings the Sun and Moon together. Thus I have, by the grace of God, interpreted to you the parabolic saying of **Isindrus**.
