## *Explanation of the Saying of Anaxagoras.*
<note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that "mind" (Nous) was the initiating force of the cosmos. Alchemists often claimed ancient philosophers as secret practitioners of their craft.</note>

God has existed from the very beginning of all things. He is compared to light and fire, and He may be compared to the latter in His very essence, because fire is the primary principle of all things that are visible and that grow. In the same way, the first principle of our **Art** <note>In this context, "the Art" refers specifically to Alchemy.</note> is fire. Heat drives Nature to perform its work, and within that work, the **Body**, **Spirit**, and **Soul** are revealed—which correspond to earth and water. Earth represents the Body, oil represents the Soul, and water represents the Spirit. All of this is achieved through Divine goodness and **lenity** <note>original: "lenitas" — here meaning gentleness or a mild, non-corrosive quality</note>, without which Nature can accomplish nothing. As the Sage says: "God's lenity rules all things; and beneath the thickness of the earth, after creation, are revealed lenity and **integrity** <note>original: "integritas" — referring to the wholeness or purity of the essential substance.</note>."

This means that if the earth is separated from the water and then dissolved into oil and water, the oil represents integrity and the water represents lenity. The water provides the soul to both the oil and the body. The body receives nothing except what is granted to it by heaven—that is, by the water—and this water is found beneath the oil, just as the oil is found beneath the earth. For fire is a subtle thing; it floats upward from the earth along with subtle waters and remains hidden within the earth. Now, the oil, air, and earth are all purified by their own spirit. Therefore, the oil acts as the "integrity" within the body, while the spirit acts as "lenity."

In the first stage of the operation, the spirit descends to the body and restores its life. Even though the oil is pure and stays with the body, it cannot help the body without the aid of the spirit; the body undergoes great struggle and distress while it is being dissolved and purified. Then, the "thickness of the earth" is transformed into a thin, refined substance like water or oil, and thus "lenity" becomes visible in the body. The body becomes so mild and soft that it changes into water or oil, even though it was completely dry before. Therefore, oil is seen within the earth; this is the richness or "fatness" and the life of the water—a union of fire, air, and water.

Now, give this water to the body to "drink," and the body will be restored to life. Although these three elements have risen up from the earth, their power remains with the body, as you can see by dissolving it into oil and water. However, the oil cannot work without the spirit, nor can the spirit produce results without the oil and the body. Therefore, they must be joined together. All "lenity" and "integrity" are finally seen in the body when it is fully transformed into the **white and red** <note>The "White" (Albedo) and "Red" (Rubedo) are the final two major stages of the Alchemical Great Work, signifying purification and total perfection/transmutation.</note>.

## *Explanation of the Opinion of Pythagoras.*
<note>Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BCE) was a Greek philosopher. Alchemists often attributed their secrets to him, believing that his theories on numbers and the harmony of the spheres mirrored the processes of their Art.</note>

This Sage asks what it is that can be touched, and yet remains unseen. He means that the substance prepared by our **Art** <note>The "Art" is the standard term for the practice of Alchemy.</note> is <term>one thing</term> <note>The "One Thing" refers to the *Prima Materia*, the single, fundamental substance from which the Alchemist creates the Stone.</note> which is both tangible and invisible. That is to say, it is felt, but not seen, and the way it operates is hidden. He who knows the substance but does not understand its operation still knows nothing as he should. This "one thing," which alone is useful for our purposes, comes from a certain dark place where it cannot be seen. Neither its operation nor its power is known to anyone except the **initiated** <note>Those who have been taught the secret wisdom of alchemy.</note>. 

A great mystery is also hidden in the **Matter** <note>The physical starting material for the alchemical work.</note> itself: namely, air and fire, or the Sun, the Moon, and the Stars. These are concealed within it and yet are invisible, as the Sage says: "What is not seen or known is only heaven." That which is felt but not seen is earth. Earth, says the Sage, is the "thickness" or "body" found at the bottom of the Matter; it has built up within the Matter and can be felt and known. 

By the words, "that which is between heaven and earth, which is not known" (meaning, in the world), the Sage means that the Matter of our Stone is found in the <term>small world</term> <note>original: "microcosmus" — the belief that the human being is a miniature version of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note>. It is not found in rocks and mountains, or simply in the dirt, but between heaven and earth—that is, in the air. 

Again, when he says that "in it are senses and the whole, such as smell, taste, hearing, and touch," he is teaching us that in human nature there is a complete mind and perception; for man can know, feel, and understand. He also teaches us how our Stone is to be found—specifically through the five senses:

*   **By sight:** Because the Matter of the Stone can be thick, or thin and clear, and it changes color from black to white and finally to red.
*   **By smell:** Because when its impurities are purged away, it gives off a most sweet fragrance.
*   **By taste:** Because it is bitter and unpleasant at first, but later becomes most pleasant.
*   **By touch:** Because that sense allows us to tell the difference between hard and soft, thick and thin, water and earth. It also lets us distinguish the different stages of the work: <term>distillation</term>, <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the "rotting" or breaking down of the substance</note>, <term>dissolution</term>, <term>coagulation</term>, <term>fermentation</term>, and <term>injection</term> <note>the final stage where the Stone is projected onto base metals to transform them</note>.

The different steps of the task are perceived through the senses, and the work should be completed within forty-six days.

### *Exposition of the Saying of Parmenides.*
<note>Parmenides was a Greek philosopher (5th century BCE) who argued that reality is a single, unchanging substance. Alchemists adopted him as a forefather who understood the "One Thing."</note>

Jealous Sages <note>The "Jealousy of the Sages" (*invidia philosophorum*) is a common alchemical trope explaining why authors wrote in riddles: they were "jealous" of their secrets and did not want them falling into the hands of the unworthy.</note> have named many waters and metals and stones, simply for the purpose of deceiving you; herein the philosophers would warn us that they have used secrecy, lest the whole mystery should be manifested before all the world. The fault, however, lies not with the Sages so much as with the ignorance of their readers. The Sages name it a stone; and so it is a stone, which is dug up from our mine. They speak of metals; and there are such things as metals liquefied from our ore. They speak of water; but our water we obtain from our own spring. The red and white <term>sulphur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulphur represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of matter.</note> they refer to are obtained from our air. ### Explanation of the Saying of Lucas <note>Lucas is a traditional figure often cited in alchemical literature, specifically as one of the participants in the "Assembly of the Philosophers" (*Turba Philosophorum*).</note>.

By the <term>living water of the Moon</term> <note>A term for the "mercury" or the animating spirit of the matter after it has been purified.</note> this Sage means our water, which is twofold. The distilled water is the Moon; the Sun, or fire, is hidden in it, and is the Father of all things. Hence it is compared to a man, because the Sun <note>The active, masculine principle associated with heat and spirit.</note> is in the water. It is also called living water; for the life of the dead body is hidden in the water. It is the water of the Moon, because the Sun is the Father and the Moon the Mother. Hence, also, they are regarded as husband and wife. The Body is the Moon, or Mother, and the distilled water, or male principle, rises upward from the earth; and for that reason is sometimes called Moon. For it is the water of the Moon, or Body. It has left the Body, and must enter it again before our <term>Art</term> <note>The "Sacred Art" of alchemy.</note> can be perfected. Hence the Body, or Moon, has well been designated the female principle, and the water, or Sun, the male principle, for reasons which have been set forth at length in this book.

Again, when the Sage says, “Coagulate <note>To "coagulate" means to solidify or "fix" a spirit into a stable physical form.</note> it after our fashion,” those last three words mean that the body must receive its spirit to drink gradually, and little by little, until it recovers its life, and health, and strength, which takes place by means of the same gentle heat which digests food in the stomach, and matures fruit in its place. For it is our custom to eat, drink, and live in gentle warmth. By this regimen our body is preserved, and all that is foul and unprofitable is driven out from our body. According to the same fashion of gentle <term>coction</term> <note>From the Latin *coctio*, meaning "cooking" or "digestion." It refers to the steady application of heat to mature the substance.</note>, all that is fetid and black <note>This refers to the *nigredo*, or "blackness," the initial stage of decay and purification in the alchemical work.</note> is gradually purged out of our <term>Stone</term>. <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the work.</note> For when the Sage says “after *our fashion*,” he wishes to teach you that the preparation of the Stone bears a strict analogy to the processes of the human body. That the chemical development of our substance is internal, and caused by the operation of Nature and of its four elements, the Sage indicates

### *Exposition of the Saying of Ethelius <note>Ethelius is a legendary figure cited in the "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers), an influential early alchemical text.</note>.*

He says: “Heat our Stone until it shines like dazzling marble; then it becomes great, and a mystic Stone; for sulphur added to sulphur preserves it on account of its fitness.” That is to say: When the moist and the dry have been separated, the dry which lies at the bottom, and is called our Stone, is as black as a raven. It must be subjected to the coction <note>A term for slow boiling, digestion, or heating.</note> of our water (separated from it), until it loses its blackness, and becomes as white as dazzling marble. Then it is the mystic Stone which by coction has been transmuted into fixed mercury <note>Mercury that has been rendered stable under heat, so it no longer evaporates.</note> with the blessing of God. The Stone is mystic, or secret, because it is found in a secret place, in an universally despised substance where no one looks for the greatest treasure of the world. Hence it may well be called THE HIDDEN STONE. By the joining of two sulphurs and their mutual preservation, he means that though, after the separation of spirit and body, there seem to be two substances, yet, in reality, there is only one substance; so the body which is below is “sulphur,” and the spirit which is above is also “sulphur.” <note>In alchemical theory, Sulphur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of matter.</note> Now, when the spirit returns to the body, one sulphur is added to another; and they are bound together by a mutual fitness, since the body cannot be without the spirit, nor the spirit without the body. ## *Explanation of the Saying of Pythagoras.*

You have good cause to wonder at the great variety of ways in which the <term>Sages</term> have expressed the same thing. Nevertheless, their descriptions apply only to one <term>Matter</term>, and their sayings refer only to a single substance. For when our <term>Sage</term> <note>Referring here to Pythagoras, whom medieval alchemists claimed as one of their own.</note> says, “We give you directions concerning these things: We tell you that it is <term>dry water</term>, like the <term>water of the Moon</term>, which you have prepared,” he means that we <term>Sages</term> must give directions, according to the best of our ability. If those directions, rightly understood, do not answer the purpose, you may justly charge us with fraud and imposture. But if you fail through not taking our meaning, you must blame your own unspeakable stupidity, which follows the letter, but not the spirit of our directions. 

When the <term>Sage</term> further says that it must drink its own water, he would teach you that after the separation of the dry from the moist, the water extracted from the body is the right water, and the <term>water of the Moon</term>, prepared by <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The process of breaking down a substance through heat and moisture to allow it to "die" and be reborn.</note> and <term>distillation</term> <note>The process of purifying a liquid by heating it into vapor and then condensing it back into a liquid.</note>. This extracted water is regarded as the <term>male principle</term>, and the earth, or body, as the <term>female principle</term>. The water of the husband must now be joined in <term>conjugal union</term> <note>Often called the "Chemical Wedding," this is the symbolic marriage of the active (male) and passive (female) aspects of the matter.</note> to that of the wife; the body must, at intervals, drink of its own prepared water, and become ever purer, the more it drinks, till it turns most wonderfully white. Then it is called “<term>our calx</term>” <note>original: "calx." A powder produced by roasting or chemically treating a metal or mineral.</note>, and you must pour the water of our

### *Explanation of the Emerald Table of Hermes.*

<note>The Emerald Tablet (*Tabula Smaragdina*) is a legendary foundational text of alchemy, said to contain the secrets of the universe and the Great Work in a few cryptic lines.</note>

<term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the "Thrice-Great Hermes," a mythical figure combining the traits of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, regarded as the father of alchemy.</note> is right in saying that our Art is true, and has been rightly handed down by the <term>Sages</term> <note>The "Wise Men" or masters of alchemy who have successfully achieved the Great Work.</note>; all doubts concerning it have arisen through false interpretation of the mystic language of the philosophers. But, since they are loth to confess their own ignorance, their readers prefer to say that the words of the Sages are imposture and falsehood. The fault really lies with the ignorant reader, who does not understand the style of the Philosophers. If, in the interpretation of our books, they would suffer themselves to be guided by the teaching of Nature, rather than by their own foolish notions, they would not miss the mark so hopelessly. By the words which follow: "That which is above is also that which is below," he describes the <term>Matter of our Art</term> <note>The "Prima Materia" or the essential starting substance of the alchemical process.</note>, which, though *one*, is divided into two things, the **volatile water** which rises upward, and the **earth** which lies at the bottom, and becomes <term>fixed</term> <note>A substance that is stable and does not evaporate or change when exposed to heat.</note>. When bodies become spirits, and spirits bodies, your work is finished; for then that which rises upward and that which descends downward become *one* body. Therefore the Sage says that that which is above is that which is below, meaning that, after having been separated into two substances (from being one substance), they are again joined together into one substance, *i.e.*, an union which can never be dissolved, and possesses such virtue and efficacy that it can do in one moment what the <term>Sun</term> <note>In alchemy, the Sun often represents gold or the celestial source of heat and life that matures metals in the earth over centuries.</note> cannot accomplish in a thousand years. And this miracle is wrought by a thing which is despised and rejected by the multitude. ### PREFACE.

We may justly wonder that the <term>Sages</term> <note>The "Wise Men" or experienced alchemists of history.</note> who have written about this most precious and secret <term>Art</term> <note>The "Sacred Art" or "Hermetic Art," another name for alchemy.</note>, have thought it necessary to invent so many occult and allegorical expressions, by means of which our <term>Art</term> is concealed not only from the unworthy, but from earnest and diligent students of the truth. Foolish persons, indeed, who read their books, and hear of the riches and all the other good things which this <term>Art</term> affords, experience a pleasant tickling sensation in their ears, and straightway behold visions of themselves sitting on golden thrones, and commanding all the treasures of the universe; they fancy that the <term>Art</term> can be learned in the twinkling of an eye, soon come to regard themselves as great Doctors, and are unable to conceive the possibility of their making a mistake, or being led astray by the <term>Sages</term>. Much less are they aware that it has always been the custom of the <term>philosophers</term> to conceal the fundamental facts of this <term>Art</term>, and to reveal them to their own sons and disciples only in sententious allegorical sayings. They want to perform the works of Nature, but they refuse to watch the hand of the one they claim to imitate. Yet our <term>Art</term> has a true foundation in natural facts. We must extract this seed from perfect, pure, and mature bodies if we hope to reach our goal. Now, so that you may more easily gain this knowledge, I have written the following treatise concerning the first principle of Nature and the creation and generation of man—which any student of our <term>Magistery</term> should carefully read, think over, and digest. # A TRACT OF GREAT PRICE

## CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE.

### CHAPTER I.

All worldly things derive their origin, their existence, and their essence from the earth, through the passage of time. Their specific properties are determined by the outward and inward influences of the stars and planets (such as the Sun and the Moon), and of the <term>four qualities</term> <note>The "four qualities" are heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—the fundamental building blocks of matter in ancient science.</note> of the elements. From these combined circumstances arise the unique forms and specific substances of all growing, fixed, and reproducing things, according to the natural order established by the Most High at the beginning of the world. 

The metals, therefore, derive their origin from the earth and are specifically composed of the <term>four qualities</term>, or the properties of the <term>four elements</term> <note>The four elements are Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>; their unique metallic character is imprinted upon them by the influences of the stars and planets. We are informed of this by Aristotle in the fourth book of his *Meteorology* <note>original: "Meteor." This refers to Aristotle’s "Meteorologica," a foundational text for medieval science that explained how minerals and metals form underground.</note>, where he says that <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Also known as mercury. In alchemy, it was believed to be the "mother" or "soul" of all metals.</note> is the common substance of all metals. 

The first matter in Nature, as we mentioned before, is the substance representing a specific gathering of the <term>four elements</term>, which the Sages <note>A term often used to describe the great alchemists and philosophers of the past.</note> call <term>Mercury</term>, or <term>quicksilver</term>. However, this <term>quicksilver</term> is still imperfect because of its coarse and earthy sulphurous nature—which makes it catch fire too easily—and because of its excess of watery parts. These have all been gathered from the <term>four elements</term> by the movements of the heavenly planets. This substance is made of a hot, sulphurous earth and a watery essence, in such a way that the Sages have named it <term>imperfect sulphur</term> <note>In alchemy, "Sulphur" represents the principle of combustibility and structure, but in its raw, "imperfect" state, it contains impurities that must be removed to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

<summary>This opening chapter explains the alchemical origin of metals, asserting that they are formed from the four elements and planetary influences, with "Mercury" acting as the foundational but imperfect substance of all metallic matter.</summary>

Now, since Nature is always striving to attain perfection, and to reach the goal set before her by the Creator of all things, she is continually at work upon the qualities of the <term>four elements</term> <note>The four elements are Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. Alchemists believed that everything in the physical world was composed of these in varying proportions.</note> of each substance; and so stirs up and rouses the inward action of the elements by the accidental heat of the Sun, and by natural warmth, that there arises a kind of vapour or steam in the veins of the earth. This vapour cannot make its way out, but is closed in; in penetrating through fat, earthy, oily, and impure <term>sulphureous</term> <note>Alchemical "Sulphur" is one of the Three Primes (Tria Prima). It represents the "soul" of a substance, its inflammability, and its oily, masculine quality.</note> substances it attracts to itself more or less of these foreign and external impurities. This is the reason that there are seen in it so great a variety of colours before it attains to purity and its own proper colour.

Those mineral and metallic substances which contain the largest proportion of efficacious <term>sulphureous</term> and <term>mercurial</term> <note>Alchemical "Mercury" represents the "spirit" of a substance, its fluidity, and its metallic volatility.</note> vapour are the best; and each quality of the <term>four elements</term> has its own peculiar operation and transmuting influence in such a conglomeration of various substances—their action being roused by the <term>sulphur</term> of the earth and the outward heat of the Sun. Through these agencies the <term>Matter</term> <note>The "First Matter" or *Prima Materia*, the foundational substance required to begin the Great Work of alchemy.</note> is often dissolved and coagulated, till that which is pure, or impure, is borne upward; and this is the work not of a few years, but of a great length of time. Nature has to purge away the peculiar characteristics of all other metals before she can make <term>gold</term>; as you may see by the fact that different kinds of metal are found in the same metallic vein. This fact may be explained in the following manner. When the <term>sulphureous</term> and <term>mercurial</term> vapours ascend, they are mixed, and united by <term>coction</term> <note>original: "coctio." A process of slow ripening or "digestion" through steady heat, which alchemists believed happened naturally inside the Earth over centuries.</note>, with the aforesaid substance.

If those <term>sulphureous</term> vapours are earthy, thick, and impure, and the heat of the Sun, or their own natural heat, have too sudden and violent an effect, the substance hardens, with all its <term>sulphureous</term> impurities, before it can be purged of its grossness, and it becomes more like metallic <term>sulphur</term>. If the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury in its liquid metallic state.</note> is hardened, the whole mass takes the form of some metal, according to the influence of the particular planet with which it is penetrated. For Nature first combines the <term>four elements</term> into some substance or body, which then receives its specific properties through the influence of some planet <note>In alchemical cosmology, each of the seven classical metals was governed by a celestial body: Gold by the Sun, Silver by the Moon, Iron by Mars, Mercury by Mercury, Tin by Jupiter, Copper by Venus, and Lead by Saturn.</note>. Such is the origin of <term>copper</term>, <term>tin</term>, <term>lead</term>, <term>iron</term>, and <term>quicksilver</term>. But it is not essential that I should here describe at length the specific—

composition and distinctive properties of each of the <term>imperfect metals</term> <note>In alchemical theory, the "imperfect" or "base" metals typically include lead, tin, copper, and iron. Nature, as I said, is ceaselessly at work upon these imperfect metals, purging and separating the pure quicksilver from the impure, and the pure sulphur from the impure, until all their grossness is removed, and they become what God designed that they should be, *viz.*, gold. But if these vapours float upward in their original pure condition, with their inward, pure, and subtle earth, without becoming mixed with gross, earthy, and sulphureous alloy, and if they succeed in breaking forth into the open air, before they become hardened into a sulphureous mass, they remain quicksilver and are not changed into any metal.

If, however, this pure quicksilver floats upward in a pure mineral earth, without any gross alloy, it is hardened into the pure and white sulphur of Nature by being subjected to a very moderate degree of gentle heat, and at length assumes the specific form of silver. Like all the other metals it may still be developed into gold, if it remain under the influence of its natural heat. But if the same pure, unalloyed quicksilver be subjected to a higher degree of natural heat, it is transmuted into the pure *red* sulphur of Nature, and becomes gold without first passing through the stage of silver. In this form it remains, because gold is the highest possible stage of metallic development.

Quicksilver is the mother of all metals, on account of its coldness and moistness <note>Alchemy inherited the Aristotelian qualities; Mercury was associated with the qualities of Water (Cold and Moist).</note>; and if it be once purified and cleansed of all foreign matter it cannot be mixed any more with grossness of any kind, neither can it be changed back into an imperfect metal. For Nature does not undo her work, and that which has once become perfectly pure can never become impure again. Sulphur, on the other hand, is the father of all metals, on account of its heat and dryness <note>Sulphur was associated with the qualities of Fire (Hot and Dry).</note>. In the following chapter we shall refer to this difference, and speak more in detail about quicksilver.

## CHAPTER III.

But we must now proceed to say a few words about the method of preparing this <term>Medicine</term>, by which the imperfection is removed from imperfect metals through the mediation of perfect mercury, and the mode of gold and silver is developed in them.

I find that the writings of the Sages are all about gold, silver, and quicksilver, which, it is said, must be reduced to the form which they wore before they became metals; that is to say, the form which they wore, perhaps, some thousands of years ago. But the operation of Nature is progressive, not retrogressive. Hence it is a great mistake to suppose that the work of Nature can be reversed by dissolution in <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Latin for "strong water," refers to nitric acid, a powerful corrosive used by early chemists to dissolve silver and other metals.</note>, or by the amalgamation of gold or silver and quicksilver. For if the metal be plunged in a solvent, if water be distilled from it, or if quicksilver be sublimed from it, it still remains the same metal that it was before. The specific properties of a metal cannot be destroyed so as to obtain the first substance. <note>The author is arguing against "vulgar" chemistry; simply dissolving a metal doesn't return it to its "First Matter" or primordial state.</note> Yet Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher Aristotle was the primary authority for alchemical theory, specifically his ideas that all matter is composed of the same fundamental ingredients and can therefore be changed.</note> says that metals cannot be changed unless they are reduced to their original substance.

## CHAPTER V.

Again, we read in the books of the Sages that <term>quicksilver</term> and <term>mercury</term> are the original substance of all metals. These words are true in a certain sense. But by many beginners they are supposed to mean ordinary <term>quicksilver</term>. Such an interpretation, however, makes nonsense of the dictum of the Sages. For ordinary <term>quicksilver</term> is an imperfect metal, and itself derived from the original substance of all metals. The Sages, indeed, say little about the *origin* of their <term>mercury</term>; but that is exactly because they use the name of <term>mercury</term>, or <term>sulphur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulphur represented the active, masculine, or combustible principle of a substance.</note>, for the first substance of their perfect metals. If common <term>mercury</term> were not a metal, there would be no metal corresponding to the celestial influence of the planet <term>Mercury</term>, as gold and silver receive their specific properties from the influence of the <term>Sun</term> <note>In the alchemical worldview, Gold was linked to the Sun (Sol).</note> and <term>Moon</term> <note>Silver was linked to the Moon (Luna).</note>. ### CHAPTER VI.

Again, the <term>Sages</term> <note>A term for the ancient and respected masters of alchemy.</note> affirm that quicksilver, or mercury, is the spirit of the specific nature of metals, collected out of the four elements by the influence of the <term>Planets</term> <note>Alchemists believed each of the seven metals was governed by a celestial body: Gold by the Sun, Silver by the Moon, Mercury by Mercury, etc.</note>, and the operation of Nature in the earth—and that from it is developed either gold, silver, or some other of seven metals, according to the peculiar effects of the predominant planetary influence.

Hence ignorant alchemists have supposed that all this is true of the common quicksilver, because it <term>amalgamates</term> <note>To alloy or blend mercury with another metal.</note> with all metals, and is soft and volatile. But why should its <term>volatile</term> <note>The tendency of a substance to evaporate or turn into vapor when heated.</note> properties prove it to be no metal? According to this definition, we might deny the metallic character of tin, lead, and other metals, because they do not remain <term>fixed</term> <note>Stable in fire; a "fixed" metal does not evaporate or change when exposed to intense heat.</note> in a fierce fire—though one can stand a greater degree of heat than another. If, again, any substance is to be called the first substance of metals because of the facility with which it amalgamates with them, copper would have a better claim to be so regarded, since it enters into a closer union with gold and silver than mercury, and shares both their <term>fusible</term> <note>Capable of being melted.</note> and malleable nature. But that is no final union, for it admits of separation; and quicksilver may, with the greatest ease, be separated from the metals with which it has amalgamated. A true union of metals can only take place in the <term>original substance</term> <note>The "Prima Materia," the foundational matter that contains the potential to become any metal.</note> which is common to all. We do find amalgams of three, or even more metals; but then this union was consummated in the first substance, which is *one*, and the whole amalgam would have been developed into gold, if its natural growth had not been retarded by gross, <term>sulphureous</term>, <term>arsenical</term> <note>Related to arsenic; these were considered "poisonous" or "clogging" impurities in the natural growth of metals.</note>, and earthy impurity, which is found among metals when purified. ## CHAPTER VII.

It is clear, then, that the final union of metals, or their perfection, cannot be attained by the mingling of any specific metals; that the metallic substance becomes useless for our purpose, as soon as it assumes a **specific form** <note>Once a metal becomes "lead" or "tin," it is considered "fixed" or "frozen" in that state, making it difficult to revert to the original liquid-like "Matter" required for the Work.</note>; but that, at the same time, all metals have a common origin, or **Matter**, which is one thing, flowing out by the operation of Nature, who ever desires the most perfect form which her own essence and her condition will admit. And this is the form of gold, highest and best of all that belong to the **metallic mode**. If, then, the purest form of this substance which it is possible for <term>Art</term> to prepare with the help of Nature, be added to the imperfect metals, then it overcomes what is impure in these, for it is not the impure, but the pure matter which is like unto it. But you must not suppose that this power belongs to **common gold**; common gold has its own specific form, which it is unable to impart to other metals. The power of gold is sufficient only for preserving its own excellence; but our prepared substance is much better and more honourable than gold, and has power to do that which gold cannot do, viz., to change the common matter of all metals into gold.

...how it may truly be affirmed that our <term>Art</term> <note>The secret practice of alchemy, often called the "Great Work."</note> is concerned with **quicksilver**, **silver**, and **gold**, or with **quicksilver** and **sulphur**, and in what sense <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "mercurius"</note> is the spirit of the metals. I will first speak about quicksilver, and at once premise that this word is not here taken to mean that common quicksilver <note>Common liquid mercury (quicksilver) found in nature, as opposed to the "Philosophical Mercury" sought by alchemists.</note> which is one of the metals, but the **first substance** of all the metals, and itself no specific metal at all. For a metal must have derived its distinctive properties through <term>planetary influences</term> <note>The belief that the seven metals were formed in the earth by the rays and movements of the seven planets (e.g., the Sun for gold, the Moon for silver).</note>; nor can any one metal be the first substance of all metals. This quicksilver is neither too hot, nor too cold, nor too moist, nor too dry; but it is a well-tempered mingling of all four. When perfectly matured quicksilver is subjected to external heat, operating thereon, it is not burned, but escapes in a volatile essence. Hence it may well be called by the philosophers a **spirit**, or a swift, and winged, and indestructible **soul**.

So long as it is palpable and visible it is also called **body**; when subjected to external cold it is congealed into a fixed body, and then these three—**body, soul, and spirit**—are one thing, and contain the properties of all the four elements. That outward part which is moist and cold is called *water*, or quicksilver; on account of its inward heat it is called *air*; if without it appear hot and dry it is *fire*, or sulphur; and on account of its internal coldness it is also styled *earth*. In this way quicksilver and sulphur are the original substance of all metals; but, of course, I do not mean that the substance is prepared by mixing common sulphur and quicksilver. The <term>sulphur and quicksilver of the Sages</term> <note>The "philosophical" versions of these elements, which were viewed as spiritual or idealized principles rather than the raw chemicals found in a shop.</note> are one and the same thing, which is first of the nature of quicksilver, or moist and watery, and is then, by constant <term>coction</term> <note>original: "coctio"; a process of steady, gentle heating or "digestion" used to mature the chemical substance.</note>, transmuted into the nature of sulphur, which may most justly be described as dry and igneous.

But I wish to confine my discourse to the quicksilver and sulphur of the philosophers, from which all metals derive their origin; and it is, according to the Sages, a heavy, earthy water, mixed with very subtle white earth, and subjected to natural coction until the moist and the dry elements have become united and coagulated into one body—through the perfect mutual...

For in its first stage the substance resembles <term>quicksilver</term>, which is sublimed by gentle natural heat, and purified in the veins of the rocks in the form of a pure vapour, as we explained above. To it we now add silver and gold, and that for the following reason, because we cannot find anywhere else in any one thing the metallic power needed for rousing the <term>sulphur</term> of the <term>quicksilver</term>, and coagulating it <note>Changing it from a liquid or vaporous state into a solid.</note>, except in gold and silver. For the Sage cannot prepare our <term>quicksilver</term> unless it be first removed from the earth, and separated from the potency of its natural surroundings; and all these natural influences can be artificially supplied only by the addition of gold and silver. Our <term>Art</term>, then, has to find a substitute for those natural forces in the precious metals. By them alone it is able to fix the volatile properties of our <term>quicksilver</term>, for in them alone do we find the powers and influences which are indispensable to our chemical process.

You should also bear in mind that the silver should be applied to our <term>quicksilver</term> before the gold, because the <term>quicksilver</term> is volatile, and cannot with safety be subjected all at once to great heat. Silver has the power of stirring up the inherent <term>sulphur</term> of the <term>quicksilver</term>, whereby it is coagulated into the form of the <term>Remedy</term> <note>Another name for the Philosopher's Stone or Elixir.</note> for transmuting metals into silver; and this coagulation is brought about by the gentle heat of the silver. Gold requires a much higher degree of heat, and if gold were added to the <term>quicksilver</term> before the silver, the greater degree of heat would at once change the <term>quicksilver</term> into a <term>red sulphur</term> <note>Representing the final, "solar" stage of the alchemical process (the Red Work or Rubedo).</note>, which, however, would be of no use for the purpose of making gold, because it would have lost its essential moisture; and our <term>Art</term> requires that the <term>quicksilver</term> should be first coagulated by means of silver into <term>white sulphur</term> <note>Representing the intermediate "lunar" stage of the process (the White Work or Albedo).</note>,

## CHAPTER X.

The <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Also known as Mercury. Alchemists distinguished between "common" quicksilver and their "Philosophical Quicksilver," which was a purified essence.</note> of the Sages has no power to transmute imperfect metals, until it has absorbed the essential qualities of gold and silver; for in itself it is no metal at all, and if it is to impart the spirit, the colour, and the hardness of gold and silver, it must first receive them itself. It is with the <term>first substance</term> <note>The "Prima Materia," the original, chaotic matter that contains the potential for all forms.</note> of metals as it is with water. If saffron is dissolved in water, the water is coloured with it, and if mixed with other water, imparts to that water, too, the colour of saffron. Unless the first substance, or <term>quicksilver</term>, is tinged with silver and gold, and coagulated by their efficacy, it cannot impart any colour, or coagulate the (water or) first substance which is latent in the imperfect metals <note>Metals like lead, tin, or iron, which were considered "unripe" or "diseased" versions of gold.</note>. For it is essentially a spirit, and volatile <note>Easily evaporated or changed; in alchemy, a "spirit" is a substance that can fly away from the fire unless it is "fixed."</note>, and if it be added to imperfect metals, it cannot act upon their water, or undeveloped first-substance, because that is partly fixed by their coagulated sulphur. But if the first-substance has been fixed by means of gold and silver, it has become a fixed and indestructible water; and, if added to imperfect metals, takes up into its own nature their first substance, or water, and mingles with it. By this means all that is combustible and impure in them is driven off by the fire. And herein is the saying true, which was uttered by the <term>Sage Haly</term> <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer and alchemist whose works were highly influential in Medieval Europe.</note>: 

> “The spirit (*i.e.*, quicksilver) is not coagulated <note>Original Latin: *coagulare*. Meaning to thicken or solidify a liquid into a solid state.</note>, unless the body (*i.e.*, gold and silver) be first dissolved.” 

For then gold and silver become spiritual, flowing, capable of being assimilated by the common substance of all metals, and of imparting to it their own metallic strength and potency. And even though this new substance be fusible in the fire, yet, when it cools again, it still remains what it was, nor is it ever again converted into a permanent spiritual substance. It is the quicksilver, then, that constitutes the chief strength and efficacy of our <term>Art</term> <note>Alchemy was commonly referred to as "The Art" or "The Royal Art."</note>; and he that has no quicksilver is without the very seed of gold and silver from which they grow in the earth.

# EPILOGUE.

We have sufficiently explained that <term>quicksilver</term> <note>In Latin, *argentum vivum*. In alchemy, this is the fundamental fluid principle required for the "Great Work."</note> is the first substance of the metals, without which no metal can become perfect, either in Nature or in our Art. But we do not yet know where to look for it, and where to find it. This is the great secret of the Sages, which they are always so careful to veil under dark words that scarcely one in many thousands is thought worthy to find the <term>philosophical Mercury</term> <note>A purified, spiritualized form of mercury, distinct from the common liquid metal, believed to be the essential "soul" of the metals.</note>. Many things have been written about it; but I will quote the words of *one* philosopher which I consider as the most helpful: In the beginning, he says, God created the earth plain, simple, rich, and very fertile, without stones, sand, rocks, hills, or valleys; it is the influences of the planets which have now covered it with stones, rocks, and mountains, and filled it with rare things of various colours, *i.e.*, the ores of the <term>seven metals</term> <note>The seven metals known to the ancient world, each associated with a celestial body: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Copper (Venus), Iron (Mars), Tin (Jupiter), Lead (Saturn), and Quicksilver (Mercury).</note>; and by these means the earth has entirely lost its original form, and that through the following causes:—

First, the earth which was created rich, great, deep, wide, and broad, was, through the daily operation of the Sun’s rays, penetrated to her very centre with a fervent, bubbling, vaporous heat. For the earth in herself is cold and saturated with the moisture of water. At length the vapours which were formed in this way in the heart of the earth became so strong and powerful as to seek to force a way out into the open air, and thus, instead of effecting their object, threw up hills and hillocks, or, as it were, bubbles on the face of the earth. And since in those places where mountains were formed the heat of the Sun must have been most powerful, and the earthy moisture rich and most plentiful, it is there that we find the most precious metals. Where the earth remained plain, this steam did not succeed in raising up mountains; it escaped, and the earth, being deprived of its moisture, was hardened into rocks. Where the earth was poor, soft, and thin, it is now covered with sand and little stones, because it never had much moisture, and, having been deprived of the little it possessed, has now become sandy and dry, and incapable of retaining moisture. No earth was changed into rocks that was not rich, viscous, and well saturated with moisture. For when the heat of the Sun has sucked up

# THE BOOK OF ALZE.

**D**o not, gentle Reader, find fault with me for speaking first about the Moon, then about the Sun, and the other planets, and only in the third place about our most excellent <term>Medicine</term><note>In alchemy, the "Medicine" refers to the Philosopher’s Stone, which was believed to "heal" base metals into gold and grant longevity to humans.</note>, <term>ALZE</term>. In this case that which is last is better and more honourable than that which is first. The substance must first become white, and then red; it cannot become red unless it have first become white. Hence <term>Simon the Sage</term><note>Likely referring to Simon of Athens, a legendary figure often cited in alchemical compendiums.</note> says: “Know that unless you first make the <term>Stone</term> white, you cannot make it red.” For by the red are the rest of the planets united, and the <term>Medicine</term> appears unawares unless this order is observed in the matter of the white and red. So is the Moon first taken and makes, with the white, <term>Elixir</term>, that is, the white of the Moon to the white of <term>Mercury</term> out of bodies comes to the red. Whence our Sages say that the red is hidden in the white, which they do not dare to extract, until the whole substance has become red. When the substance has been subjected to the influence of the Moon, it may then, in the second place, be brought under the influence of the Sun, which will bring the <term>Medicine</term> to perfection without any aid from the other planets. By which you may understand why the <term>Medicine</term> comes last, even as from the Father proceeds the Son, and the Holy Spirit from both of these. He that hath ears to hear let him hear, and comprehend the brief statement of our <term>Art</term>, which is given in “The Crowd”<note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among assembly of philosophers.</note>: “Know that the true <term>Tincture</term><note>The potent liquid or powder derived from the Stone used to transform metals.</note> can be prepared only out of our ore.” Concerning this ore I therefore propose to give you the only explanation that is required, and I shall be careful to supplement and confirm my own opinion by quotations from other Sages. I shall speak not only about our ore, but also about our union or conjunction of water and mercury. Although the water is naturally cold, yet we must beware of too fierce a degree of heat; for if the moisture of the substance be dried up, our work must come to nothing.

That which is called the spirit is the active, or male principle, and can only be obtained by the dissolution of the body. Accordingly, we must understand this as the humidity which results—namely, that which is produced as long as two spouses are conjoined in a lawful manner, even until the "white" stage. Would you know when the body has been rendered liquid by <term>coction</term><note>A process of slow, steady heating or "digestion" used to mature the substance over time.</note>? Hear what **Bonellus**<note>An alchemical authority frequently cited in early texts like the "Turba Philosophorum."</note> answers:

> "When you see a black substance floating in the water, you may know that the body has been dissolved."

These two, body and spirit, have a third thing which represents their common substance, and is, in its turn, called their body. It is also called a round cloud, death, blackness, darkness, shadow, ashy lead, or a metallic and subtle ore; or it is described, based on what is obtained from it, as gold that was hidden in the body of <term>Magnesia</term><note>In alchemy, Magnesia is not the modern chemical, but a name for the "Prime Matter" or the raw, transformative material of the Work.</note>. Hence it is said:

> "Extract the shadow thereof from the splendor."

This also is the substance of which so many have spoken. Three things constitute the true ore: namely, body, soul, and spirit. Hence it is compared to an egg, because in an egg, too, the chicken is developed out of three things. Thus also <term>Alchemy</term> is produced out of the above-mentioned three things, as many philosophers do testify in **"The Crowd"**<note>A reference to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note>. The male principle, or the water, is also called "nature"; for water is a natural agent which dissolves the elements of bodies and then unites them again. Concerning this water, it is said by **Fictes**, that its nature has the wonderful power of transmuting the body into spirit. Where it is found alone it overcomes all...

This <term>dissolution</term><note>The act of breaking down a solid body into a liquid form, often the first major step in the alchemical process.</note> first imparts a black appearance to the body. Then the soul must be restored to the powder by a powerful fire; and both [be] subjected to <term>coction</term> until they become first black, then white, afterwards red, and finally good venom <note>original: "venenum." In alchemy, "venom" or "poison" often refers to the potent, concentrated medicinal power of the Stone, which "attacks" and transforms the imperfections of base metals.</note>, the whole being accomplished by the separation of waters. And now, the waters being divided, cook the matter and the vapour till <term>coagulation</term> takes place, and there is made a white stone. Then are the waters divided. Therefore preserve this Book with care,
And take heed that you study it again and again.
Thus shall you receive and learn the truth,

You will soon be free from the bonds of error.

For you must subject to gentle <term>coction</term> the seeds and the

### FIGURE III.

The <term>Sages</term> <note>Wise men or master alchemists.</note> say truly
That two animals are in this forest:
One glorious, beautiful, and swift,
A great and strong deer;
The other an unicorn.
They are concealed in the forest,
But happy shall that man be called
Who shall snare and capture them.
The Masters shew you here clearly
That in all places
These two animals wander about in forests
(But know that the forest is but one).
If we apply the parable to our <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, often called the "Sacred Art" or the "Great Work."</note>,
We shall call the forest the Body.
That will be rightly and truly said.
The unicorn will be the Spirit at all times.
The deer desires no other name
But that of the Soul; which name no man shall take away from it.
He that knows how to tame and master them by Art,
To couple them together,
And to lead them in and out of the forest,
May justly be called a Master.
For we rightly judge
That he has attained the <term>golden flesh</term> <note>A symbolic term for the perfected, incorruptible state of the alchemist's soul and body, akin to the creation of the Philosopher’s Stone.</note>,
And may triumph everywhere;
Nay, he may bear rule over great Augustus. <note>A reference to the Roman Emperor Augustus, symbolizing the highest earthly power and wealth, which the successful alchemist surpasses.</note>

<summary>This page uses the allegory of a deer and a unicorn in a forest to represent the Soul and Spirit residing within the human Body. It explains that the goal of the alchemist is to master and unite these internal forces to achieve spiritual and physical perfection.</summary>

<term>Alexander</term> <note>Alexander the Great was frequently cited in alchemical lore as a possessor of secret wisdom, particularly through the "Secret of Secrets" (Secretum Secretorum), a text falsely attributed to Aristotle written for Alexander.</note> writes from Persia
That a **wolf** and a **dog** are in this field,

<note>original Latin motto: "Pater et Filius & Ductor iungunt manus: Scitote hos tres esse Corpus, Animam, & Spiritum." This represents the alchemical 'Tria Prima', or the three essential components of all matter: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>

The Father, the Son, and the Guide,
Are now joined together by the hand.
<term>The Three: In this allegory, the Father represents the Body (the solid physical matter), the Son represents the Soul (the transformative fire or sulfur), and the Guide represents the Spirit (the mediating mercury that allows them to interact).</term>
Know that these three are Body, Soul, and Spirit;
They are now made one and shall never be separated.
For unless the <term>Spirit</term> is joined with the Soul and the Body,
It is impossible for them to bring forth any fruit.
<note>In alchemy, 'fruit' refers to the successful creation of the Philosophers' Stone or the "Tincture" that has the power to heal or transform.</note>
But when they are truly united,
The Work is perfected and the Tincture is produced.
Observe that the Spirit is the life of the Soul,
And it is the Spirit that gives life to the Body.
<note>This emphasizes the Guide's role as the vitalizing force that bridges the gap between the material world and the divine soul.</note>
In this way, the Stone is made whole.

By dedicating the work to the "Invisible King" <note>original Latin: "Regi saeculorum invisibili," a reference to 1 Timothy 1:17</note>, the author acknowledges that while the physical results of alchemy are visible, the source of the wisdom is a spiritual, hidden deity.</note>

# THE GOLDEN TRIPOD,

->OR,<-

## THREE SELECT CHEMICAL TREATISES,

->NAMELY:<-

(i.) That of **BASILIUS VALENTINUS**, a Monk of the Benedictine Order; entitled **THE PRACTICE**, <note>original Latin: "Practica." In an alchemical context, this refers to the practical laboratory application of theory.</note> with twelve Keys and an Appendix.

(ii.) The **BELIEVE ME**, <note>original Latin: "Crede Mihi." This was a common title for authoritative medieval and Renaissance texts, emphasizing the reliability of the author's secrets.</note> or Ordinal <note>An "Ordinal" is a book of rules or a sequence of operations; here it refers to the specific order of the alchemical process.</note>, of **THOMAS NORTON**, an English Sage.

(iii.) The **TESTAMENT** of a certain **CREMER**, Abbot of **WESTMINSTER**.

->EDITED BY<-

## MICHAEL MAIER,

->DOCTOR OF MEDICINE.<-

<note>The "Golden Tripod" is a metaphorical title. Just as a tripod is held up by three legs, Michael Maier suggests that the "truth" of alchemy is supported by these three specific authors. Maier was a prominent German physician and counselor to Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II, and he was known for his efforts to present alchemy as a serious, ancient, and respectable science.</note>

<note>The three authors selected represent different traditions: Basilius Valentinus (the legendary German monk), Thomas Norton (the 15th-century English poet-alchemist), and Abbot Cremer (a semi-legendary figure associated with the monastery at Westminster). By grouping them, Maier aims to show a consensus across different eras and nations regarding the "Great Work."</note>

<summary>This is the title page for "The Golden Tripod," a collection of three foundational alchemical texts edited by Michael Maier. It introduces works by Basilius Valentinus, Thomas Norton, and Abbot Cremer, framing them as essential "keys" to chemical wisdom.</summary>

## DEDICATED

->TO<-

->THE MOST LEARNED AND CULTURED OF PHYSICIANS, THE<-
->TRUEST, SINCEREST, NOBLEST, AND MOST<-
->EXPERT OF HIS KIND,<-

# JOHN HARTMANN BEYER,

->DOCTOR OF MEDICINE,<-
->A RENOWNED PHYSICIAN AND COUNCILLOR OF THE IMPERIAL<-
->FREE CITY, FRANKFURT-ON-THE-MAIN,<-

->BY<-

# MICHAEL MAIER,

->DOCTOR OF MEDICINE AND PHILOSOPHY, <term>COUNT PALATINE</term>, KNIGHT, AND FORMERLY<-
->COURT PHYSICIAN TO HIS IMPERIAL MAJESTY.<-

Finding myself in the midst of a fierce debate between the followers of <term>Dogmatic Medicine</term> and <term>Hermetic Medicine</term> <note>This refers to the 17th-century conflict between traditional doctors who followed ancient Greek theories and the new "chemical" physicians who used alchemical preparations.</note>, I believed it would provide significant and unexpected clarity to this controversy if I published, in the Latin tongue, three major classical treatises on this subject. These are the works of the Benedictine monk <term>Basilius Valentinus</term>, and those of the two great English sages, <term>Thomas Norton</term> and <term>John Cremer</term>. This triad of treatises...

<note>
<term>Dogmatic Medicine</term> — Traditional medical practice based on the teachings of Galen and Hippocrates, primarily focusing on balancing the body's "four humors."
<term>Hermetic Medicine</term> — Also called Spagyric medicine; a school of thought influenced by Paracelsus that used alchemical processes to create potent mineral-based medicines.
<term>Count Palatine</term> — A high-ranking title of nobility (<note>original: "Comes Palatinus"</note>) granted to Maier by the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II in recognition of his service and learning.
<term>Basilius Valentinus</term> — A legendary 15th-century alchemist and monk; many modern scholars believe his writings were actually composed by his "discoverer," Johann Thölde.
<term>Norton</term> — Thomas Norton (c. 1433–1513), an English alchemist famous for his rhyming alchemical book, "The Ordinal of Alchemy."
<term>Cremer</term> — John Cremer, identified as an Abbot of Westminster in the 14th century, though his historical existence is debated among researchers.
</note>

Maier positions these works as essential contributions to the ongoing debate between traditional Galenic medicine and the emerging field of alchemical healing.</summary>

I have ventured to call the **GOLDEN TRIPOD**, and the name suggests to me, as appropriate to our controversy, the answer returned to the enquiring Ionians by the priestess of Delphi <note>The Pythia, the famous oracle of Apollo who provided cryptic prophecies.</note>:

> “The feud between the Meropes <note>A legendary people associated with the island of Cos, the birthplace of the physician Hippocrates.</note> and the Ionians”
> “will not cease until the Golden Tripod, which”
> “Vulcan <note>The god of fire and smithing, known as Hephaestus in Greek; in alchemy, "Vulcan" often represents the fire of the laboratory.</note> cast into the sea, be brought into the”
> “house of the man who knows the things that”
> “are, that were, and that are to come.”

Thus I believe our controversy, too, may be determined, if I dedicate *my* golden Tripod <term>Golden Tripod</term> <note>Referring to the title of this work, *Tripus Aureus*, which contains three essential alchemical texts.</note> to the most learned of modern physicians. For, as Homer says, “A physician is worth many ordinary men,” and if I searched through the whole of Germany, nay, Europe, I could not find a fitter person than him who is set upon the lofty tower of world-wide celebrity, and whose skill is admired and courted far and wide by princes and nobles. Accept, then, this **GOLDEN TRIPOD**, forged by the hands of the Hermetic Vulcan. Value it as a token of affection and esteem, as well as because of its inward worth. I firmly trust that it will assuage the feud between the adherents of <term>Dogmatic Medicine</term> and of <term>Hermetic Medicine</term> <note>The conflict between traditional Galenic medicine and the new chemical or Paracelsian medicine.</note>, as its namesake of old did that between the Meropes and Ionians; and that it will establish amity and concord among physicians of both schools. In order that its beneficial influence might be as widely spread as possible, I have set it forth in the common language of European scholars <note>original: "lingua Latina" — Latin was the universal language of science and medicine in the 17th century.</note>. In conclusion, let me pray you to love me, even as I love you—as I also know that you do.

->Written at Frankfurt-on-the-Main in the month of<-
->January, 1618.<-

### FIRST TRACT.

THE HERMETIC MUSEUM.

I have ventured to call the **GOLDEN TRIPOD** <term>Golden Tripod</term> <note>Referring to the title of this book, *Tripus Aureus*, which brings together three essential alchemical texts like the three legs of a tripod.</note>, and the name suggests to me, as appropriate to our controversy, the answer returned to the enquiring Ionians by the priestess of Delphi <note>The Pythia, the famous oracle of Apollo who provided cryptic prophecies while seated on a tripod.</note>:

> “Vulcan <note>The god of fire and smithing, known as Hephaestus in Greek; in alchemy, "Vulcan" represents the controlled fire of the laboratory.</note> cast into the sea, be brought into the”
> “house of the man who knows the things that”
> “are, that were, and that are to come.”

Thus I believe our controversy, too, may be determined, if I dedicate *my* golden Tripod to the most learned of modern physicians. For, as Homer says, “A physician is worth many ordinary men,” and if I searched through the whole of Germany, nay, Europe, I could not find a fitter person than him who is set upon the lofty tower of world-wide celebrity, and whose skill is admired and courted far and wide by princes and nobles. Accept, then, this **GOLDEN TRIPOD**, forged by the hands of the Hermetic Vulcan. Value it as a token of affection and esteem, as well as because of its inward worth. I firmly trust that it will assuage the feud between the adherents of <term>Dogmatic Medicine</term> <note>The traditional medical system based on the theories of Galen and the balance of the four humors.</note> and of <term>Hermetic Medicine</term> <note>The "new" chemical medicine, which used laboratory-prepared minerals and metals to treat disease, often following the teachings of Paracelsus.</note>.

# THE PREFACE
### OF
## BASILIUS VALENTINUS, THE BENEDICTINE,
### CONCERNING
## THE GREAT STONE OF THE
## ANCIENT SAGES.
<note>The "Great Stone" is the Philosopher's Stone, the ultimate goal of alchemy, believed to possess the power of transmutation and healing.</note>

WHEN I had emptied to the dregs the cup of human suffering, I was led to consider the wretchedness of this world, and the fearful consequences of our first parents’ disobedience <note>A reference to the Fall of Man in Genesis, which alchemists often linked to the corruption of nature that alchemy sought to "cure."</note>. Then I saw that there was no hope of repentance for mankind, that they were getting worse day by day, and that for their impenitence God’s everlasting punishment was hanging over them; and I made haste to withdraw myself from the evil world, to bid farewell to it, and to devote myself to the service of God.

When I had spent some years at the monastery, I found that after I had performed my work and my daily devotions I still had some time on my hands. This I did not wish to pass in idleness, lest my evil thoughts should lead me into new sins; and so I determined to use it for the study and investigation of those <term>natural secrets</term> <note>In this context, "natural secrets" refers to the hidden laws of chemistry and physics through which God governs the material world.</note> by which God has shadowed out eternal things. So I read a great many books in our monastery written in olden times by philosophers who had pursued the same study, and was thereby stimulated to a more ardent desire of knowing that which they also knew. Though I did not make much progress at first, yet at last God granted my earnest prayer, and opened my eyes that I might see what others had seen before me.

<summary>This preface introduces Basilius Valentinus, a monk who turned to alchemical study to avoid idleness and to better understand God’s creation. He frames his scientific pursuit as a spiritual journey sanctioned by divine grace after his retirement from the world.</summary>
<keywords>Basilius Valentinus, Benedictine, Philosopher's Stone, monastery, natural secrets, alchemy, repentance, spiritual chemistry</keywords>

--- Page 330 ---
<meta>This page continues the autobiographical preface of Basilius Valentinus. Following his decision to enter the monastery, he now describes his transition from unsuccessful herbal medicine to the "higher" art of metallic and mineral alchemy, which he believes was revealed to him through divine grace and his successful cure of a fellow monk.</meta>

->THE HERMETIC MUSEUM.<-

In the convent there was a brother who was afflicted with a severe disease of the kidneys <note>In the 15th century, "disease of the kidneys" often referred to painful kidney stones or "the gravel," conditions that were frequently fatal and extremely difficult to treat with period medicine.</note>, and to whom none of the many physicians he had consulted had been able to give even momentary relief. So he had committed himself to the hand of God, and despaired of all human aid.

As I loved him, I gathered all manner of herbs, extracted their salts <note>In alchemical pharmacy, "salts" were the purified mineral remains of plants, thought to hold the plant’s essential healing power.</note>, and distilled various medicines. But none of them seemed to do him the slightest good, and after six years I found that I had tried every possible vegetable substance, without any beneficial effect.

At last I determined to devote myself to the study of the powers and virtues which God has laid into metals and minerals; and the more I searched the more I found. One discovery led to another, and, after God had permitted unto me many experiments, I understood clearly the nature and properties, and the secret potency, imparted by God to minerals and metals.

Among the mineral substances I found one which exhibited many colours, and proved to be of the greatest efficacy in art. The <term>spiritual essence</term> <note>The "spiritual essence" or "spirit" was considered the volatile, energetic part of a substance that could be separated via distillation to create potent medicines.</note> of this substance I extracted, and therewith restored our sick brother, in a few days, to perfect health. For the strength of this spirit was so great as to quicken the prostrate spirit of my diseased brother, who, from that day to the day of his death, remembered me in his hourly prayers. And his prayers, together with my own diligence, so prevailed with God, that there was revealed to me that great secret which God ever conceals from those who are wise in their own conceits.

Thus have I been wishing to reveal to you in this treatise, as far as may be lawful to me, the <term>Stone of the Ancients</term> <note>Another name for the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of curing all diseases and turning base metals into gold.</note>, that you, too, might possess the knowledge of this highest of earthly treasures for your health and comfort in this valley of sorrow. I write about it, not for my own good, but for that of posterity; and though my words be few and simple, that which they import is of immeasurable magnitude. Ponder them well, that you also may find the Rock which is the <term>foundation Stone of truth</term>, the temporal blessing, and the eternal reward.

<summary>Basilius Valentinus describes how his failed attempts to heal a fellow monk with herbal remedies led him to discover the superior medicinal power of minerals, eventually resulting in the revelation of the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>

# THE TRACT
->OF<-
## BASILIUS VALENTINUS, THE BENEDICTINE,
->CONCERNING<-
## THE GREAT STONE OF THE ANCIENT SAGES.

---

I N the preface, gentle Reader, and zealous Student of this **Art** <note>In alchemical literature, "The Art" refers to Alchemy itself—the "Great Work" of purifying and perfecting matter.</note>, I promised to communicate to you a knowledge of our **Corner Stone**, or **Rock** <note>These are metaphors for the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical process.</note>, of the process by which it is prepared, and of the substance from which it was already derived by those **ancient Sages** <note>Alchemists often claimed their knowledge descended from a lineage of "Sages" including figures like Hermes Trismegistus, Aristotle, or biblical figures like Noah.</note>, to whom the secret of our Art was first revealed by God for the health and happiness of earthly life. 

Let me assure you that I fully intend to fulfil my promise, and to be as plain with you as the rules of our Art permit, not misleading you by **sophistical deceptions** <note>Basilius is warning the reader against "puffers"—fraudulent alchemists who used confusing terminology to trick people out of money.</note>, but opening up to you the spring of all blessings even unto the fountain head. I propose to set forth what I have to say in a few simple, straightforward words, for I am no <term>adept</term> <note>An "adept" is a master who has successfully achieved the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> in the art of multiplying words; nor do I think that exuberance of language tends to clearness; on the contrary, I am convinced that it is many words that darken council.

Let me tell you, then, that although many are engaged in the search after this **Stone**, it is nevertheless found but by very few. For God never intended that it should become generally known. It is rather to be regarded as a gift which He reserves for those favoured few, who love the truth, and hate falsehood, who study our Art earnestly by day and by night, and whose hearts are set upon God with an unfeigned affection.

<summary>This page introduces the formal treatise of Basilius Valentinus, where he promises to reveal the secrets of the Philosopher's Stone in plain language. He emphasizes that alchemical success is a divine gift granted only to the sincere, the hardworking, and the God-fearing.</summary>
<keywords>Basilius Valentinus, Philosopher's Stone, Alchemical Art, Adept, Sages, Hermeticism, Divine Grace</keywords>

# THE HERMETIC MUSEUM.

Hence, if you would prepare our great and ancient <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance sought by alchemists to transmute base metals into gold and achieve spiritual perfection.</note>, I testify unto you in all truth that you must give diligent heed to my teaching, and before all things implore the gracious blessing of the Creator of all things. You must also truly repent you of all your sins, confessing the same, and firmly resolve to lead a good and holy life. It is also necessary that you should determine to shew your gratitude to God for His unspeakable Gift, by succouring the poor and the distressed, and by opening your hand and your heart to the needy. Then God will bless your labour, and reward your search with success, and yourself with a seat in Heaven as the fruit of your faith.

Do not despise the truthful writings of those who possessed the <term>Stone</term> before us. For, after the enlightening grace of God, it is from them that I received my knowledge. Let your study of them be increased and repeated often, lest you lose the thread of insight, and the lamp of understanding be extinguished.

Give yourself wholly to study, and be not flighty or double-minded. Let your mind be like a firm Rock, in which all the various sayings of the <term>Sages</term> <note>The "Sages" are the historical and mythical masters of alchemy, such as Hermes Trismegistus, whose writings formed the basis of the "Hermetic" tradition.</note> are reduced to the unity of their common meaning. For a man who is easily influenced in different directions is not likely to find the right path.

As our most ancient <term>Stone</term> is not derived from combustible things, you should cease to seek it in substances which cannot stand the test of fire. For this reason it is absurd to suppose that we can make any use of vegetable substances, though the <term>Stone</term>, too, is endowed with a principle of growth.

If our <term>Stone</term> were a vegetable substance, it would, like other vegetables, be consumed by fire, leaving only a certain <term>salt</term> <note>In alchemical theory, salt is the "body" or fixed principle that remains after a substance is burned or decomposed.</note>. Ancient writers have, indeed, described our <term>Stone</term> as the *vegetable Stone*. But that name was suggested to them by the fact that it grows and increases in size, like a plant.

Know also that animals only multiply after their kind, and within their own species. Hence our <term>Stone</term> can only be prepared out of its own **seed**, from which it was taken in the beginning; and hence also you will perceive that the soul of an animal must not be the subject of this investigation. Animals are a class by themselves; nor can anything ever be obtained from them that is not animal in its nature. But our <term>Stone</term>, as it

...has been bequeathed to me by the <term>Ancients</term> <note>The "Ancients" refers to the long lineage of hermetic philosophers and alchemists, stretching back to mythical figures like Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, is derived from two things, and one thing, in which is concealed a third thing. This is the purest truth, and a most faithful saying. For male and female have from of old been regarded as one body, not from any external or visible consideration, but on account of the ardour of that mutual love which naturally draws them together into one; and as the male and female seed jointly represent the principle of propagation, so also the sperm of the matter out of which our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals and perfecting the human soul.</note> is made can be sown and increased. There are in our substance two supplementary kinds of seed, from which our Stone may be prepared and multiplied.

If you are a true lover of our <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" is a common term for Alchemy, emphasizing that it is both a practical skill and a spiritual discipline.</note>, you will carefully weigh and ponder these words, lest, with other <term>sophisticators</term> <note>A term used by alchemists to describe "puffers" or false practitioners who used deceptive methods or sought only material wealth without understanding the spiritual philosophy.</note>, you fall into the dangerous pit prepared by the common enemy of man.

But whence are you to obtain this seed? This question you may most easily answer by asking yourself another question. What do you want to develop from this seed, and what use do you wish to make of it? There can be no doubt, then, that it must be the root, or first substance, of metals, from which all metals derive their origin. It is, therefore, necessary that we should now proceed to speak of the generation of the metals.

In the beginning, when the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters, and as yet all was involved in darkness, Almighty and Eternal God, Whose beginning and wisdom are from everlasting, by His inscrutable counsel created heaven and earth, and all that in them is, both visible and invisible, out of nothing. How the act of creation was accomplished I will not attempt to explain. This is a matter which is set forth to us in Holy Scripture, and must be apprehended by faith.

To each creature God gave its own <term>seed</term> <note>In the alchemical worldview, "seed" is the vital spark or formal cause within matter that directs its growth and specific identity.</note>, wherewith to propagate its kind, that in this way there might always be an increase of men and animals, plants and metals. Man was not to be able to produce *new* seed: he was only permitted to educe new forms of life out of that which already existed. The creating of seed God reserved to Himself. For if man could *create* seed he would be equal to the Creator.

Know that our seed is produced in the following way. A celestial influence descends from above, by the decree and...

When this union has taken place, the two bring forth a third, namely, an earth-like substance, which is the principle of our seed, of its first source, so that it can shew an ancestry, and from which three the elements, such as water, air, and earth, take their origin. If these three substances be mixed, they are hardened and coagulated into a perfect body, which represents the seed chosen and appointed by the Creator. This is a most important and certain truth. If the metallic soul, the metallic spirit, and the metallic *form* of body be present, there will also be metallic quicksilver, metallic sulphur, and metallic salt, which together make up the perfect metallic body.

If you cannot perceive what you ought to understand herein, you should not devote yourself to the study of philosophy.

Moreover, I tell you in few words, that you cannot obtain a metallic body except by perfectly joining these three principles into one. Know, also, that all animals are, like man, composed of flesh and blood, and also possess a vitalizing spirit, but are destitute of the rational soul which the Creator gave to man alone. Therefore, when animals die, they perish for ever. But when man yields up his mortal life into the hands of his Creator, his soul does not die. It returns, and is united to the glorified body, in which, after the Resurrection <note>Alchemists frequently used the theological concept of the Resurrection as an analogy for the "exaltation" or "perfection" of matter at the end of the Great Work.</note>, soul and spirit dwell together once more in eternal glory, never to be separated again throughout all eternity.

Hence the rational soul of man makes him an abiding creature, and, though his body may seem to die, yet we know that he will live for ever. For to him death is only a process of purification <note>original: "purgatio"</note>, by means of which he is freed from his sins, and translated to another and better place. But there is no resurrection for the brute beasts, because they have no rational soul, for which alone our Lord and Saviour shed His blood.
