-># THE GOLDEN TRIPOD.<-

For though a body may be vitalized by a spirit, yet it need not, therefore, be fixed, unless, indeed, it possess a <term>rational soul</term> <note>In alchemical philosophy, the "soul" (often associated with Sulphur) is the mediating force that prevents the "spirit" (Mercury) from evaporating when the "body" (Salt) is heated.</note>, that strong bond between body and spirit, which represents their union, and resists all efforts to separate them. Where there is no soul, there is no hope of redemption. Nothing can be perfect or lasting without a soul. This is a profound and most important truth, which I feel in conscience bound to make known to my readers. Now, the <term>spirits of metals</term> have this property of <term>fixedness</term> <note>A "fixed" substance is one that remains stable in the heat of a furnace and does not evaporate or change state.</note> in a greater or less degree; they are more or less <term>volatile</term> in proportion to the mutual fitness of their bodies and souls. A metal that has the three conditions of fixedness is not affected by fire or overcome by any other outward agent. But there is only one metal that fulfils these conditions, namely, <term>gold</term>. <term>Silver</term> also contains <term>fixed mercury</term>, and is not so quickly volatilised as the <term>imperfect metals</term> <note>Base metals like lead, tin, or iron were considered "imperfect" because they degrade or oxidize when exposed to fire, unlike "noble" gold.</note>, but stands the trial of fire, and yields no food to <term>voracious Saturn</term> <note>original: "Saturnus vorax." In alchemy, Saturn is the symbol for lead. Lead was used in a process called cupellation to purify gold and silver, "devouring" or absorbing the base metal impurities.</note>.

Amatory <term>Venus</term> <note>Venus is the alchemical name for copper.</note> is clothed with abundant colour, and her whole body is one pure <term>tincture</term> <note>A "tincture" refers to the spiritualized essence or color of a metal that has the power to transform other substances.</note>, not unlike the red colour which is found in the most precious of metals. But though her spirit is of good quality, her body is leprous, and affords no permanent substratum to the fixed tincture. Hence the soul has to share the fate of the imperfect body, and when the body dies the soul has to leave it. For its dwelling has been destroyed by fire, and it is without a house wherein to abide.

<term>Fixed salt</term> has imparted to warlike <term>Mars</term> <note>Mars is the alchemical name for iron.</note> a hard, firm, and durable body, which is evidence of the generosity of his soul; nor can fire be said to have much power over it. And if its strength be united to the beauty of <term>Venus</term>, I do not say but that a precious and harmonious result may be obtained. For the phlegmatic or humid quality of <term>the Moon</term> <note>The Moon is the alchemical name for silver.</note> may be heated with the ardent blood of <term>Venus</term>, and the blackness of <term>Venus</term> removed with the strong <term>salt of Mars</term>.

You need not look for our <term>metallic seed</term> among the elements. It need not be sought so far back. If you can only rectify the <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Sulphur</term>, and <term>Salt</term> (understand, those of the <term>Sages</term> <note>The "Sages" are the historical alchemists. Valentinus warns that these three principles are not common mercury, sulphur, and salt, but specialized substances prepared through the Art.</note>) until the <term>metallic spirit</term> and body are inseparably joined together by means of the <term>metallic soul</term>, you thereby firmly rivet the chain of love, and prepare the palace for the coronation.

Then you must join the husband and wife together, that each may feed upon the other's flesh and blood, and that so they may propagate their species a thousandfold.

Though I would fain reveal this matter to you more plainly and openly, I am prohibited from doing so by the law of God, and by the fear of His wrath, and of eternal punishment, lest the gift of the Most High should be abused.

If, however, you do not understand the theoretical part of my work, perhaps the practical part will serve to enlighten you more fully. I will therefore proceed to shew how, by the help of God, I was enabled to prepare the <term>Stone of the Ancients</term>, and, for your further instruction, I will add twelve keys, in which I give a figurative account of our <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" or "Great Work" is the traditional name for the practice of alchemy.</note>.

Take a quantity of the best and finest gold, and separate it into its component parts by those media which Nature vouchsafes to those who are lovers of <term>Art</term>, as an anatomist dissects the human body. Thus change your gold back into what it was before it became gold; and thou shalt find the seed, the beginning, the middle, and the end—that from which *our gold* and its female principle are derived, viz., the pure and subtle spirit, the spotless soul, and the astral salt and balsam. When these three are united, we may call them the mercurial liquid: a water which was examined by Mercury, found by him to be pure and spotless, and therefore espoused by him as his wife. Of the two was born an incombustible oil; for Mercury became so proud that he hardly knew himself. He put forth eagle feathers, and devoured the slippery tail of the Dragon, and challenged Mars to battle.

Then <term>Mars</term> <note>In alchemy, Mars usually represents the metal iron or a state of vigorous chemical reaction.</note> summoned his horsemen, and bade them enclose Mercury in prison under the ward of <term>Vulcan</term> <note>Vulcan, the god of fire, represents the alchemical furnace or the application of heat.</note>, until he should be liberated by one of the female sex.

When this became known, the other Planets assembled and held a deliberation on the question, what would be the best and wisest course to adopt. When they were met together, <term>Saturn</term> <note>Saturn represents the metal lead and the stage of "putrefaction" or "blackening," characterized by slow, cooling heat.</note> first came forward, and delivered himself as follows:

### FIRST KEY.

<note>The Twelve Keys are a series of alchemical instructions and allegories. Basilius Valentinus was purportedly a 15th-century Benedictine monk, though historians now believe the name was a pseudonym for Johann Thölde, a 17th-century salt-maker and editor.</note>

<note>image: The First Key of Basil Valentine. An alchemical woodcut featuring a King (representing gold) and a Queen (representing silver) in ceremonial attire standing before a landscape with a castle. A wolf leaps over a flaming crucible on the left, representing the purification of gold using antimony (often called the "grey wolf"). On the right, an old man with a scythe represents Saturn, symbolizing time, lead, and the process of "mortification" or breaking down the material.</note>

<summary>This page concludes an allegorical discourse on the unity of nature and introduces the "Twelve Keys" by Basilius Valentinus, a foundational text on the preparation of the Philosophers' Stone.</summary>

Let my friend know that no impure or spotted things are useful for our purpose. For there is nothing in their leprous nature capable of advancing the interests of our <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, specifically the "Great Work" of transmuting base metals into gold and achieving spiritual perfection.</note>. There is much more likelihood of that which is in itself good being spoiled by that which is impure. Everything that is obtained from the mines has its value, unless, indeed, it is adulterated. Adulteration, however, spoils its goodness and its efficacy.

As the physician purges and cleanses the inward parts of the body, and removes all unhealthy matter by means of his medicines, so our metallic substances must be purified and refined of all foreign matter, in order to ensure the success of our task. Therefore, our Masters require a pure, immaculate body, that is untainted with any foreign admixture, which admixture is the leprosy of our metals.

Let the diadem of the <term>King</term> <note>The King is the standard alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> be of pure gold, and let the <term>Queen</term> <note>The Queen usually represents Silver or the "philosophical mercury" that will be joined with the gold.</note> that is united to him in wedlock be chaste and immaculate.

If you would operate by means of our bodies, take a fierce <term>grey wolf</term> <note>In the "Twelve Keys" of Basil Valentine, the "Grey Wolf" is a secret name for the mineral antimony. Because antimony "consumes" other metals when melted with them—leaving only gold behind—it was used as a purifying agent.</note>, which, though on account of its name it be subject to the sway of warlike <term>Mars</term> <note>Mars is the alchemical name for Iron; iron was often used in the chemical process to prepare the antimony.</note>, is by birth the offspring of ancient <term>Saturn</term> <note>Saturn represents Lead, suggesting the heavy, base mineral origin of the wolf.</note>, and is found in the valleys and mountains of the world, where he roams about savage with hunger. Cast to him the body of the <term>King</term>, and when he has devoured it, burn him entirely to ashes in a great fire. By this process the <term>King</term> will be liberated; and when it has been performed thrice the <term>Lion</term> <note>The "Lion" here refers to the gold once it has been purified and "revitalized" by the antimony.</note> has overcome the wolf, and will find nothing more to devour in him. Thus our Body has been rendered fit for the first stage of our work.

Know that this is the only right and legitimate way of purifying our substance: for the <term>Lion</term> purifies himself with the blood of the wolf, and the tincture of its blood agrees most wonderfully with the tincture of the <term>Lion</term>, seeing that the two liquids are closely akin to each other. When the <term>Lion</term>’s hunger is appeased, his spirit becomes more powerful than before, and his eyes glitter like the <term>Sun</term>. His internal essence is now of inestimable value for the removing of all defects, and the healing of all diseases. He is pursued by the ten lepers <note>A metaphor for base metals (like lead, tin, or copper) which the alchemists believed were "diseased" and required the "blood" (tincture) of the purified gold to be cured or transmuted.</note>, who desire to drink his blood; and all that are tormented with any kind of sickness are refreshed with this blood.

For whoever drinks of this golden fountain, experiences a renovation of his whole nature, a vanishing of all unhealthy

## SECOND KEY.

<note>This "Key" describes the preparation of the philosophical solvent—the "Mercury of the Sages"—which is necessary to dissolve the purified gold from the previous step.</note>

*An engraving accompanies this stage, showing a winged, two-headed figure—a hermaphrodite—standing upon a winged globe. This figure represents the union of opposites: the fixed and the volatile. To the left stands the Sun (Gold) and a man with a staff; to the right stands the Moon (Silver) and a man with a sword. The figure holds two caducei, symbols of the dual nature of Mercury.*

In the houses of the great are found various kinds of drink, of which scarcely two are exactly like each other in odour, colour, or taste. For they are prepared in a great variety of different ways. Nevertheless they are all drunk, and each is designed for its own special use <note>This refers to the different "spirits" or volatile liquids produced during alchemical distillation, each serving a specific purpose in the Work.</note>.

When the **Sun** gives out his rays, and sheds them abroad upon the clouds, it is commonly said that he is attracting water, and if he do it frequently, and thereby cause rain, it is called a fruitful year <note>This is an allegory for the process of distillation and "circulation" within a sealed glass vessel. The "rain" is the condensed vapor that falls back onto the material, "fertilizing" it.</note>.

If it be intended to build a **palace**, the services of many different craftsmen must be employed, and a great variety of materials is required. Otherwise the palace would not be worthy the name. It is useless to use wood where stone is necessary <note>The "Palace" is the Philosopher’s Stone. The different "craftsmen" represent the various chemical operations (calcination, solution, etc.), and the "stone" vs "wood" warns the alchemist to use the correct "Prime Matter" rather than inferior substances.</note>.

The daily ebb and flow of the sea, which are caused by the **sympathetic influence** <note>The Hermetic belief that the heavens and earth are linked; here, specifically the Moon's influence on the tides.</note> of heavenly bodies, impart great wealth and blessing to the earth. For whenever the water comes rolling back, it brings a blessing with it.

<term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurius". In this context, not common quicksilver, but the "Mercury of the Philosophers," a specialized substance capable of dissolving metals without corroding them.</note> is the essential tool of this Key. It must be prepared with the <term>Caduceus</term> <note>The staff of Hermes/Mercury, representing the reconciliation of the two snakes (competing forces) into a balanced whole.</note> of wisdom, uniting the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>The masculine/fixed and feminine/volatile principles.</note> into a single, potent essence.

<summary>This page introduces the Second Key of Basil Valentine, using metaphors of architecture and nature to explain the preparation of the philosophical Mercury. It emphasizes that the Great Work requires multiple stages of preparation and the harmonious union of opposing forces.</summary>
<keywords>Second Key, Basil Valentine, Mercury of the Philosophers, distillation, Hermetic allegory, Sun and Moon, Caduceus, Sympathetic Influence</keywords>

A bride, when she is to be brought forth to be married, is gloriously adorned in a great variety of precious garments, which, by enhancing her beauty, render her pleasant in the eyes of the bridegroom. But the rites of the bridal night she performs without any clothing but that which she was arrayed withal at the moment of her birth <note>In alchemical allegory, "garments" represent the external impurities or "accidental" qualities of a metal. To reach the "bridal night" (the union of substances), the metals must be reduced to their pure, "naked" prime matter.</note>.

In the same way our bridal pair, <term>Apollo</term> <note>Representing the Sun or Gold; the active, masculine principle.</note> and <term>Diana</term> <note>Representing the Moon or Silver; the passive, feminine principle.</note>, are arrayed in splendid attire, and their heads and bodies are washed with various kinds of water, some strong, some weak, but not one of them exactly like another, and each designed for its own special purpose. Know that when the moisture of the earth ascends in the form of a vapour, it is condensed in the upper regions, and precipitated to the earth by its own weight. Thus the earth regains the moisture of which it had been deprived, and receives strength to put forth buds and herbs. In the same way you must repeatedly distil the water which you have extracted from the earth, and then again restore it to your earth, as the water in the <term>Strait of Euripus</term> <note>A channel in Greece famous in antiquity for its powerful and alternating currents; here it symbolizes the "reflux" or the constant rising and falling of vapors in a sealed vessel.</note> frequently leaves the shore, and then covers it again until it arrives at a certain limit.

When thus the palace has been constructed by the hands of many craftsmen, and the **sea of glass** <note>The "sea of glass" refers to the alchemical flask or retort, which must be clear and strong to contain the "Great Work."</note> has absolved its course, and filled the palace with good things, it is ready for the King to enter, and take his seat upon the throne.

But you should notice that the King and his spouse must be quite naked when they are joined together. They must be stripped of all their glorious apparel, and must lie down together in the same state of nakedness in which they were born, that their seed may not be spoiled by being mixed with any foreign matter.

Let me tell you, in conclusion, that the bath in which the bridegroom is placed, must consist of two hostile kinds of matter, that purge and rectify each other by means of a continued struggle. For it is not good for the <term>Eagle</term> <note>Usually represents the volatile principle or the "Mercury of the Sages."</note> to build her nest on the summit of the <term>Alps</term> <note>High mountains representing the highest degree of sublimation or coldness.</note>, because her young ones are thus in great danger of being frozen to death by the intense cold that prevails there.

But if you add to the <term>Eagle</term> the icy <term>Dragon</term> <note>Often represents the "fixed" sulfurous body or a corrosive acid that "devours" the metal.</note> that has long had its habitation upon the rocks, and has crawled forth from...

It explains the process of circulation and the necessity of balancing volatile and fixed substances, personified as the Eagle and the Dragon.</summary>

### THIRD KEY.

<note>The emblem for this Key depicts a dragon in the foreground and a winged creature, likely an eagle, in a mountainous landscape, symbolizing the union of the "fixed" (earthly dragon) and the "volatile" (heavenly eagle).</note>

By means of water fire may be extinguished, and utterly quenched. If much water be poured upon a little fire, the fire is overcome, and compelled to yield up the victory to the water. In the same way our <term>fiery sulphur</term> <note>Sulphur was considered the active, masculine, and "combustible" principle of metals, responsible for their color and "soul."</note> must be overcome by means of our prepared water. But, after the water has vanished, the fiery life of our sulphurous vapour must triumph, and again obtain the victory. But no such triumph can take place unless the King imparts great strength and potency to his water, and <term>tinges</term> <note>To "tinge" is to fundamentally change the color and nature of a substance. In alchemy, the "tinging" power is the ability of the Stone to transform base metals into gold.</note> it with his own colour, that thereby he may be consumed...

and become invisible, and then again recover his visible form, with a diminution of his simple essence, and a development of his perfection.

A painter can set yellow upon white, and red or crimson upon yellow; for, though all these colours are present, yet the latter prevails on account of its greater intensity. When you have accomplished the same thing in our Art, you have before your eyes the light of wisdom, which shines in the darkness, although it does not burn. For our <term>sulphur</term><note>In alchemical theory, Sulphur represents the active, masculine, and "combustible" principle of matter. However, the "Sulphur of the Sages" described here is a spiritualized, stable form that provides the "seed" of gold.</note> does not burn, but nevertheless its brilliancy is seen far and near. Nor does it colour anything until it has been prepared, and dyed with its own colour, which it then imparts to all weak and imperfect metals. This sulphur, however, cannot impart this colour until it have first by persevering labour been prevailed upon to abjure its original colour. For the weaker does not overcome the stronger, but has to yield the victory to it. The gist of the whole matter lies in the fact that the small and weak cannot aid that which is itself small and weak, and a combustible substance cannot shield another substance from combustion. That which is to protect another substance against combustion must itself be safe from danger. The latter must be stronger than the former, that is to say, it must itself be essentially incombustible. He, then, who would prepare the incombustible sulphur of the Sages, must look for our sulphur in a substance in which it is incombustible—which can only be after its body has been absorbed by the <term>salt sea</term><note>The "salt sea" typically refers to the specialized solvent or "mercurial water" used to dissolve the starting material during the purification process.</note>, and again rejected by it. Then it must be so exalted as to shine more brightly than all the stars of heaven, and in its essence it must have an abundance of blood, like the <term>Pelican</term><note>The Pelican is a famous alchemical symbol for the "Rubedo" or reddening stage. Just as the legendary pelican wounds its breast to feed its young with blood, the Alchemical Stone is said to "nourish" base metals, transforming them into its own nature.</note>, which wounds its own breast, and, without any diminution of its strength, nourishes and rears up many young ones with its blood. This <term>Tincture</term><note>The Tincture is another name for the Philosophers' Stone in its liquid or powder form, capable of "staining" or transforming the quality of metals.</note> is the <term>Rose of our Masters</term>, of purple hue, called also the <term>red blood of the Dragon</term><note>The "blood of the dragon" refers to the deep red color the matter takes on at the end of the work, signifying its power to fix and transform.</note>, or the purple cloak many times folded with which the <term>Queen of Salvation</term><note>An allegorical name for the perfected Stone, emphasizing its "saving" power to heal both metals and the human body.</note> is covered, and by which all metals are regenerated in colour.

Carefully preserve this splendid mantle, together with the <term>astral salt</term> which is joined to this sulphur, and screens it from harm. Add to it a sufficient quantity of the volatility of the bird; then the <term>Cock</term> will swallow the <term>Fox</term><note>The Cock (volatile) and the Fox (fixed) represent the interaction of different states of matter. Their mutual "swallowing" refers to the cycle of distillation and condensation (Solve et Coagula) where the solid becomes liquid and the liquid becomes solid again.</note>, and, having been drowned in the water, and quickened by the fire, will in its turn be swallowed by the Fox.

# FOURTH KEY.

All flesh that is derived from the earth, must be decomposed and again reduced to earth; then the earthy salt produces a new generation by celestial resuscitation. For where there was not first earth, there can be no resurrection in our <term>Magistery</term><note>The "Magistery" refers to the entire alchemical process or "Great Work" of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. For in earth is the balm of Nature, and the salt of the Sages.

At the end of the world, the world shall be judged by fire, and all those things that God has made of nothing shall by fire be reduced to ashes, from which ashes the Phœnix is to produce her young. For in the ashes slumbers a true and genuine tartaric substance <note>In alchemy, "tartaric substance" refers to the fixed, stable salt that remains after combustion—a symbol of the permanent essence that survives the fire.</note>, which, being dissolved, will enable us to open the strongest bolt of the royal chamber <note>The "royal chamber" is a metaphor for the inner secret of the chemical process or the heart of the alchemical vessel.</note>.

After the conflagration, there shall be formed a new heaven and a new earth, and the new man will be more noble in his glorified state than he was before.

When the sand and ashes have been well matured and ripened with fire, the glass-blower makes out of it glass, which remains hard and firm in the fire, and in colour resembles a crystal stone. To the uninitiated this is a great mystery, but not to the master whom long experience has familiarized with the process.

Out of stones the master also prepares <term>lime</term><note>In alchemy, lime (calcium oxide) represents a powerful, caustic force produced by fire, capable of breaking down substances and initiating change.</note> by burning, which is very useful for our work. But before they are prepared with fire, they are mere stones. The stone must be matured and rendered fervent with fire, and then it becomes so potent that few things are to be compared to the <term>fiery spirit of lime</term>.

By burning anything to ashes you may gain its <term>salt</term>. If in this dissolution the <term>sulphur</term> and <term>mercury</term><note>Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt are the "Three Primes" of alchemy, representing the soul, spirit, and body respectively.</note> be kept apart, and restored to its salt, you may once more obtain that form which was destroyed by the process of combustion. This assertion the wise of this world denounce as the greatest folly, and count as a rebellion, saying that such a transformation would amount to a new creation, and that God has denied such creative power to sinful man. But the folly is all on their side. For they do not understand that our <term>Artist</term><note>The "Artist" is the alchemist, who does not create from nothing but works in harmony with natural laws.</note> does not claim to create anything, but only to evolve new things from the seed made ready to his hand by the Creator.

If you do not possess the ashes, you will be unable to obtain our salt; and without our salt you will not be able to impart to our substance a bodily form; for the <term>coagulation</term><note>Coagulation is the process of turning a liquid or spiritual substance into a solid, "fixing" it so it can exist in the physical world.</note> of all things is produced by salt alone.

As salt is the great preserving principle that protects all things from decay, so the Salt of our <term>Magistery</term><note>The Magistery refers to the mastery of the "Great Work," the process of creating the Philosopher’s Stone.</note> preserves metal from decomposition and utter annihilation. If their Balm were to perish, and the Spirit to leave the body, the body would be quite dead, and no longer available for any good purpose. The metallic spirit would have departed, and would have left its habitation empty, bare, and lifeless.

Observe also, thou who art a lover of this Art, that the salt that is gained from ashes has great potency, and possesses many concealed virtues. Nevertheless, the salt is unprofitable, until its inward substance has been extracted. For the spirit alone gives strength and life. The body by itself profits nothing. If you know how to find this spirit, you have the Salt of the Sages, and the <term>incombustible oil</term><note>The "incombustible oil" is a metaphor for the "Fixed" state of the Stone—a substance that has been so purified by fire that fire can no longer destroy or change it.</note>, concerning which many things have been written before my time.

> Although many philosophers
> Have sought for me with eagerness,
> Yet very few succeed at length
> In finding out my secret virtue.

## FIFTH KEY.

<note>The emblem for the Fifth Key depicts a woman holding a floral branch, standing before a crowned lion. In the sky, a personified sun shines, while in the background, a figure works with bellows at a furnace, symbolizing the application of heat to the work of nature.</note>

The <term>quickening power</term><note>The "quickening power" refers to the life-giving force (vis vitalis) that initiates growth and movement in seemingly dormant matter.</note> of the earth produces all things that grow forth from it, and he who says that the earth has no life makes a statement which is flatly contradicted by the most ordinary facts. For what is dead cannot produce life and growth, seeing that it is devoid of the quickening spirit. This spirit is the life and soul that dwell in the earth, and are nourished by heavenly and <term>sidereal influences</term><note>The alchemical belief that the stars and planets emit subtle energies or "effluvia" that penetrate the earth to "cook" or mature minerals and plants.</note>. For all herbs, trees, and roots, and all metals and minerals, receive their growth and nutriment from the <term>spirit of the earth</term><note>Known in Latin as the *Spiritus Mundi*, this is the invisible vital breath that alchemists sought to capture and use in their experiments.</note>, which is the spirit of life. This spirit is itself fed by the stars, and is thereby rendered capable of imparting nutriment to all things that grow, and of nursing them as a mother does her child while it is yet in the womb. The minerals are hidden in the <term>womb of the earth</term><note>A common Hermetic metaphor: the earth acts as a biological mother, and the veins of metal in the ground are seen as growing embryos or fetuses.</note>, and nourished by her with the spirit which she receives from above.

Ultimately we obtain the indestructible medicine of human and metallic bodies, which is fitter to be known to angels than to men, except such as seek it at God’s hands in heartfelt prayer, and give genuine proofs of their gratitude by service rendered to Him, and to their needy neighbour.

The male without the female is looked upon as only half a body, nor can the female without the male be regarded as more complete. For neither can bring forth fruit so long as it remains alone. But if the two be conjugally united, there is a perfect body, and their seed is placed in a condition in which it can yield increase. <note>This "chemical wedding" or *Coniunctio* is a central pillar of alchemy, representing the union of the active (male/sulfur) and passive (female/mercury) principles to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

If too much seed be cast into the field, the plants impede each other's growth, and there can be no ripe fruit. But if, on the other hand, too little be sown, weeds spring up and choke it.

If a merchant would keep a clear conscience, let him give just measure to his neighbour. If his measure and weight be not short, he will receive praise from the poor. <note>Alchemists often used moral or commercial parables to emphasize the absolute precision required in their laboratory work.</note>

In too much water you may easily be drowned; too little water, on the other hand, soon evaporates in the heat of the sun.

If, then, you would attain the longed-for goal, observe just measure in mixing the <term>liquid substance of the Sages</term><note>Often referring to "Philosophical Mercury," the specialized solvent used to dissolve the base metals.</note>, lest that which is too much overpower that which is too little, and the generation be hindered. For too much rain spoils the fruit, and too much drought stunts its growth. Therefore, when <term>Neptune</term><note>A mythological code-word for the liquid solvent or the "water" of the work.</note> has prepared his bath, measure out carefully the exact quantity of <term>permanent water</term><note>Original: *aqua permanens*. A solvent that does not evaporate when heated, or a substance that has reached a stable, liquid state through alchemical art.</note> needed, and let there be neither too little nor too much.

The twofold <term>fiery male</term><note>The active, hot, and dry principle, usually associated with Sulfur.</note> must be fed with a <term>snowy swan</term><note>The swan represents the "White Work" or *Albedo* stage; its white color and association with water link it to purified Mercury.</note>, and then they must mutually slay each other and restore each other to life; and the air of the imprisoned <term>fiery male</term> will occupy three of the four quarters of the world, and make up three parts of the imprisoned <term>fiery male</term>, that the death-song of the swans may be distinctly heard; <note>The "death-song" refers to the hissing or chemical reactions occurring within the sealed vessel as the substances transform.</note> then the swan roasted will become food for the <term>King</term>, and the fiery <term>King</term> will be seized with great love towards the <term>Queen</term>, and will take his fill of delight in embracing her, until they both vanish and coalesce into one body.

It is commonly said that two can overpower one, especially if they have sufficient room for putting forth their strength. Know also that there must come a twofold wind, and a single wind, and that they must furiously blow from the east and from the south. If, when they cease to rage, the air has become water, you may be confident that the spiritual will also be transmuted. <note>The winds represent the volatile gases and heat directions applied to the vessel during the distillation and condensation phases.</note>

## SEVENTH KEY.

Natural heat preserves the life of man. If his body lose its natural heat his life has come to an end.

A moderate degree of natural heat protects against the cold ; an excess of it destroys life. It is not necessary that the substance of the Sun should touch the earth. The Sun can heat the earth by shedding thereon its rays, which are intensified...

When its fruit is about to be matured, the vine stands in greater need of the Sun’s warmth than in the spring; and if the Sun shine brightly in the autumn, the grapes will be better than if they had not felt his autumnal warmth.

In the winter the multitude suppose everything to be dead, because the earth is bound in the chains of frost, so that nothing is allowed to sprout forth. But as soon as the spring comes, and the cold is vanquished by the power of the Sun, everything is restored to life, the trees and herbs put forth buds, leaves, and blossoms, the hibernating animals creep forth from their hiding places, the plants give out a sweet fragrance, and are adorned with a great variety of many coloured flowers; and the summer carries on the work of the spring, by changing its flowers into fruit.

Thus, year by year, the operations of the universe are performed, until at length it shall be destroyed by its Creator, and all the dwellers upon earth shall be restored by resurrection to a glorified life. Then the operations of earthly nature shall cease, and the heavenly and eternal dispensation shall take its place.

When the Sun in the winter pursues his course far away from us, he cannot melt the deep snow. But in the summer he approaches nearer to us, the quality of the air becomes more fiery, and the snow melts and is transmuted by warmth into water. For that which is weak is always compelled to yield to that which is strong.

# THE HERMETIC MUSEUM.
<page-num>340</page-num>

Neither human nor animal bodies can be multiplied or propagated without decomposition; the grain and all vegetable seed, when cast into the ground, must decay before it can spring up again; moreover, <term>putrefaction</term><note>In alchemy, putrefaction is the "nigredo" or blackening stage, where matter is broken down to its primary essence so it can be reborn in a purified state.</note> imparts life to many worms and other <term>animalculæ</term><note>A historical term for microscopic or tiny living creatures; here used to show how life seemingly "spontaneous" arises from decay.</note>. The process of augmentation and quickening is mostly performed in the earth, while it is caused by spiritual seed through the other elements.

The farmer’s wife knows that she cannot hope to obtain chickens except through the decomposition of the egg.

If bread is placed in honey, and suffered to decay, ants are generated; worms are bred in the putrefying bodies of men, horses, and other animals; maggots are also developed by the decay of nuts, apples, and pears.

The same thing may be observed in regard to vegetable life. Nettles and other weeds spring up where no such seed has ever been sown. This occurs only by <term>putrefaction</term>. The reason is that the soil in such places is so disposed, and, as it were, impregnated, that it produces these fruits, which is a result of the properties of <term>sidereal influence</term><note>The belief that stars and planets emit a spiritual energy or "virtue" that shapes and gives life to matter on Earth.</note>; consequently the seed is spiritually produced in the earth, and putrefies in the earth, and by the operation of the elements generates corporeal matter according to the species of Nature. Thus the stars and the elements may generate new spiritual, and, ultimately, new vegetable seed, by means of <term>putrefaction</term>. But man cannot create new seed; for it is not in his power to order the operation of the elements and the essential influences of the stars. By natural conditions, however, new plants are generated simply through <term>putrefaction</term>. This fact is not noticed by the farmer, simply because it is a thing that he has always been used to, and for which he is unable to find an explanation. But you who should know more than the vulgar herd, must search into the causes of things, and endeavour to understand how the process of <term>generation</term> and <term>resuscitation</term><note>Literally "bringing back to life"; the alchemist seeks to "kill" the base metal so it can be "resuscitated" as gold.</note> is accomplished by means of <term>decomposition</term>, and how all life is produced out of decay.

Each element is in its turn decomposed and regenerated by that which is contained in it. For you should know that every element contains the three others. In air, for instance, there is fire, water, and earth. This assertion may appear incredible, but it is nevertheless true. In like manner, fire—

...includes air, water, and earth, since otherwise it could generate nothing. Water contains fire, air, and earth; for if it did not, there could be no growth. At the same time, each element is distinct, though each contains the others. All this is found by distillation in the separation of the elements.

In order to rationally prove this to you, who are investigating the separation of Nature, and purpose to understand the division of the elements, lest you should think my words inventions, and not true, I tell you that if you distil earth, you will find that, first of all, there is an escape of air, which, in its turn, always contains fire, as they are both of a spiritual essence, and exercise an irresistible mutual attraction. In the next place, there issues water from the earth, and the earth, in which is the precious <term>salt</term><note>In alchemy, 'salt' is the third of the Three Primes, representing the physical body, stability, and the non-volatile residue that remains after firing.</note>, remains by itself at the bottom of the vessel.

When water is distilled, air and fire issue from it, and the water and material earth remain at the bottom. Again, when the invisible part of elementary fire is extracted, you get water and earth by themselves. Nor can any of the three other elements exist without air. It is air that gives to earth its power of production, to fire its power of burning, to water its power of generating fruit. Again, air can consume nothing, nor dry up any moisture, without that natural heat which must be imparted to it by fire. For everything that is hot and dry contains fire. From these considerations we conclude that no element can exist without the others, and that in the generation of all things there is a mingling of the four elements.

He who states the contrary in no wise understands the secrets of Nature, nor has he investigated the properties of the elements. For if anything is to be generated by <term>putrefaction</term><note>Putrefaction, or the 'Nigredo' stage, is the essential breakdown of matter into its constituent parts so that it can be reformed into a higher state.</note>, the process must be as follows: The earth is first decomposed by the moisture which it contains; for without moisture, or water, there can be no true decay; thereupon the decomposed substance is kindled and quickened by the natural heat of fire: for without natural heat no generation can take place. Again, if that which has received the spark of life, is to be stirred up to motion and growth, it must be acted upon by air. For without air, the quickened substance would be choked and stifled in the germ. Hence it manifestly appears that no one element can work effectually without the aid of the others, and that all must contribute...

...and then the spirit. And though the substance remains the same, its properties have become very different. This excellent powder is dissolved in a moist place into a liquid which is profitably employed as a painless agent in surgery.

Let me sum up in few words what I have to say. The substance is of heavenly birth, its life is preserved by the stars, and nourished by the <term>four elements</term><note>Fire, Air, Water, and Earth—the fundamental building blocks of the universe in ancient and medieval science.</note>; then it must perish, and be putrefied; again, by the influence of the stars, which works through the elements, it is restored to life, and becomes once more a heavenly thing that has its habitation in the highest region of the <term>firmament</term><note>The celestial sphere or the heavens, representing the highest state of spiritual and physical refinement.</note>. Then you will find that the heavenly has assumed an earthly body, and that the earthly body has been reduced to a heavenly substance.

# THE GOLDEN TRIPOD.

In our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and acting as a universal medicine.</note>, as composed by me and by those who have long preceded me, are contained all elements, all mineral and metallic forms, and all the qualities and properties of the whole world. In it we find most powerful natural heat, by which the icy body of Saturn <note>In alchemy, Saturn is the symbolic name for the metal lead.</note> is gently transmuted into the best gold. It contains also a high degree of cold, which tempers the fervent heat of Venus <note>Venus is the symbolic name for the metal copper.</note>, and coagulates the mercury, which is thereby also changed into the finest gold. All these properties slumber in the substance of our <term>Stone</term>, and are developed, perfected, and matured by the gentle <term>coction</term> <note>The process of "cooking" or digesting a substance over a steady heat for a long period.</note> of natural fire, until they have attained their highest perfection.

If the fruit of a tree be plucked before it is ripe, it is unfit for use; and if the potter fail to harden his vessels in the fire, they cannot be employed for any good purpose.

In the same way you must exercise considerable patience in preparing our <term>Elixir</term> <note>A liquid preparation of the Stone, often intended for medicinal use or for the "projection" onto metals.</note>, if it is to become all that you wish it to become. No fruit can grow from a flower that has been plucked before the time. He who is in too great a hurry, can bring nothing to perfection, but is almost sure to spoil that which he has in hand. Remember, then, that if our <term>Stone</term> be not sufficiently matured, it will not be able to bring anything to maturity.

The substance is dissolved in a bath, and its parts reunited by <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage of decomposition or "blackening" (nigredo), where the material is broken down to be reborn.</note>. In ashes it blossoms. In the form of sand all its excessive moisture is dried up. Maturity and fixity are obtained by living fire. The work does not actually take place in the <term>Bath of St. Mary</term> <note>original: "Balneum Mariae." A gentle heating method using water, similar to a modern double-boiler.</note>, in horse-dung, in ashes, or in sand, but the grades and regimen of the fire proceed after the degrees which are represented by these. The <term>Stone</term> is prepared in an empty furnace, with a threefold line of <term>circumvallation</term> <note>A series of defensive walls; here referring to the structural layers of the furnace designed to retain and regulate heat.</note>, in a tightly closed chamber. It is subjected to continued <term>coction</term>, till all moisture and clouds are driven off, and the <term>King</term> <note>A common alchemical symbol for the completed Gold or the Stone itself.</note> attains to indestructible fixedness, and is no longer liable to any danger or injury, because he has become unconquerable. Let me express my meaning in a somewhat different manner. When you have dissolved your earth with your water, dry up the water with its own inward fire. Then the air will breathe new life into the body, and you will have that which can only be regarded as that <term>Great Stone</term> which in a spiritual manner pervades human and metallic bodies, and is the universal and immaculate <term>Medicine</term>, since it drives out that

## ELEVENTH KEY.

The eleventh Key to the Knowledge of the <term>augmentation</term> <note>Also known as "multiplication," this is the process by which the alchemist increases the quantity and the transmuting power of the Stone after it has been successfully created.</note> of our **Stone**, I will put before you in the form of a parable.

I have concealed nothing; and if you will but remove the veil of ignorance from your eyes, you will behold that which many have sought and few found.

## TWELFTH KEY.

If an athlete know not the use of his sword, he might as well be without it; and if another warrior that is skilled in the use of that weapon come against him, the first is like to fare badly. For he that has knowledge and experience on his side, must carry off the victory.

In the same way, he that possesses this <term>tincture</term> <note>From the Latin *tinctura*; in alchemy, this refers to the concentrated essence or "dye" capable of instantly transforming the properties of a substance, usually turning base metals into gold.</note>, by the grace of Almighty God, and is unacquainted with its uses, might as well not have it at all. Therefore this twelfth and last Key must serve to open up to you the uses of this <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance that is the goal of the alchemist's "Great Work."</note>. In dealing with this part of the subject I will drop my parabolic and figurative style, and plainly set forth all that is to be known.

When the <term>Medicine</term> <note>Alchemists often called the Stone a "Medicine" because they believed it could "cure" base metals of their impurities (turning them to gold) and cure the human body of all diseases.</note> and <term>Stone</term> of all the Sages has been perfectly prepared out of the true **virgin’s milk** <note>original: *lac virginis*. A symbolic term for a purified mercurial solvent or the white stage of the process; it represents the "purity" of the substance before it is joined with "sulfur."</note>, take one part of it to three parts of the best gold purged and refined with <term>antimony</term> <note>A metallic element used by alchemists to "devour" impurities in gold. In the laboratory, antimony alloys with base metals, allowing the pure gold to be separated more easily.</note>, the gold being previously beaten into plates of the greatest possible thinness. Put the whole into a smelting pot, and subject it to the action of a gentle fire for twelve hours; then let it be melted for three days and three nights more.

<note>The accompanying illustration depicts the alchemist in his laboratory, a place where spiritual prayer and physical chemistry meet. The lion being consumed by the serpent in the foreground is a classic symbol of the "fixed" (gold/sulfur) being "dissolved" or overcome by the "volatile" (mercury/solvent) to create the final Tincture.</note>

For without the <term>ferment of gold</term> <note>In alchemy, a "ferment" is a small amount of a perfected substance—like yeast in bread—added to a larger mass to trigger a transformation into that same substance.</note> no one can compose the **Stone** or develop the <term>tinging virtue</term> <note>The "tinging virtue" refers to the power of the Stone to "dye" or permeate base metals, changing their internal nature and outward color into gold.</note>. For the same is very subtle and penetrating if it be fermented and joined with a ferment like unto itself; then the prepared <term>tincture</term> <note>The final, liquid form of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> has the power of entering into other bodies, and operating therein. Take then one part of the prepared ferment for the tinging of a thousand parts of molten metal, and then you will learn in all faith and truth that it shall be changed into the only good and <term>fixed gold</term> <note> "Fixed" gold refers to gold that is stable and pure, able to withstand the heat of fire without evaporating or degrading.</note>. For one body takes possession of the other; even if it be unlike to it, nevertheless, through the strength and potency added to it, it is compelled to be assimilated to the same, since like derives origin from like.

Whoever uses this as a medium shall find whither the vestibules of the palace lead, and there is nothing comparable to the subtlety thereof. He shall possess all in all, performing all things whatsoever which are possible under the sun.

O principle of the prime principle, consider the end! O end of the final end, consider the beginning! And be this medium commended unto your faithful care, wherein also God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, shall give unto you whatsoever you need both in soul and body.

### *Concerning the First Matter of the Philosophical Stone.*

Seek for that **Stone** which has no fleshly nature, but out of which a <term>volatile fire</term> <note>A paradoxical term for a substance that is both active (fire) and elusive or easily evaporated (volatile).</note> is extracted, whence also this stone is made, being composed of white and red <note>These represent the "White Work" (silver) and "Red Work" (gold), the two final stages of the alchemical process.</note>. It is a stone, and no stone; therein Nature alone operates. A fountain flows from it. The fixed part submerges its father, absorbing it, body and life, until the soul is returned to it. And the volatile mother like to him, is produced in her own kingdom; and he by his virtue and power receives greater strength. The volatile mother when prepared surpasses the sun in summer. Thus the father by means of <term>Vulcan</term> <note>The Roman god of fire; here, he represents the alchemist's furnace and the controlled heat required for the work.</note> was produced from the spirit. Body, soul, and spirit exist in both, whence the whole matter proceeds. It proceeds from one, and is one matter. Bind together the fixed and the volatile; they are two, and three, and yet one only. If you do not understand you will attain nothing. **Adam** <note>Symbolizes the "First Man" or the primal, unrefined matter of the work.</note> was in a bath—wherein **Venus** <note>Often represents the planet/metal copper or the feminine principle of receptivity and love in the chemical marriage.</note> found her like, which bath the aged **Dragon** <note>A common symbol for the raw, "poisonous" or volatile state of the material before it is purified.</note> had prepared when his strength was deserting him.

### *A short Appendix and clear Recapitulation of the preceding Treatise concerning the Great Stone of the Ancient Sages.*

I, **Basil Valentine** <note>Traditionally identified as a 15th-century Benedictine monk, though historians believe these writings were likely authored by Johann Thölde in the late 16th century.</note>, a brother of the **Benedictine Order**, testify that I have written this little book. **Salt of tartar** <note>Potassium carbonate, often obtained from the crusty sediments in wine barrels.</note> by itself is a powerful fixative, particularly if the heat of **quicklime** <note>Calcium oxide, a caustic alkaline substance produced by heating limestone.</note> be incorporated with it. In the same way, the vegetable salt of wine fixes and volatilizes according to the manner of its preparation. Its use is one of the <term>arcana</term> <note>From the Latin "arcanum," meaning a profound secret or mystery of nature.</note> of Nature, and a miracle of the philosopher's art.

When a man drinks wine, there may be gained from his urine a clear salt, which is volatile, and renders other fixed substances volatile, causing them to rise with it in the <term>alembic</term> <note>An early distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling pot and a cooling cap with a spout.</note>. But the same does not fix. If a man drank nothing but wine, yet for all that the salt obtained from his urine would have a different property from that gained out of the lees of wine. For it has undergone a chemical change in the human body, having become transmuted from a vegetable into an animal salt—just as horses that feed on oats, straw, etc., change those vegetable substances into flesh and fat, while the bee prepares honey out of the precious juices of flowers and herbs.

The great change which takes place in these and other substances is due to <term>putrefaction</term> <note>In alchemy, this refers to the decomposition or breaking down of a substance to release its constituent parts.</note>, which separates and transmutes the constituent elements.

The common **spirit of salt** <note>Hydrochloric acid.</note>, which is extracted according to the direction given in my last declaration, if there be added to it a small quantity of the <term>spirit of the dragon</term> <note>A metaphorical term for a sharp, corrosive acid or a specific reactive chemical agent.</note>, dissolves, volatilizes, and raises together with itself in the <term>alembic</term>, gold and silver; just as the <term>eagle</term> <note>Often an alchemical symbol for sal ammoniac or the act of sublimation (rising as vapor).</note>, together with the spirit of the dragon (which is found in stony places), before the spirit is separated from its body, is much more powerful in producing fixation than volatility.

This I also say, that if the spirit of common salt be joined to the spirit of wine, and distilled together with it, it becomes sweet, and loses its acidity. This prepared spirit does not dissolve gold bodily, but if it be poured on prepared <term>calx</term> of gold <note>Gold that has been reduced to a fine, crumbly powder through heating or chemical action.</note>, it extracts the essence of its colour and redness. If this be rightly done, it reduces the white and pure <term>moon</term> <note>The alchemical name for silver.</note> to the colour of that body from which it was itself extracted. The old body may also receive back its former colour through the love of

alluring <term>Venus</term> <note>The alchemical name for copper.</note>, from whose blood it, in the first instance, derived its origin.

But observe, likewise, that the <term>spirit of salt</term> <note>Commonly known today as hydrochloric acid.</note> also destroys the <term>moon</term> <note>The alchemical name for silver.</note>, and reduces it to a spiritual essence, according to my teaching, out of which the "<term>potable moon</term>" <note>Latin: *luna potabilis*. A liquid, drinkable form of silver believed to have high medicinal value.</note> may be prepared. This spirit of the <term>moon</term> belongs to the spirit of the <term>sun</term> <note>The alchemical name for gold.</note>, as the female answers to the male, by the <term>copulation</term> <note>A term used by alchemists to describe the chemical union or bonding of two substances.</note> or <term>conjunction</term> of the <term>spirit of mercury</term> or its <term>oil</term>.

The <term>spirit</term> lies hid in <term>mercury</term>, the colour you must seek in <term>sulphur</term>, and their <term>coagulation</term> <note>The process of turning a liquid into a solid or semi-solid state.</note> in <term>salt</term>; then you have three things which together are capable of once more generating a perfect thing. The <term>spirit</term> is fermented in the <term>gold</term> with its own proper <term>oil</term>; the <term>sulphur</term> is found in abundance in the property of precious <term>Venus</term> <note>Copper.</note>. This kindles the <term>fixed blood</term> <note>A reference to the deep red color of the completed alchemical "Tincture" or Stone.</note> which is sprung from it, the <term>spirit of the salt of the Sages</term> imparts strength and firmness, though the <term>spirit of tartar</term> <note>Potassium carbonate essence.</note> and the <term>spirit of urine</term> <note>Ammonia-rich salts.</note>, together with true <term>vinegar</term> <note>Often referring to "Philosophical Vinegar," a potent acidic solvent.</note>, have great virtue. For the <term>spirit of vinegar</term> is cold, and the <term>spirit of lime</term> <note>Calcium oxide essence.</note> is intensely hot, and thus the two <term>spirits</term> are found to be of opposite natures. I do not here speak according to the customary manner of the <term>Sages</term>. But I must not say too openly how the <term>inner gates</term> <note>The most guarded secrets of the alchemical process.</note> are to be unlocked.

In bidding farewell, let me impart to you a faithful word. Seek your material in a metallic substance. Thence prepare <term>mercury</term>. This <term>ferment</term> with the <term>mercury</term> of its own proper <term>sulphur</term>, and <term>coagulate</term> them with <term>salt</term>. <term>Distil</term> them together; mix all according to weight. Then you will obtain *one thing*, consisting of elements sprung from *one thing*. <term>Coagulate</term> and <term>fix</term> <note>To make a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated.</note> it by means of continuous warmth. Thereupon <term>augment</term> and <term>ferment</term> it a third time, according to the teaching of my two last <term>Keys</term>, and you will find the object and goal of your desire. The uses of the <term>Tincture</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, used for both transmuting metals and healing the body.</note> are set forth plainly in my <term>twelfth Key</term>.

->THANKS BE TO GOD.<-

As a parting kindness to you, I am constrained to add that the <term>spirit</term> may also be extracted from black <term>Saturn</term> <note>The alchemical name for lead.</note> and benevolent <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The alchemical name for tin.</note>. When it has been reduced to a <term>sweet oil</term>, we have a means of robbing the common liquid <term>quicksilver</term> of its vivacity, or rendering it firm and solid, as is also set forth in my book.

He provides a final instruction on the use of acids and spirits to fix volatile substances into a solid, perfect Tincture.</summary>

<page-num>357</page-num>
<header>THE GOLDEN TRIPOD.</header>

->*Postscript.*<-

When you have thus obtained the material, the <term>regimen of the fire</term> <note>The specific method and schedule for managing the heat during the chemical process.</note> is the only thing on which you need bestow much attention. This is the sum and the goal of our search. For our fire is a common fire, and our furnace a common furnace. And though some of my predecessors have left it in writing, that our fire is not common fire, I may tell you that it was only one of their devices for hiding the mysteries of our Art. For the material is common, and its treatment consists chiefly in the proper adjustment of the heat to which it is exposed.

The fire of a spirit lamp is useless for our purpose. Nor is there any profit in "<term>horse-dung</term>," <note>Alchemists often used the natural, steady heat produced by decomposing manure to warm their vessels for long periods, a process called "digestion."</note> nor in the other kinds of heat in the providing of which so much expense is incurred.

Neither do we want many kinds of furnaces. Only our <term>threefold furnace</term> <note>A specialized stove designed to allow the alchemist to regulate heat across different stages of the work.</note> affords facilities for properly regulating the heat of the fire. Therefore do not let any <term>babbling sophist</term> <note>A term of contempt for those who use clever but false arguments to sell expensive or overly complicated equipment.</note> induce you to set up a great variety of expensive furnaces. Our furnace is cheap, our fire is cheap, and our material is cheap—and he who has the material will also find a furnace in which to prepare it, just as he who has flour will not be at a loss for an oven in which it may be baked. It is unnecessary to write a special book concerning this part of the subject. You cannot go wrong, so long as you observe the proper degree of heat, which holds a middle place between hot and cold. If you discover this, you are in possession of the secret, and can practise the Art, for which the CREATOR of all nature be praised world without end. AMEN.

The manuscript is bound in a **pebbled, gold-colored leather**. The front surface is decorated with a simple, rectangular **blind-stamped border** with rounded corners.

<note>A "blind stamp" is a decorative mark pressed into the leather using a heated tool or die without the application of gold leaf or ink. This creates a subtle, recessed texture that provides a classic, understated aesthetic common in various periods of bookbinding.</note>

<note>The "pebbled" texture—small, raised bumps on the surface of the leather—was often used to provide a better grip and to make the binding more resistant to showing scratches or wear from frequent use by students of alchemy.</note>
